GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 1

Water, Acids, Bases and Buffers

Where the body’s water is, how water and salts move between compartments, what pH means, and how buffers, lungs and kidneys keep blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 1: Water, pH & Buffers

In 60 seconds

  • About two-thirds of body water is inside cells (ICF) and one-third outside (ECF).
  • Water is a dipole (δ– oxygen, δ+ hydrogens), so it forms hydrogen bonds and dissolves polar molecules and salts.
  • ECF is rich in Na⁺ and Cl⁻; ICF is rich in K⁺ and phosphate. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase keeps it that way.
  • Water moves from low osmolality to high osmolality.
  • pH = –log₁₀[H⁺]. Normal blood pH is 7.4 (range 7.35–7.45).
  • The main blood buffer is bicarbonate (pKa 6.1); lungs remove CO₂ fast, kidneys handle H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ slowly.
  • Four disorders: respiratory and metabolic acidosis, respiratory and metabolic alkalosis. Acidosis pushes K⁺ out of cells (hyperkalemia).

Learning objectives

From the syllabus for Week 1 (Marks’ Basic Medical Biochemistry, 6th ed., Chapter 4, pages 83–98). By the end you can:

  • describe the body’s fluid compartments and the electrolytes in each;
  • explain why water is a good solvent and how it helps control body temperature;
  • explain osmolality, osmotic pressure and why water moves between compartments;
  • define pH, acids, bases, pKa and buffers, and use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation;
  • explain the bicarbonate, hemoglobin, respiratory and renal buffering systems;
  • recognise the four acid–base disturbances, their causes, compensation and effect on potassium.

Body water compartments

Biochemistry starts with a simple question: what is the normal body made of? The biggest answer is water. Almost two-thirds of an adult’s body weight is water.

That water sits in separate spaces called compartments, divided by cell membranes and capillary walls.

Where total body water is
CompartmentShare of total body waterWhat it includes
Intracellular fluid (ICF)About ⅔Water inside all cells
Extracellular fluid (ECF)About ⅓Plasma (inside vessels) and interstitial fluid (between cells)
Transcellular waterA small part of ECFFluid in special epithelium-lined cavities: cerebrospinal fluid (brain and spinal cord), ocular fluid (eyes), synovial fluid (joints)

Water as the solvent of life

Structure: a dipole

A water molecule (H₂O) is one oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms by covalent bonds. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself.

  • The oxygen carries a partial negative charge (δ–).
  • Each hydrogen carries a partial positive charge (δ+).
  • So the molecule has a negative end and a positive end: an electrical dipole.

Two kinds of bond

BondWhereStrength
Covalent O–H bondWithin one water molecule (intramolecular)Strong
Hydrogen bondBetween two water molecules (intermolecular): the δ+ H of one molecule is attracted to the δ– O of anotherWeak, but very many of them

Why water dissolves so much

Because water is dipolar, it forms hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions with other charged or polar substances. That is why polar organic molecules (such as glucose) and inorganic salts (such as NaCl) dissolve readily in water. Nonpolar molecules (fats) cannot do this and stay apart from water.

Water and temperature control

The syllabus also lists “water and thermal regulation”. From the textbook chapter: the many hydrogen bonds mean water absorbs a lot of heat before its temperature rises (high heat capacity), and it takes a lot of heat to evaporate it. So body water buffers temperature changes, and evaporating sweat carries heat away from the skin.

Electrolytes and ion transport

Electrolytes is the general name for bicarbonate and the inorganic anions and cations dissolved in body fluids. Both ECF and ICF contain them, but they are unevenly distributed.

CompartmentMain cationMain anion
ECF (plasma and interstitial fluid)Na⁺Cl⁻
ICF (inside cells)K⁺Phosphates such as HPO₄²⁻

How the difference is kept

  • Water diffuses freely across most cell membranes.
  • Ions and neutral molecules cannot move freely; their movement is restricted to channels and transporters.
  • The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the sodium pump) uses ATP to keep Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside.
In the clinic: digoxin

Digoxin, a heart drug, inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Na⁺ builds up inside heart muscle cells. With less Na⁺ gradient, the cell pushes out less calcium, so more Ca²⁺ stays inside and the heart contracts more strongly. This stronger contraction is the drug’s positive inotropic effect.

The anion gap

Blood is electrically neutral: total positive charge equals total negative charge. But a routine blood test measures only some ions. The anion gap (AG) is the difference between the measured cations and the measured anions. It stands for the anions we don’t measure (proteins such as albumin, phosphate, sulfate, organic acids).

Plasma ions in the lecture
IonTypical plasma concentration
All cations togetherAbout 150 mmol/L
Sodium (Na⁺)About 140 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)About 4 mmol/L
Chloride (Cl⁻)About 100 mmol/L
Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)About 25 mmol/L

The lecture gives two versions of the formula:

  • With potassium: AG = (Na⁺ + K⁺) – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). With the numbers above: (140 + 4) – (100 + 25) = 19 mmol/L.
  • Without potassium (used in the metabolic acidosis slide): AG = Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Normal range 8–12 mEq/L.

For a monovalent ion such as Na⁺ or Cl⁻, 1 mmol/L = 1 mEq/L, so the units are interchangeable here.

Osmolality and water movement

  • Osmolality is the total concentration of all dissolved particles (ions, organic metabolites such as glucose and urea, and proteins) in a fluid. Unit: milliosmoles per kilogram of water (mOsm/kg).
  • Water distributes between compartments according to osmolality.
  • Water moves from the side with lower osmolality (fewer solutes) to the side with higher osmolality (more solutes), until both sides are equal.
  • Osmotic pressure is the minimum pressure needed to stop pure solvent flowing into a solution through a semipermeable membrane. The more solute, the higher the osmotic pressure.

When ECF osmolality changes

ECF osmolalityWater movesEffect on cells
Rises (e.g. high plasma Na⁺)Out of cells into ECFCells shrink: cellular dehydration
Falls (e.g. low plasma Na⁺)From ECF into cellsCells swell: cell edema
Memory hook

“Water follows solute.” Water always goes towards the side that has more dissolved particles.

Regulating water and salt: RAAS

The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) controls salt and water balance. When blood pressure or blood volume falls, the kidney releases renin; this leads to angiotensin II, which makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the kidney keep Na⁺ (and with it water) and lose K⁺ and H⁺.

TypeCauseHow common
Primary hyperaldosteronismAbnormal activity of the adrenal gland itself, e.g. a single adrenal tumour (adenoma) = Conn’s syndromeRare
Secondary hyperaldosteronismToo much renin drives the adrenal to make aldosteroneMore common

pH, acids and bases

What pH means

pH = –log₁₀[H⁺], with [H⁺] in moles per litre. pH is usually a positive number between 0 and 14. Because of the minus sign, more H⁺ means a lower pH (more acidic). Because it is a log scale, one pH unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺].

Body fluids differ in pH

Blood pH is 7.4 and is kept within a narrow range of 7.35–7.45. Outside this range, medical problems follow: below 7.35 is acidemia, above 7.45 is alkalemia. Other body fluids have their own pH (the slide shows a chart): for example, stomach juice is strongly acidic and pancreatic juice is alkaline.

Acids and bases

TermMeaningExamples from the slides
AcidReleases H⁺ when dissolved in waterHydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), acetic acid (CH₃COOH)
Strong acidCompletely dissociates in water, releasing all its H⁺; high KaHCl, H₂SO₄
Weak acidOnly partly dissociates; only a small fraction of molecules release H⁺; low KaAcetic acid, carbonic acid
BaseReleases OH⁻ (or takes up H⁺) in waterSodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH), ammonia (NH₃)

A weak acid HA (the conjugate acid) dissociates into H⁺ and A⁻ (the conjugate base): HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻. Ka is the dissociation constant: the bigger Ka, the stronger the acid.

Buffers

A buffer is a solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid). It keeps the pH change small when a little strong acid or strong base is added.

  • Add acid → the buffer’s base part takes up the extra H⁺.
  • Add base → the buffer’s acid part releases H⁺, which neutralises the OH⁻.

The bicarbonate buffer system

The most important buffer in blood and ECF:

CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

SituationWhat happens
pH too low (too much H⁺)H⁺ binds HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃ (which can leave as CO₂ through the lungs)
pH too high (too little H⁺)H₂CO₃ dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, releasing H⁺

The first step, CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃, is sped up by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, found especially in red blood cells and kidney tubule cells.

The hemoglobin buffer in red blood cells

  1. In the tissues, cells produce CO₂.
  2. CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
  3. Hemoglobin binds the H⁺ (forming HHb), so the blood does not become too acidic.
  4. At the same time, hemoglobin releases O₂ to the tissues.

So hemoglobin has two jobs at once: it carries oxygen and it buffers H⁺. In the lungs the process reverses: Hb takes up O₂, releases H⁺, and the H⁺ combines with HCO₃⁻ to make CO₂, which is breathed out.

Intracellular pH

Inside cells, the main buffers are phosphate (HPO₄²⁻/H₂PO₄⁻) and proteins, because these are what cells contain most. Intracellular pH is kept slightly lower than blood pH.

Henderson–Hasselbalch and pKa

The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation links pH to the ratio of base to acid in a buffer:

pH = pKa + log ( [A⁻] / [HA] )

  • [A⁻] = concentration of the conjugate base.
  • [HA] = concentration of the weak acid.
  • pKa = –log Ka. It measures how strong an acid is: lower pKa = stronger acid.
  • pKa is the pH at which the acid is exactly half dissociated: 50% HA and 50% A⁻. Then [A⁻]/[HA] = 1, log 1 = 0, so pH = pKa.

For blood

For the bicarbonate buffer, pKa = 6.1, and the acid part is represented by dissolved CO₂ (0.03 × PCO₂ in mmHg). This lets you calculate pH from HCO₃⁻ and PCO₂:

pH = 6.1 + log ( [HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PCO₂) )

Worked example with normal values (HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L, PCO₂ 40 mmHg): 0.03 × 40 = 1.2; 24 / 1.2 = 20; log 20 ≈ 1.3; pH = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4.

Key idea

Blood pH depends on the ratio of HCO₃⁻ (controlled by the kidneys) to CO₂ (controlled by the lungs). Normal ratio ≈ 20 : 1. Anything that changes this ratio changes pH.

Lungs and kidneys

Respiratory buffering (the slide is a diagram)

  • CO₂ is an acid-forming gas: more CO₂ means more H₂CO₃, more H⁺, lower pH.
  • Breathing faster and deeper (hyperventilation) blows off CO₂ → pH rises.
  • Breathing slower (hypoventilation) keeps CO₂ → pH falls.
  • The respiratory centre responds within minutes.

Renal mechanisms

The kidneys have two main tools: they reabsorb HCO₃⁻ from the urine back into the blood, and they secrete H⁺ into the urine. They act more slowly (hours to days) but can truly remove acid from the body.

StateKidney response
AcidosisSecrete more H⁺ into urine (carried as ammonium NH₄⁺ and phosphate), reabsorb and make more HCO₃⁻ → urine becomes more acidic
AlkalosisSecrete less H⁺, reabsorb less HCO₃⁻ and excrete it → urine becomes more alkaline

Acid–base disorders

There are four primary disorders. The name tells you two things: the direction of pH (acidosis or alkalosis), and what changed first (respiratory = PCO₂, metabolic = HCO₃⁻). The body then compensates with the other system to bring the ratio back towards 20 : 1.

Most of these slides are diagrams; the details below follow the textbook chapter the syllabus names.

The four disorders at a glance
DisorderpHPrimary changeCompensationTypical causes
Respiratory acidosis↓↑ PCO₂ (CO₂ is not eliminated)Kidneys keep more HCO₃⁻ (↑ HCO₃⁻), over daysHypoventilation: chronic lung disease (COPD), airway obstruction, drugs that depress breathing (opioids, sedatives), weak breathing muscles
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓ PCO₂Kidneys excrete HCO₃⁻ (↓ HCO₃⁻)Hyperventilation: anxiety or panic, high altitude, fever, early aspirin (salicylate) overdose
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ HCO₃⁻Hyperventilation lowers PCO₂ (fast)Ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure, poisons, diarrhea
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ HCO₃⁻Hypoventilation raises PCO₂Vomiting (loss of stomach HCl), diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, too much antacid or bicarbonate

Metabolic acidosis in detail

Metabolic acidosis is a primary fall in plasma bicarbonate, which lowers extracellular pH. Its causes fall into three groups:

  1. More acid produced: e.g. ketone bodies in diabetic ketoacidosis, lactate in shock.
  2. Less acid eliminated: e.g. kidney failure.
  3. Bicarbonate lost: e.g. severe diarrhea.

The anion gap splits metabolic acidosis into two kinds:

TypeWhyExamples
High anion gap (above 8–12 mEq/L)Unmeasured organic acid anions are added; HCO₃⁻ falls with no rise in Cl⁻Lactate, ketones, oxalic acid, formic acid, glycolic acid (the last three from poisons such as ethylene glycol or methanol)
Normal anion gap (hyperchloremic)HCO₃⁻ is lost and replaced by Cl⁻, so the gap stays normalDiarrhea, some kidney tubule disorders

Compensation: hyperventilation removes more CO₂ and lowers PCO₂, which pulls pH back up.

In the clinic

A patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes breathes deeply and fast. Ketone bodies (acids) have used up bicarbonate (high anion gap metabolic acidosis), and the deep breathing is the lungs’ compensation, blowing off CO₂.

In the clinic

Repeated vomiting removes stomach HCl. The body loses H⁺ and Cl⁻ and is left with extra HCO₃⁻: metabolic alkalosis.

Potassium shifts in pH disorders

K⁺ is mainly inside cells. When blood pH changes, H⁺ and K⁺ swap places across the cell membrane to keep the charges balanced (electroneutrality). The shift is temporary.

StateH⁺ movesK⁺ movesResult
Acidosis (↑ H⁺ in blood)Into cellsOut of cellsHyperkalemia
Alkalosis (↓ H⁺ in blood)Out of cellsInto cellsHypokalemia
Memory hook

K⁺ and H⁺ move in opposite directions, so blood K⁺ follows blood H⁺: acidosis → high K⁺, alkalosis → low K⁺.

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
Covalent vs hydrogen bond in waterCovalent: inside one molecule (O–H). Hydrogen: between molecules.
ECF vs ICF ionsECF: Na⁺ and Cl⁻. ICF: K⁺ and phosphate.
Strong vs weak acidStrong: dissociates completely, high Ka, low pKa. Weak: partly, low Ka, high pKa.
Conjugate acid vs conjugate baseHA is the conjugate acid; A⁻ is its conjugate base.
Respiratory vs metabolic disorderRespiratory starts with PCO₂; metabolic starts with HCO₃⁻.
Primary vs secondary hyperaldosteronismPrimary: the adrenal is the problem (Conn’s adenoma), rare. Secondary: too much renin, more common.
Cell dehydration vs cell edemaDehydration when ECF osmolality rises; edema when it falls.
High vs normal anion gap acidosisHigh: extra organic anions, Cl⁻ normal. Normal: HCO₃⁻ replaced by Cl⁻.

Watch out

Watch out: bonds in water

Slide 5 says “Covalent bonds intermolecular”. That is the wrong way round. Covalent bonds are intramolecular (the O–H bonds inside one molecule). Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular (between molecules). Use this in the exam.

Watch out: “aceto acetic acid”

Slide 15 lists “Aceto acetic acid (CH₃COOH)”. CH₃COOH is acetic acid, a weak acid. Acetoacetic acid is a different molecule (CH₃COCH₂COOH), one of the ketone bodies.

Watch out: two anion gap formulas

Slide 9 includes K⁺ in the formula; slide 26 uses Na⁺ only and gives the normal range 8–12 mEq/L. The 8–12 range belongs to the formula without K⁺. If a question gives K⁺ and asks for the gap “with potassium”, add it; otherwise use Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻).

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • “Water moves towards lower osmolality” is false: it moves towards higher osmolality.
  • A higher [H⁺] means a lower pH, not higher.
  • At pH = pKa the acid is half dissociated, not fully.
  • Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; it does not stimulate it.
  • In metabolic acidosis the lungs compensate by hyperventilating, not hypoventilating.
  • Acidosis causes hyperkalemia, alkalosis hypokalemia.
  • Conn’s syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism.

Check yourself

  1. About what fraction of total body water is in the intracellular fluid?

    1. One-tenth
    2. One-third
    3. Two-thirds
    4. Nine-tenths
    Show answer

    C. About two-thirds is ICF and one-third ECF.

  2. Which pair are the major electrolytes inside cells?

    1. Na⁺ and Cl⁻
    2. K⁺ and phosphate
    3. Ca²⁺ and HCO₃⁻
    4. Na⁺ and HCO₃⁻
    Show answer

    B. K⁺ and phosphates (e.g. HPO₄²⁻) dominate the ICF; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ dominate the ECF.

  3. Digoxin produces a positive inotropic effect because it:

    1. Activates the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
    2. Blocks K⁺ channels
    3. Inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so less Ca²⁺ is pushed out of the cell
    4. Increases Ca²⁺ excretion by the kidney
    Show answer

    C. Intracellular Na⁺ rises, Ca²⁺ extrusion falls, and more Ca²⁺ strengthens contraction.

  4. If ECF osmolality rises, what happens to cells?

    1. Water enters them and they swell
    2. Water leaves them and they shrink
    3. Nothing, because water cannot cross membranes
    4. They take up Na⁺ to balance it
    Show answer

    B. Water moves towards higher osmolality, out of the cells: cellular dehydration.

  5. Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 104 and HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L. What is the anion gap, and is it normal?

    1. 12, normal
    2. 20, high
    3. 36, high
    4. 4, low
    Show answer

    A. 140 – (104 + 24) = 12 mEq/L, within 8–12.

  6. An acid has a pKa of 6.1. At pH 6.1, the acid is:

    1. Fully dissociated
    2. Not dissociated at all
    3. 50% dissociated
    4. 90% dissociated
    Show answer

    C. pKa is the pH at which an acid is half dissociated: 50% HA, 50% A⁻.

  7. What does the bicarbonate buffer do when blood pH falls?

    1. H₂CO₃ releases more H⁺
    2. HCO₃⁻ binds H⁺ to form H₂CO₃
    3. Hemoglobin releases H⁺
    4. The kidneys excrete HCO₃⁻
    Show answer

    B. At low pH, HCO₃⁻ takes up the extra H⁺; the H₂CO₃ formed can leave as CO₂.

  8. In the tissues, hemoglobin acts as a buffer by:

    1. Binding H⁺ while releasing O₂
    2. Releasing H⁺ while binding O₂
    3. Binding Cl⁻
    4. Making HCO₃⁻ directly
    Show answer

    A. Hb binds H⁺ (HHb) produced from CO₂ and at the same time gives O₂ to the tissues.

  9. Which finding fits metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation?

    1. ↓ HCO₃⁻ and ↓ PCO₂
    2. ↑ HCO₃⁻ and ↑ PCO₂
    3. ↑ PCO₂ and ↑ HCO₃⁻
    4. ↓ PCO₂ and normal HCO₃⁻
    Show answer

    A. HCO₃⁻ falls first; hyperventilation then lowers PCO₂.

  10. Which is a cause of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis?

    1. Severe diarrhea
    2. Repeated vomiting
    3. Diabetic ketoacidosis
    4. Hyperventilation from anxiety
    Show answer

    C. Ketone body anions are unmeasured anions. Diarrhea gives a normal-gap acidosis; vomiting gives alkalosis; anxiety gives respiratory alkalosis.

  11. A patient is in acidosis. Which change in plasma potassium do you expect?

    1. Hypokalemia, as K⁺ enters cells
    2. Hyperkalemia, as K⁺ leaves cells
    3. No change
    4. Hypokalemia, as K⁺ is lost in sweat
    Show answer

    B. H⁺ moves into cells and K⁺ moves out to keep electroneutrality.

  12. Conn’s syndrome is:

    1. Secondary hyperaldosteronism from high renin
    2. Primary hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma
    3. A lack of aldosterone
    4. A kidney tumour making renin
    Show answer

    B. A single adrenal adenoma causes primary hyperaldosteronism, which is rare.

Key terms

ICF / ECF
Intracellular fluid (inside cells) / extracellular fluid (plasma and interstitial fluid).
Transcellular water
Fluid in epithelium-lined cavities: CSF, eye fluid, synovial fluid.
Dipole
A molecule with a partly negative end and a partly positive end, like water.
Hydrogen bond
A weak attraction between a δ+ hydrogen and a δ– atom such as oxygen on another molecule.
Electrolytes
Bicarbonate and the inorganic anions and cations of body fluids.
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Membrane pump using ATP to keep Na⁺ outside and K⁺ inside cells.
Anion gap
Measured cations minus measured anions; reflects unmeasured anions.
Osmolality
Total concentration of dissolved particles, in mOsm per kg of water.
Osmotic pressure
The minimum pressure that stops pure solvent flowing into a solution across a semipermeable membrane.
Aldosterone
Adrenal hormone that makes the kidney keep Na⁺ and lose K⁺ and H⁺.
pH
The negative log₁₀ of the hydrogen ion concentration in mol/L.
Ka / pKa
Acid dissociation constant / its negative log; pKa is the pH at which an acid is half dissociated.
Conjugate base
What is left of an acid after it gives up H⁺ (A⁻ from HA).
Buffer
A weak acid plus its conjugate base that keeps pH nearly steady when acid or base is added.
Carbonic anhydrase
Enzyme that speeds up CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃.
Acidosis / alkalosis
A process that lowers / raises blood pH.
Compensation
The other system (lungs or kidneys) changing to bring pH back towards normal.
Hyperkalemia / hypokalemia
High / low plasma potassium.

gct/biochemistry/wk02-major-compounds:
GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 2

Structures of the Major Compounds of the Body

The building blocks of every later lecture: carbon skeletons and functional groups, then carbohydrates, lipids and the nitrogen-containing compounds.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 2: Major Biological Compounds

In 60 seconds

  • Body molecules are built mainly from C, H, O, N, S and P; carbon forms 4 covalent bonds.
  • Oxidation = loss of electrons (lose H or gain O); reduction = gain of electrons (gain H or lose O).
  • Aldehyde sugar = aldose; ketone sugar = ketose. Natural glucose is D-glucose.
  • Glucose and galactose are epimers at C4; glucose and mannose are epimers at C2.
  • Lactose = galactose β(1→4) glucose. Glycogen = α1→4 chains with α1→6 branches, built on glycogenin.
  • Oleic acid is 18:1, Δ9 and an ω9 fatty acid. Phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) is the main lung surfactant lipid.
  • Sphingomyelin is the only significant sphingophospholipid; cholesterol is the precursor of all steroid hormones and of bile salts.

Learning objectives

Marks’ Basic Medical Biochemistry, 6th ed., Chapter 5, pages 110–135. By the end you can:

  • name the main functional groups and say whether a group is oxidised or reduced;

Carbon and functional groups

The organic molecules of the body are made mostly of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus, joined by covalent bonds.

  • Carbon is the key element: it forms four covalent bonds, through single or double bonds, building carbon backbones of any size.
  • Aliphatic: carbon chains (straight or branched, single or double bonds) that contain no ring.
  • Rings are common too. The most common is the six-membered benzene ring, also called a phenyl group when attached to a molecule.

Functional groups

A molecule is defined by its carbon skeleton and its functional groups: groups where carbon is bonded to oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur or phosphate. Their names often appear in the compound’s name.

GroupStructureName ending / example
Hydroxyl (alcohol)–OH-ol: ethanol
KetoneC=O inside a chain-one: acetone
Aldehyde–CHO at the end of a chain-al: glyceraldehyde
Carboxyl (carboxylic acid)–COOH (–COO⁻ when charged)-ic acid / -ate: pyruvate
Amino–NH₂ (–NH₃⁺ when charged)-amine
Sulfhydryl (thiol)–SHcysteine
Phosphate–PO₄²⁻ (ester)glucose 6-phosphate

Groups that carry a charge at body pH (carboxylate –COO⁻, amino –NH₃⁺, phosphate, sulfate) make a molecule more water-soluble.

Oxidised and reduced groups

Carbon–carbon and carbon–oxygen groups are called oxidised or reduced according to the number of electrons around the carbon.

OxidationReduction
ElectronsLoss of electronsGain of electrons
Seen asLoss of H atoms (with one or two electrons), or gain of an O atom or OH groupGain of H atoms, or loss of an O atom

Order from most reduced to most oxidised carbon: alkane (–CH₃) → alcohol (–CH₂OH) → aldehyde (–CHO) → carboxylic acid (–COOH) → CO₂. This is why fats (very reduced) give more energy than sugars when they are oxidised.

Mnemonic: OIL RIG

Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

Carbohydrates: types

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones (or their derivatives), and their main job is to supply energy.

Monosaccharides and isomers

Aldoses and ketoses

A simple monosaccharide is a chain of three or more carbons. One carbon forms a carbonyl group (C=O).

  • Carbonyl is an aldehyde (at the end of the chain) → aldose (e.g. glucose).
  • Carbonyl is a ketone (inside the chain) → ketose (e.g. fructose).
Carbons34567
NameTrioseTetrosePentoseHexoseHeptose

Chiral carbons, D and L sugars

  • A carbon attached to four different groups is an asymmetric (chiral) centre.
  • Its groups can be arranged in two ways that are mirror images and cannot be superimposed. Such mirror-image pairs are enantiomers, named D and L.
  • D and L are still used in medicine for sugars and amino acids.
  • Natural glucose is D-glucose. L-glucose is made synthetically in small amounts and is less biologically active.

Epimers

Epimers are stereoisomers that differ at only one of their asymmetric carbons.

PairDiffer atNote
D-glucose and D-galactoseCarbon 4Interconverted in human cells by epimerases
D-glucose and D-mannoseCarbon 2
Enantiomer or epimer?

Enantiomers are mirror images: opposite at every chiral centre. Epimers differ at one chiral centre only.

Substituted sugars and glycosidic bonds

Substituted sugars

Sugars often carry extra groups: phosphate (PO₄³⁻), amino (NH₂), sulfate (SO₄²⁻) or N-acetyl (NHCOCH₃). Most free monosaccharides inside cells are phosphorylated at their terminal carbon (for example glucose 6-phosphate). The charged phosphate stops the sugar leaving the cell, trapping it inside.

Glycosidic bonds

A glycosidic bond is a covalent bond that joins a sugar, through its anomeric carbon (the carbonyl carbon, C1 of glucose), to another molecule. It builds disaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and links sugars to alcohols and amines (forming glycosides and nucleosides).

BondAnomeric carbon bonds toFound in
O-glycosidicThe oxygen of a hydroxyl (alcohol) groupDisaccharides, glycogen, O-linked glycoproteins
N-glycosidicThe nitrogen of an amineNucleosides (sugar to base), N-linked glycoproteins

Disaccharides, oligo- and polysaccharides

Disaccharides

Two monosaccharides joined by an O-glycosidic bond.

DisaccharideMade ofNotes
Lactose (milk sugar)Galactose + glucoseβ(1→4) bond: the β-OH of galactose’s anomeric carbon to the OH on carbon 4 of glucose
Sucrose (table sugar)Glucose + fructoseListed as a disaccharide on the slides
MaltoseGlucose + glucoseComes from starch digestion
In the clinic: lactase deficiency

Lactase is a brush-border enzyme of the small intestine that splits lactose into absorbable monosaccharides. Without enough lactase, lactose is almost not digested or absorbed, causing lactose intolerance.

  • Primary: lactase declines with age after childhood (no lactase-persistence allele). Common in people of Asian, African or Native American descent.
  • Secondary: the brush border is damaged, e.g. by gastroenteritis (rotavirus) or autoimmune disease.
  • Congenital: rare, from a defective gene.

Oligosaccharides

From 3 to roughly 10 (one slide says 12) monosaccharides. They are often attached to proteins by N- or O-glycosidic bonds, forming glycoproteins.

Polysaccharides

Tens to thousands of monosaccharides in linear or branched chains. Starch (plants) and glycogen (animals) contain thousands of glucose units.

  • Glycogen: chains of glucose linked α1→4, with branch points made by α1→6 bonds.
  • At the centre of every glycogen molecule is glycogenin, the protein primer on which glycogen synthesis starts.

Fatty acids

A fatty acid is usually a straight aliphatic chain with a methyl group at one end (the ω-carbon) and a carboxyl group at the other.

  • Most human fatty acids have an even number of carbons, usually 16–20.
  • Saturated: only single bonds. Most common: palmitic acid (C16) and stearic acid (C18).
  • Unsaturated: one or more double bonds. Monounsaturated = one; polyunsaturated = two or more.

How to read the shorthand

Oleic acid is 18:1, Δ9:

  • 18 = number of carbons;
  • 1 = number of double bonds;
  • Δ9 = the double bond is between carbons 9 and 10, counting from the carboxyl carbon (C1).

The ω (omega) number counts from the other end, the methyl (ω) carbon, to the nearest double bond. Oleic acid is an ω9 fatty acid; linolenic acid is an ω3 fatty acid.

Δ versus ω

Δ counts from the carboxyl end. ω counts from the methyl end. For oleic acid (18 carbons, double bond at 9–10), both happen to give 9.

Acylglycerols and phosphoacylglycerols

Acylglycerols

An acylglycerol is glycerol with one or more fatty acids (acyl groups) attached by ester bonds.

  • Mono-, di- and triacylglycerols carry one, two and three fatty acids.
  • Triacylglycerols (fats) rarely have the same fatty acid at all three positions, so they are called mixed triacylglycerols.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids are most often on carbon 2.

Phosphoacylglycerols (glycerophospholipids)

Fatty acids on carbons 1 and 2 of glycerol, and a phosphate (alone or with a substituent) on carbon 3.

  • Phosphatidylcholine (also called lecithin) is one of the major membrane phosphoacylglycerols.
  • It is the main component of pulmonary surfactant.
In the clinic: surfactant

Surfactant lines the alveoli (air sacs) and reduces surface tension. Without it the alveoli would collapse during exhalation. Premature babies who have not yet made enough surfactant develop breathing difficulty for this reason.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Metabolism | The Metabolic Map: Lipids Watch from 4:12 to 7:53: glycerol, fatty acids and how triacylglycerols are built.

Sphingolipids and Niemann–Pick

Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine, not glycerol.

  1. A long-chain fatty acid is attached to the amino group of sphingosine by an amide bond → ceramide.
  2. The alcohol group at carbon 1 of sphingosine is esterified to phosphorylcholine → sphingomyelin.
  • Sphingomyelin is the only significant sphingophospholipid in humans.
  • It is an important part of the myelin sheath of nerve fibres.
In the clinic: Niemann–Pick disease (syllabus correlation)

An inherited deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme sphingomyelinase, which breaks down sphingomyelin. Sphingomyelin builds up in lysosomes, especially of the liver, spleen and brain, causing enlarged liver and spleen and, in the severe form, nerve damage in infancy.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Tay-Sachs, Fabry, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick Disease Watch from 29:01 to 31:25: Niemann–Pick disease.

Steroids

  • Steroids have a four-ring structure called the steroid nucleus.
  • Cholesterol is the precursor of all steroid hormones, made by changing the rings or the C20 side chain.
  • Cholesterol itself is poorly soluble in water, but it is converted into amphipathic, water-soluble bile salts such as cholic acid.
  • Bile salts coat fat droplets in the intestine, forming micelles, which keep the fat emulsified in the watery gut contents so it can be digested.

Amino acids and nitrogen rings

Amino acids

  • Contain an amino group and a carboxylic acid group.
  • In proteins they are always L-α-amino acids.
  • D-amino acids are not normally put into proteins, but bacteria use them, e.g. to build cross-links in their cell walls.

Nitrogen-containing rings

The body’s nitrogen rings are purines, pyrimidines and pyridines (e.g. niacin and pyridoxine, vitamin B6). The ending “-ine” shows nitrogen (amine) in the ring.

StructureMade ofExample
BasePurine or pyrimidine ringAdenine
NucleosideBase + pentose sugar (N-glycosidic bond)Adenosine
Nucleoside monophosphateNucleoside + 1 phosphate on the 5′ carbon of the pentoseAMP
Nucleoside di- / triphosphateA second / third phosphate addedADP / ATP

Adding one or more phosphates to a nucleoside makes a nucleotide.

Watch out

Watch out: how many sugars in an oligosaccharide?

Slide 6 says “3 to roughly 12”; slide 14 says “3 to roughly 10”. Both are approximate. If an option says “3 to about 10”, that matches the textbook slide on oligosaccharides.

Watch out: sucrose

Sucrose is a glucose + fructose disaccharide (α1→β2 bond). The slides list it but do not give its sugars; this is from the textbook.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and of H; gaining O is also oxidation.
  • Glucose/galactose differ at C4, not C2 (that is mannose).
  • Lactose has a β(1→4) bond; glycogen chains are α1→4.
  • Proteins use L-amino acids, while natural sugars are D.
  • Phosphorylating a sugar traps it in the cell; it does not help it leave.
  • The “ω” carbon is the methyl end, not the carboxyl end.

Check yourself

  1. A carbon chain with no ring is described as:

    1. Aromatic
    2. Aliphatic
    3. Phenyl
    4. Chiral

  2. Which change is an oxidation?

    2. Gain of electrons
    3. Gain of an oxygen atom

    2. Aldohexose
    3. Ketopentose
    4. Aldopentose

  4. D-glucose and D-galactose are:

    1. Enantiomers
    2. Epimers at carbon 2
    3. Epimers at carbon 4
    4. Identical

    C. They differ only at C4 and are interconverted by epimerases.

  5. Why are most free sugars inside cells phosphorylated?

    1. To make them sweeter
    2. To stop them being transported out of the cell
    3. To make them nonpolar
    4. To link them to proteins

    B. Phosphorylation at the terminal carbon traps the sugar in the cell.

  6. The bond between a sugar and a base in a nucleoside is:

    1. O-glycosidic
    2. N-glycosidic
    3. Peptide
    4. Ester

    1. Caused by rotavirus
    2. An age-dependent decline after childhood
    3. Always present at birth
    4. Caused by autoimmune disease

    2. β1→4 bonds

Key terms

Functional group
A group of atoms (e.g. –OH, –COOH, –NH₂) that gives a molecule its chemical behaviour.
Aliphatic
A carbon chain without a ring.
Phenyl group
A benzene ring attached to a molecule.
Aldose / ketose
Sugar with an aldehyde / a ketone group.
Chiral carbon
A carbon with four different groups attached.
Enantiomers
Non-superimposable mirror-image isomers (D and L).
Epimers
Stereoisomers differing at one chiral carbon.
Epimerase
Enzyme that converts one epimer into another.
Anomeric carbon
The carbonyl carbon of a sugar, which forms glycosidic bonds.
Glycosidic bond
Covalent bond from a sugar’s anomeric carbon to an O (O-glycosidic) or N (N-glycosidic).
Glycoprotein
Protein with oligosaccharide chains attached.
Glycogenin
Protein primer at the centre of glycogen.
Saturated fatty acid
Fatty acid with only single C–C bonds.
ω-carbon
The methyl-end carbon of a fatty acid.
Triacylglycerol
Glycerol with three fatty acids in ester bonds (a fat).
Lecithin
Phosphatidylcholine; main surfactant lipid.
Ceramide
Sphingosine with a fatty acid on its amino group.
Sphingomyelin
Ceramide + phosphorylcholine; in the myelin sheath.
Micelle
A droplet of fat coated by amphipathic molecules such as bile salts.
Nucleoside / nucleotide
Base + sugar / base + sugar + phosphate.

GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 3

Amino Acids in Proteins

The 20 (plus one) building blocks of proteins: their structure, how they are grouped, what special jobs some of them do, how proteins are modified after they are made, and how protein sequences vary.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 3: Amino Acids

In 60 seconds

  • Every amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain (R); proteins use only L-amino acids.
  • Glycine is the only achiral amino acid. Proline is an imino acid.
  • Methionine starts every protein (AUG) and makes SAM; cysteine forms disulfide bridges; two cysteines = cystine.
  • Arg → urea and nitric oxide; His → histamine; Glu → GABA (by GAD with vitamin B6).
  • Cystinuria: poorly soluble cystine forms hexagonal crystals and kidney stones.
  • Post-translational changes: glycosylation (N on Asn, O on Ser/Thr), fatty acylation, phosphorylation (Ser/Thr/Tyr), acetylation (Lys), ADP-ribosylation (cholera toxin).
  • HbF (α₂γ₂) binds O₂ more tightly than HbA (α₂β₂). Creatine kinase has tissue-specific isozymes.

Learning objectives

Marks’ Basic Medical Biochemistry, 6th ed., Chapter 6, pages 148–170. By the end you can:

  • draw the general structure of an amino acid and explain L and D forms;
  • classify amino acids by side chain, polarity, nutrition and metabolic fate;
  • explain modified amino acids and post-translational modifications;
  • describe species, developmental and tissue variations in primary structure;
  • explain the clinical correlation cystinuria (and cholera toxin).

General structure and stereochemistry

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Each contains:

  • an amine group (–NH₂),
  • a carboxyl group (–COOH),
  • a side chain (the R group), which is different for each amino acid,

all attached to the same central carbon, the α-carbon, which also carries a hydrogen. The main elements are carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen. At body pH the groups are charged: –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻.

L and D forms

Because the α-carbon has four different groups, each amino acid (except glycine) exists as two non-superimposable mirror images, called enantiomers (L and D). Only L-enantiomers are found in proteins.

Classification by side chain (R group)

Amino acids can be grouped in four ways: by R group, by polarity, by nutritional requirement and by metabolic fate.

The side-chain groups and the facts the slides attach to each
GroupMembersKey facts

Alanine: methyl (–CH₃) side chain; carries nitrogen in blood in the glucose–alanine cycle.
Leucine, isoleucine, valine: essential branched-chain amino acids; defects in their breakdown cause maple syrup urine disease.
Aromatic (six-carbon ring with alternating double bonds) Phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan The ring gives special chemical and physical properties (e.g. they absorb ultraviolet light).
Sulfur-containing Methionine (methyl thioether), cysteine (thiol, –SH) Methionine: starts protein synthesis (start codon AUG), so it is the first amino acid of most proteins; precursor of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the methyl donor in methylation reactions.
Cysteine: forms disulfide bridges, covalent links within one chain or between chains that stabilise protein structure.
Cystine = two cysteines joined by a disulfide bond (a dimer).
Hydroxy (–OH in side chain) Serine, threonine, tyrosine Form hydrogen bonds and are the sites of regulatory phosphorylation, especially in enzymes. Serine is a precursor of sphingolipids.
Amide (polar, uncharged; C=O attached to N in side chain) Asparagine, glutamine Asparagine: main target of N-glycosylation in the ER, a cotranslational modification.
Glutamine: carries nitrogen in the body.
Acidic (side-chain –COOH, negative at body pH) Aspartic acid (aspartate), glutamic acid (glutamate) Aspartate: its amino group provides one nitrogen of urea in the urea cycle.
Glutamate: main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS; converted to the inhibitory transmitter GABA by glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), which needs pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6).

Arginine: its R group gives urea in the urea cycle; precursor of the vasodilator nitric oxide (NO).
Histidine: found in the active site of many enzymes; precursor of the allergic mediator histamine.
Imino acid Proline Its nitrogen is part of a ring, so it has an –NH– (imino) group instead of –NH₂. Proline is converted to hydroxyproline, a hallmark component of collagen.
The 21st amino acid Selenocysteine (Sec) Cysteine with selenium in place of sulfur. Proteins containing it are selenoproteins; humans have 25 known ones, many of which maintain redox balance, e.g. thioredoxin reductases and glutathione peroxidases.

Essential and non-essential

  • Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from the diet.
  • Arginine and histidine may become essential when demand rises: during illness and growth phases such as pregnancy or childhood (conditionally essential).

The nine essential amino acids (textbook list): phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, lysine.

Cystinuria (clinical correlation)

In cystinuria, an inherited defect of the amino acid transporter in the kidney tubule (and gut) means cystine (with ornithine, lysine and arginine) is not reabsorbed and spills into the urine.

  • Cystine is less soluble than cysteine, so it crystallises: hexagonal cystine crystals and kidney stones.

Post-translational modifications

After a protein is made, enzymes can add chemical groups to some residues, oxidise them or change them in other ways. This is post-translational modification. More than 100 different modified residues are known in human proteins.

ModificationWhat is added and whereEffect / example
N-linked glycosylationOligosaccharide on the amide nitrogen of asparagineOn cell-surface proteins; protects against proteolysis and immune attack
O-linked glycosylationOligosaccharide on the –OH of serine or threonineCommon in secreted proteins
Fatty acylationPalmitoyl (C16) often on plasma membrane proteins; myristoyl (C14) often on proteins of intracellular vesicle membranesThe lipid anchors the protein in the membrane by hydrophobic interaction
PhosphorylationPhosphate on the –OH of serine, threonine or tyrosine, by a protein kinaseAdds a large negative charge, changing structure and activity
AcetylationAcetyl on lysine of histonesRemoves lysine’s positive charge, loosening its grip on DNA phosphates, which changes gene expression
ADP-ribosylationADP-ribose on a specific residueCholera toxin acting on Gs (below)

ADP-ribosylation: cholera toxin

Cholera is a small-intestine infection by Vibrio cholerae.

  1. Cholera toxin binds intestinal cells (enterocytes) and enters them.
  2. It ADP-ribosylates the G protein Gs, locking it in its GTP-bound (active) form.
  3. Gs keeps stimulating adenylate cyclase → cAMP rises continuously.
  4. Cl⁻ and water are secreted into the gut, and Na⁺ and water entry into enterocytes falls.
  5. Rapid fluid loss from the intestine → severe dehydration (watery diarrhea).

Variations in primary structure

The primary structure of a protein is its linear amino acid sequence. Almost every residue contributes to the protein’s shape, but the sequence can still vary a little.

Between species

  • Hypervariable region: many different amino acids are tolerated at a position.
  • Invariant region: binding sites and parts critical for the 3-D shape; exactly the same sequence between individuals, tissues and species.

During development: hemoglobin

HemoglobinChainsWhenO₂ affinity

HbA (adult)2 α + 2 βReplaces HbF after birthLower

Between tissues: isoforms (isozymes)

Proteins that differ somewhat in sequence and properties from tissue to tissue but keep the same function are tissue-specific isoforms or isozymes. Example: creatine kinase (CK), made of two subunits with 60–72% sequence homology. From the textbook: CK-MM (skeletal muscle), CK-MB (heart), CK-BB (brain); CK-MB in blood points to heart muscle damage.

gct/biochemistry/wk04-protein-structure:
GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 4

Structure–Function Relationships in Proteins

The four levels of protein structure, what holds each one together, how proteins fold, unfold and get destroyed, and the diseases of misfolding: Alzheimer disease and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 4: Protein Structure & Function

In 60 seconds

  • Primary = sequence joined by peptide bonds; it decides the final shape.
  • Secondary = α-helix and β-sheet, held by backbone hydrogen bonds. The α-helix is right-handed with 3.6 residues per turn; proline breaks helices.
  • Tertiary = whole 3-D shape, from R-group interactions (including disulfide bonds). Quaternary = how subunits fit together (Hb = α₂β₂).
  • Denaturation unfolds secondary and tertiary structure without breaking peptide bonds.
  • Hsp70 works cotranslationally; Hsp60 post-translationally (uses much ATP). Bad proteins get ubiquitin (E1, E2, E3) and go to the proteasome.
  • Alzheimer: extracellular Aβ42 plaques (β-secretase + γ-secretase) and intracellular tau tangles.
  • CJD: infectious prion PrPSc; rapid dementia, myoclonus, death within 1 year.

Learning objectives

Marks’ Basic Medical Biochemistry, 6th ed., Chapter 7, pages 179–190 and 208–216. By the end you can:

  • describe primary, secondary (α-helix, β-sheet, non-repetitive), tertiary and quaternary structure, and structural motifs;
  • explain denaturation and renaturation;
  • explain protein folding, chaperones, the ubiquitin–proteasome system and prions;
  • describe Alzheimer disease and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease at the molecular level.

Contents

  1. The four levels
  2. Primary structure
  3. Secondary structure
  4. Tertiary structure
  5. Quaternary structure
  6. Denaturation
  7. Chaperones and misfolding
  8. Ubiquitin and the proteasome
  9. Alzheimer disease
  10. Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease

The four levels

Proteins are macromolecules made of amino acid monomers. The linear sequence of amino acids contains all the information needed to form one unique 3-D shape, and that shape determines function.

LevelWhat it isHeld together by
PrimaryLinear amino acid sequencePeptide bonds (covalent)
SecondaryLocal folding: α-helix, β-sheet, turns and loopsHydrogen bonds between backbone atoms (C=O and N–H)
TertiaryThe whole 3-D shape of one chainInteractions between R groups: hydrophobic, ionic, hydrogen bonds, disulfide bonds
QuaternaryHow several subunits fit togetherCovalent and noncovalent interactions between subunit surfaces

Primary structure

  • The linear sequence of amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds into a polypeptide chain. This sequence determines the shape of the protein.
  • A peptide bond is an amide linkage between the α-carboxyl group of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the next.
  • It forms by a dehydration (condensation) reaction: one molecule of water is removed.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · Proteins & Amino Acids | Biochemistry Watch from 2:00 to the end: how amino acids join into polypeptides.

Secondary structure

Locally folded regions formed by interactions between atoms of the polypeptide backbone (not the side chains). The two regular forms are the α-helix and the β-sheet.

The α-helix

  • A rigid, right-handed spiral with a tightly coiled backbone core.
  • Side chains point outward from the central axis so they don’t get in each other’s way.
  • 3.6 residues per turn, so side chains three or four residues apart come close together in space.
  • Stabilised by extensive hydrogen bonds between carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens of the backbone, within the same strand (each C=O bonds to the N–H four residues further on).
  • Proline is a “helix breaker”: its ring doesn’t fit inside the helix (and its nitrogen has no H to donate). It is usually not in the middle of a helix, but can be at the start or in the second position.

The β-sheet (β pleated sheet)

  • Two or more segments of a chain line up side by side, forming a sheet.
  • The carbonyl O of one peptide bond is hydrogen-bonded to the amide H of a peptide bond on an adjacent strand.
  • Strands can run in the same direction (parallel) or opposite directions (antiparallel).

Non-repetitive structures and motifs

Not every region is a helix or sheet. Turns and loops connect them (β-turns often contain glycine and proline). Common combinations of secondary structures are called structural motifs, for example the helix–turn–helix, the zinc finger, and β-hairpins.

α-helixβ-sheet
ShapeRight-handed coilFlat, pleated sheet of strands
H bondsWithin the same strandBetween adjacent strands
Side chainsPoint outward from the axisPoint above and below the sheet
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Protein Structure - Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary Watch from 8:05 to 14:30: primary and secondary structure.

Tertiary structure

  • The overall 3-D shape of a protein: the sum of its secondary structural elements.
  • Mainly due to interactions between the R groups.
  • It is flexible and dynamic: side chains and domains keep moving rapidly.
  • A disulfide bond (–S–S–) is a covalent link made from the –SH groups of two cysteine residues, producing a cystine residue.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Protein Structure - Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary Watch from 14:30 to 18:50: tertiary structure.

Quaternary structure

Proteins with more than one subunit have quaternary structure, determined by covalent and noncovalent interactions between subunit surfaces.

TermMeaningExample
ProtomerRepeating unit made of non-identical subunitsAdult hemoglobin, a tetramer α₂β₂; one α–β pair is a protomer
OligomerMultisubunit protein of identical subunitsF-actin, made of identical G-actin subunits
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Protein Structure - Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary Watch from 18:50 to the end: quaternary structure and a review of all four levels.

Denaturation

  • Denaturation = unfolding and disorganisation of a protein’s secondary and tertiary structure without hydrolysis of peptide bonds. The primary structure stays.
  • Denaturing agents: heat, urea, organic solvents, strong acids or bases, detergents, and heavy metal ions such as lead.
  • Under some conditions a denatured protein can refold into its native shape and regain function (renaturation), which shows that the sequence carries the folding information.

Chaperones and misfolding

Chaperones are proteins that help other proteins fold and prevent misfolding. They give a favourable environment for folding and stop unfolded proteins from aggregating. (The word once meant an older woman accompanying a young unmarried lady in public.) Many are heat-shock proteins (Hsp).

FamilyWhenWhat it does
Hsp70Cotranslational (while the chain is being made)Stops new chains folding too early; can also help unfold proteins when needed
Hsp60Post-translational (after synthesis)Folds already-made proteins; uses a lot of ATP

Misfolding

Folding is complex and sometimes goes wrong. Misfolded proteins are usually tagged and degraded, but this quality control is not perfect. Aggregates of misfolded proteins can build up inside or outside cells, and such deposits cause several diseases.

Possible fates of a new protein (slide diagram): correct folding (with or without chaperones) → function; or misfolding → refolding by chaperones, degradation by the proteasome, or aggregation (amyloid).

Ubiquitin and the proteasome

  • The proteasome is an abundant, ATP-dependent protease that destroys incompletely folded proteins.
  • It acts processively: it cuts the whole protein into short peptides.
  • Proteins to be destroyed are marked with polyubiquitin chains, added in a multistep process by three enzyme classes:
  1. E1, ubiquitin-activating enzyme: uses ATP to activate ubiquitin.
  2. E2, ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme: carries the activated ubiquitin towards the substrate.
  3. E3, ubiquitin ligase: recognises the specific substrate protein and attaches ubiquitin to it.
Which E decides the target?

E3 (the ligase) gives the specificity: it chooses which protein is tagged.

Alzheimer disease

  • A progressive neurodegenerative disease and the leading cause of dementia.
  • Risk factors: age > 65 years and genes. People with Down syndrome are at higher risk because the gene for amyloid precursor protein (APP) is on chromosome 21.
  • Main microscopic feature: extraneuronal β-amyloid (Aβ) plaques.
  • Usually begins with short-term memory loss, slowly progressing to dementia with other cognitive deficits; often with depression, anxiety and apathy.

How amyloid plaques form

PathwayFirst cutThen γ-secretase givesResult
Non-amyloidogenic (normal, predominant)α-secretase → sAPPα + C83p3 + AICDNon-toxic fragments
Amyloidogenic (increases in disease)β-secretase → sAPPβ + C99Aβ42 + AICDAβ aggregates into insoluble extracellular plaques

AICD = APP intracellular domain. Aβ42 is hydrophobic and aggregates; the plaques disrupt synaptic signalling, trigger inflammation and promote neuron death.

Tau and neurofibrillary tangles

  • Normally tau stabilises microtubules in neurons, which carry nutrients and signals.
  • In Alzheimer disease tau is hyperphosphorylated, detaches from microtubules and aggregates into neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) inside neurons → cytoskeleton collapses → neuron dies.

Cholinergic hypothesis

There is a marked loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain (less acetylcholine).

Memory hook

Plaques outside, tangles inside. Aβ plaques are extracellular; tau tangles are intracellular.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · Dementia & Alzheimer’s Disease Watch from 5:10 to 13:20: amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (clinical correlation)

  • A progressive, fatal, dementing illness caused by an infectious protein, a prion, called PrPSc.
  • PrPSc is highly resistant to proteolysis and forms insoluble aggregates of fibrils.
  • The normal, non-infectious form PrPC (C = cellular) is encoded by the same gene and sits on the surface of neurons and glial cells. The two differ in folding, not sequence: PrPSc has more β-sheet and converts PrPC into more PrPSc.
FeatureDetails
Early (prodromal) symptomsNonspecific: fatigue, sleep disturbance, weight loss, headache, anxiety, vertigo
Main signsRapidly progressive dementia (weeks to months), ataxia, startle myoclonus (jerks triggered by minimal stimuli)
OutcomeDeath usually in less than 1 year
Definite diagnosisNeuropathologically confirmed spongiform encephalopathy in progressive dementia
Gold standardBrain biopsy, but rarely done because there is no treatment or cure

Numbers to remember

3 or 4Residues apart for side chains that meet in a helix

Hsp70 / Hsp60Cotranslational / post-translational chaperones
E1, E2, E3Ubiquitin-activating, -conjugating, ligase

Chromosome 21Location of the APP gene
Aβ42 / C99 / C83Toxic peptide / β-secretase fragment / α-secretase fragment
< 1 yearSurvival in CJD

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
Secondary vs tertiary bondsSecondary: backbone H bonds. Tertiary: R-group interactions.
Protomer vs oligomerNon-identical subunit unit (Hb α–β pair) vs identical subunits (F-actin).
Denaturation vs hydrolysisDenaturation unfolds; hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds.
Hsp70 vs Hsp60During synthesis vs after synthesis (ATP-heavy).
α- vs β-secretaseα: non-amyloidogenic (C83, p3). β: amyloidogenic (C99, Aβ42).
Plaques vs tanglesAβ outside neurons vs hyperphosphorylated tau inside neurons.
PrPC vs PrPScNormal cellular form vs infectious, protease-resistant misfolded form; same gene.

Watch out

Watch out: the α-helix hydrogen bonds

Slide 7 says side chains three or four residues apart are brought together “and so” the helix is stabilised by hydrogen bonds. The stabilising hydrogen bonds are between backbone C=O and N–H groups (each C=O to the N–H four residues along), not between side chains. Side chains point outward.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Denaturation does not break peptide bonds; primary structure survives.
  • The α-helix is right-handed.
  • Proline is a helix breaker, but can appear at the start of a helix.
  • In β-sheets H bonds are between strands; in α-helices within the strand.
  • E3, not E1, chooses the protein to be destroyed.
  • Down syndrome raises Alzheimer risk because of the APP gene on chromosome 21.
  • PrPC and PrPSc come from the same gene.

Check yourself

    1. Two side chains
    2. The α-carboxyl of one amino acid and the α-amino of the next
    3. Two cysteine –SH groups
    4. Two α-carbons directly
    Show answer

  2. How many residues per turn does an α-helix have?

    1. 2.0
    2. 3.6
    3. 4.5
    4. 10
    Show answer

    B. So residues 3–4 apart meet in space.

  3. Why is proline called a helix breaker?

    1. It is negatively charged
    2. Its ring structure cannot fit inside the α-helix
    3. It forms disulfide bonds
    4. It is too large
    Show answer

    B. It is usually found at the start of a helix, not in the middle.

  4. Tertiary structure mainly results from:

    1. Peptide bonds
    2. Backbone hydrogen bonds only
    3. Interactions between R groups
    4. Subunit contacts
    Show answer

  5. F-actin made of identical G-actin subunits is an example of:

    1. A protomer

  6. Which statement about denaturation is correct?

    1. It hydrolyses peptide bonds
    2. It destroys secondary and tertiary structure without breaking peptide bonds
    3. It can never be reversed

  7. Which chaperone family folds already-synthesised proteins and uses a lot of ATP?

gct/biochemistry/wk05-phospholipids:
GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 5

Phospholipids, Sphingolipids and Eicosanoids

The membrane lipids built on glycerol and on sphingosine, what they do in signalling, the lung, the mitochondrion and the nerve, the storage diseases when their breakdown fails, and the eicosanoids that drive inflammation and clotting.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 5: Phospholipids & Sphingolipids

In 60 seconds

  • Membrane lipids are amphipathic; the backbone is glycerol or sphingosine. All glycerophospholipids come from phosphatidic acid.
  • DPPC (made by type II pneumocytes) is the main surfactant lipid; too little → neonatal RDS.
  • PLC splits PIP₂ into IP₃ (releases Ca²⁺ from ER) and DAG (activates PKC). GPI anchors fail in PNH (no CD55/CD59).
  • Cardiolipin: inner mitochondrial membrane; antigen in the Wassermann syphilis test.
  • Ceramide → sphingomyelin, cerebrosides, gangliosides, sulfatides. Missing lysosomal enzymes cause sphingolipidoses (Niemann–Pick, Tay–Sachs, Gaucher, Fabry, Krabbe, MLD).
  • Eicosanoids come from 20-carbon ω-6/ω-3 fatty acids (arachidonic acid). Aspirin blocks COX irreversibly; low dose (< 300 mg/day) is antiplatelet.
  • Leukotrienes: LTB4 attracts neutrophils; LTC4/D4/E4 drive asthma. Zileuton blocks 5-lipoxygenase; montelukast and zafirlukast block the receptor.

Learning objectives

Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 8th ed., Chapter 17, pages 563–605. By the end you can:

  • describe glycerophospholipids and sphingophospholipids, including phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylinositol, cardiolipin and plasmalogens;
  • outline the synthesis and breakdown of sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids;
  • explain the sphingolipidoses and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome;
  • describe eicosanoids, how anti-inflammatory drugs block them, and their role in asthma.

Membrane lipids

The major membrane lipids are amphipathic: they have a hydrophilic (water-loving) part and a hydrophobic (water-fearing) part.

  • Backbone: glycerol or sphingosine.
  • Hydrophilic head: a phosphate group plus an alcohol (e.g. choline, ethanolamine, serine, inositol).
  • Hydrophobic tail: fatty acids or fatty-acid-derived hydrocarbons.

Glycerophospholipids

Phospholipids with a glycerol backbone. They are the major class of phospholipids. All are derivatives of phosphatidic acid (PA): a diacylglycerol (DAG) with a phosphate on carbon 3.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Membrane Structure & Function Watch from 2:09 to 8:20: the membrane lipids and why they are amphipathic.

Phosphatidylcholine and neonatal RDS

Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) has palmitate (a saturated long-chain fatty acid) at both positions 1 and 2 of glycerol.

  • Made and secreted by type II pneumocytes.
  • A major lipid of lung surfactant.
  • Surfactant lowers surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli, so less pressure is needed to reinflate them; this prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis).
In the clinic: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  • In preterm infants, from too little surfactant made or secreted.
  • Incidence is inversely proportional to gestational age: the earlier the birth, the more likely.
  • Maternal diabetes raises the risk: the baby’s hyperinsulinemia inhibits surfactant synthesis.
  • Prevention: glucocorticoids to the mother shortly before delivery speed lung maturation.
  • Treatment: give the baby natural or synthetic surfactant after birth.
Watch: explains the section above

Phosphatidylinositol

Signal transduction: the PIP₂ pathway

  1. A signal activates phospholipase C (PLC).
  2. PLC splits phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP₂) into two second messengers.
  3. IP₃ (inositol trisphosphate) → releases Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum. DAG (diacylglycerol) → activates protein kinase C (PKC).
  4. Together they control secretion, contraction and gene expression.

Anchoring proteins: GPI anchors

Some proteins are fixed to the outer surface of the membrane by a glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, which links the protein to PI in the membrane.

  • Lipoprotein lipase, which breaks down triglycerides, is held on capillary walls by a GPI anchor.
  • DAF (CD55) stops complement activation on the cell surface; CD59 blocks formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC). Without them, red cells are treated as “non-self” and destroyed.
In the clinic: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)

A rare acquired disorder: a mutation in the PIGA gene of blood stem cells means GPI anchors are not made, so red cells lack CD55 and CD59. Complement destroys them inside vessels (intravascular hemolysis), giving:

  • hemoglobinuria: dark urine, especially in the morning;
  • anemia and fatigue;
  • thrombosis, the major cause of death;
  • pancytopenia in some patients.

Cardiolipin

  • Two phosphatidic acids esterified through their phosphates to an extra glycerol = cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol).
  • Found in membranes of prokaryotes and eukaryotes. In eukaryotes it is almost only in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it keeps certain electron transport chain complexes working.
  • It is antigenic: people infected with Treponema pallidum (syphilis) make anti-cardiolipin antibodies. The Wassermann test detects them using cardiolipin as the antigen.

Plasmalogens and platelet-activating factor

These are ether glycerophospholipids: carbon 1 of glycerol carries an alkyl chain joined by an ether bond, not an ester bond.

LipidCarbon 1Carbon 2Notes
PlasmalogenUnsaturated alkyl group, ether bondFatty acidNamed “-al” not “-yl”, e.g. phosphatidalethanolamine in nerve tissue
Platelet-activating factor (PAF)Saturated alkyl group, ether bondAcetyl group (not a fatty acid)Released by many cells; binds receptors and causes strong clotting and inflammation

An unsaturated alkyl group contains one or more C=C double (or C≡C triple) bonds.

Phospholipases

  • Glycerophospholipids are broken down by phospholipases, present in all tissues and in pancreatic juice.
  • Many toxins and venoms have phospholipase activity, and several pathogenic bacteria make phospholipases that dissolve cell membranes and help infection spread.

Sphingophospholipids

  • Backbone: sphingosine, made from serine + palmitate.
  • Ceramide = sphingosine + long-chain fatty acid by an amide bond. Ceramide is the precursor of cerebrosides and gangliosides.
  • Sphingomyelin = ceramide whose C1–OH binds phosphorylcholine. It is the major sphingophospholipid, essential for the myelin sheath and fast nerve conduction.
  • Ceramides maintain the skin’s water-permeability barrier; low ceramide levels are linked to several skin disorders.

Synthesis of sphingomyelin

  1. Palmitoyl CoA + serine condense → (via 3-ketosphinganine) sphinganine. Needs PLP (vitamin B6).
  2. Sphinganine is acylated on its amino group with a long-chain fatty acid, then desaturated → ceramide.
  3. Phosphorylcholine is transferred from phosphatidylcholine (PC) to ceramide → sphingomyelin + DAG.

Breakdown of sphingomyelin

  1. Sphingomyelinase (a type of phospholipase C) removes phosphorylcholine → ceramide.
  2. Ceramidase splits ceramide → sphingosine + free fatty acid.

Niemann–Pick disease

Cause: sphingomyelinase deficiency → sphingomyelin builds up. Type C is different: NPC1/NPC2 mutations → cholesterol and sphingomyelin build up.

TypeDefectFeatures
A: severe infantileSphingomyelinaseProgressive neurodegeneration, developmental delay, cherry-red spot on the macula, hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages); fatal in early childhood
B: chronic visceralSphingomyelinaseLittle or no nerve involvement; affects liver and spleen; later onset, longer survival
C: lipid transport defectNPC1/NPC2Cholesterol + sphingomyelin accumulate; variable nerve involvement
Why a cherry-red spot?

Lipid builds up in the retinal ganglion cells, making the retina pale. The macula has no ganglion cells, so it stays red from the choroidal vessels underneath. Pale retina + red macula = cherry-red spot.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Tay-Sachs, Fabry, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick Disease Watch from 29:01 to 31:25: Niemann–Pick disease.

Glycosphingolipids

Glycosphingolipids differ from sphingomyelin: they contain no phosphate. Their head is a mono- or oligosaccharide attached directly to ceramide by an O-glycosidic bond.

  • Act as cell-surface antigens (ABO blood groups, fetal and tumour antigens); the sugar part decides the antigen.
  • Act as receptors for toxins (cholera, tetanus) and some viruses.
ClassTypeStructureWhere
NeutralCerebrosides (simplest)Ceramide + one galactose (galactocerebroside) or glucose (glucocerebroside)Brain and peripheral nerves, high in myelin
Acidic (negative at body pH)GangliosidesCeramide oligosaccharide + one or more NANA (N-acetylneuraminic acid, a sialic acid)CNS, especially nerve endings
SulfatidesSulfated galactocerebrosidesBrain and kidneys

Synthesis

  • Mainly in the Golgi, by adding sugars one at a time from UDP-sugar donors.
  • The enzymes are glycosyltransferases, each specific for the type and position of the bond.
  • Sulfate for sulfatides comes from PAPS (3′-phosphoadenosine-5′-phosphosulfate).

Sphingolipidoses (glycosphingolipid breakdown)

Glycosphingolipids are broken down in lysosomes, one sugar at a time. A missing enzyme causes the lipid to accumulate. The slide lists six enzymes; the matching diseases are from the textbook.

Missing enzymeDiseaseWhat accumulatesHallmarks
1. Hexosaminidase ATay–SachsGM2 gangliosideNeurodegeneration, cherry-red spot, no hepatosplenomegaly
2. α-Galactosidase AFabry (X-linked)GlobotriaosylceramidePain in hands and feet, skin lesions, kidney and heart disease
3. Arylsulfatase AMetachromatic leukodystrophySulfatidesDemyelination
4. GalactocerebrosidaseKrabbeGalactocerebrosideGloboid cells (slide 20), demyelination
5. GlucocerebrosidaseGaucher (most common)GlucocerebrosideHepatosplenomegaly, bone problems, Gaucher cells
6. SphingomyelinaseNiemann–Pick A and BSphingomyelinCherry-red spot, hepatosplenomegaly, foam cells

  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Tay-Sachs, Fabry, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick Disease Watch from 17:59 to 29:01: Tay–Sachs and Gaucher disease (start at 0:43 if you want lysosomes explained first).

Eicosanoids

  • Made from 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids, either ω-6 or ω-3 (“eicosa” = 20).
  • ω-6 and ω-3 fatty acids are essential: humans cannot make them and must eat them.
  • The sn-2 position of PI and PC often stores arachidonic acid, which phospholipase A₂ can release quickly for inflammation and signalling.
  • From arachidonic acid, cyclooxygenase (COX) makes prostaglandins and thromboxanes; 5-lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes.
  • In the stomach and duodenum, acid triggers release of PGE2, which increases bicarbonate and mucus secretion and protects the epithelium from acid.

Prostacyclin versus thromboxane

Prostacyclin (PGI2)Thromboxane A2 (TXA2)
Made byEndothelial and smooth muscle cells of the vessel wallActivated platelets
Effect on plateletsInhibits aggregationActivates nearby platelets → aggregation
Effect on vesselsVasodilationVasoconstriction

Aspirin and acetaminophen

DrugHow it blocks COXWhere
Acetaminophen (paracetamol)ReversiblyMostly in the CNS; inactivated in the periphery, so little anti-inflammatory effect
Aspirin (an NSAID)Irreversibly (acetylates the enzyme), both COX-1 and COX-2Everywhere

Aspirin blocks TXA2 synthesis more than prostacyclin synthesis (platelets have no nucleus, so they cannot make new COX; endothelial cells can). Net effect: less clotting.

Aspirin effects by dose
DoseEffect
Low: < 300 mg/dayLess platelet aggregation (antiplatelet)
Intermediate: 300–2400 mg/dayAntipyretic and analgesic
High: 2400–4000 mg/dayAnti-inflammatory
Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · NSAIDs | Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs Watch from 4:45 to the end: prostaglandins and how NSAIDs block COX.

Leukotrienes and asthma

  • Made from arachidonic acid by macrophages, mast cells and leukocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes), via 5-lipoxygenase.
  • LTA4 is inactive; it gives rise to active LTB4 and LTC4.
  • LTC4 is made by adding glutathione. Removing Glu then Gly gives LTD4 and then LTE4. LTC4, D4 and E4 are the cysteinyl leukotrienes (CysLTs).
  • LTB4 attracts neutrophils, dendritic cells and T cells (chemotaxis).
  • LTC4 increases the permeability of postcapillary venules (and CysLTs constrict bronchi).
In the clinic: asthma

Inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles → smooth muscle contraction and recruitment of leukocytes. Long term: hypertrophy of smooth muscle and of mucus glands.

Drugs for prevention and chronic treatment: zileuton (inhibits 5-lipoxygenase), and montelukast and zafirlukast (block the CysLT receptor 1).

Numbers to remember

ValueWhat it is
C3Carbon of glycerol carrying the phosphate in phosphatidic acid
C1 and C2Both palmitate in DPPC
4,5Phosphate positions on inositol in PIP₂
2 PA + 1 glycerolCardiolipin
sn-2Position storing arachidonic acid in PI and PC
20Carbons in eicosanoid precursors
< 300 mg/dayAntiplatelet aspirin dose
300–2400 mg/dayAntipyretic/analgesic aspirin dose
2400–4000 mg/dayAnti-inflammatory aspirin dose
CD55 / CD59GPI-anchored complement regulators lost in PNH

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
IP₃ vs DAGIP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from ER; DAG activates PKC.
CD55 vs CD59CD55 (DAF) stops complement activation; CD59 blocks MAC formation.
Plasmalogen vs PAFUnsaturated alkyl + fatty acid at C2 vs saturated alkyl + acetyl at C2.
Sphingomyelin vs glycosphingolipidPhosphorylcholine head (has phosphate) vs sugar head (no phosphate).
Ganglioside vs sulfatideNegative from NANA vs from sulfate.
Niemann–Pick A/B vs CSphingomyelinase deficiency vs NPC1/NPC2 cholesterol transport defect.
Tay–Sachs vs Niemann–Pick ABoth have a cherry-red spot; only Niemann–Pick has hepatosplenomegaly.
Zileuton vs montelukastBlocks 5-lipoxygenase (synthesis) vs blocks the CysLT1 receptor.
Aspirin vs acetaminophenIrreversible, COX-1 and -2, peripheral too vs reversible, mainly CNS.

Watch out

Watch out: the leukotriene label

Slide 24 writes “Leukotriene C4 (LTB5) increases the permeability of postcapillary venules”. “LTB5” is a typo: the molecule meant is LTC4. LTB4 is the one that attracts neutrophils.

Watch out: different textbook

This week follows Lippincott (Chapter 17), not Marks. Use Lippincott’s wording for sphingolipid diseases.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • DPPC is made by type II, not type I, pneumocytes.
  • Maternal diabetes raises RDS risk (fetal insulin inhibits surfactant).
  • PNH is acquired (PIGA mutation in stem cells), not inherited.
  • Cardiolipin is in the inner, not outer, mitochondrial membrane.
  • Sphingomyelinase is a type of phospholipase C.
  • Glycosphingolipids have no phosphate.
  • Aspirin inhibits COX irreversibly; acetaminophen reversibly.
  • LTA4 is inactive.

Check yourself

  1. All glycerophospholipids are derivatives of:

    1. Sphingosine
    2. Phosphatidic acid
    3. Ceramide
    4. Cholesterol

  2. Which factor increases the risk of neonatal RDS?

  3. Phospholipase C acting on PIP₂ produces:

  4. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from loss of:

    1. Cardiolipin
    2. GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59
    3. Sphingomyelinase
    4. Surfactant

    B. A PIGA mutation stops GPI-anchor synthesis; complement lyses red cells.

  5. The Wassermann test for syphilis uses which lipid as antigen?

    1. Phosphatidylcholine
    2. Sphingomyelin
    3. Cardiolipin
    4. Ganglioside

    C. Infected patients make anti-cardiolipin antibodies.

  6. Platelet-activating factor has, on carbon 2 of glycerol:

    1. A fatty acid
    2. An acetyl group

    B. C1 carries a saturated alkyl group by an ether bond.

  7. The first step of sphingosine synthesis needs which vitamin-derived coenzyme?

    1. Thiamine pyrophosphate

    3. Biotin

    B. Palmitoyl CoA + serine condensation is PLP (B6)-dependent.

  8. A cherry-red spot with hepatosplenomegaly and foam cells in an infant suggests deficiency of:

    1. Hexosaminidase A
    2. Sphingomyelinase

GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 6

The Extracellular Matrix and Fibrous Proteins

What fills the space between cells: collagen, elastin, laminin, proteoglycans, integrins, fibronectin and the enzymes that remodel them, plus the diseases when any of these go wrong.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 6: ECM & Fibrous Proteins

In 60 seconds

  • ECM = collagen (strength) + elastin (stretch) + adhesive proteins (fibronectin, laminin) + proteoglycans.
  • Collagen is the most abundant body protein: a triple helix of Gly-X-Y repeats; glycine every third residue.
  • Synthesis needs vitamin C (hydroxylation) and copper (lysyl oxidase cross-links). Lack of C → scurvy; lack of Cu → Menkes.
  • Collagen diseases: osteogenesis imperfecta (type I), Ehlers–Danlos (I, III, V, processing enzymes), Alport (type IV).
  • Elastin: Gly 31%, Ala 22%, Pro 11%, cross-linked by desmosine; built on fibrillin microfibrils (defective in Marfan).
  • α1-antitrypsin from the liver inhibits neutrophil elastase; deficiency → early panacinar emphysema and cirrhosis.
  • Proteoglycans are about 95% GAG; mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler, Hunter) come from missing lysosomal enzymes. MMPs are Ca²⁺-dependent zinc endopeptidases, blocked by TIMPs.

Learning objectives

Marks, 6th ed., Chapter 47 (pages 1659–1679) and Lippincott, 8th ed., Chapter 4 “Fibrous Proteins” (pages 137–161). By the end you can:

  • list the components of the ECM and describe laminin, proteoglycans, integrins, adhesion molecules and matrix metalloproteinases;
  • describe collagen types, structure and synthesis, and the collagenopathies (scurvy, osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers–Danlos, Alport);
  • describe elastin, α1-antitrypsin, α1-antitrypsin deficiency and Marfan syndrome;
  • explain the mucopolysaccharidoses Hurler and Hunter.

The extracellular matrix

The extracellular matrix (ECM) is the network that fills the spaces between cells. It gives structure, determines the shape of tissues, and links cells and tissues together.

ComponentExamplesMain job
Structural proteinsCollagen; elastinStrength; elasticity
Specialised adhesive proteinsFibronectin; lamininLink cells to the matrix
ProteoglycansCore protein + GAG chainsHydration, gel, resistance to compression

Fibrous proteins

Fibrous proteins fold into long filaments or sheets with repeated amino acid sequences. They are not very soluble in water and give tissues strength and support.

  • Collagen: strength of skin, bone, tendons, cartilage.
  • Keratin: hair, nails, skin.
  • Elastin: elasticity of ligaments and blood vessels.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · Connective Tissue | Everything you need to know! Watch from 4:04 to 12:14: the fibres and ground substance of connective tissue.

Collagen structure and types

  • The most abundant protein in the human body.
  • A long, rigid molecule: three polypeptide α chains wound around one another in a rope-like triple helix, held together by interchain hydrogen bonds.
  • Rich in glycine and proline:
    • Proline’s ring causes kinks, helping each α chain take its helical shape.
    • Glycine, the smallest amino acid, is in every third position. It fits the tight space where the three chains meet in the middle.
  • Contains hydroxyproline (Hyp) and hydroxylysine (Hyl), which most other proteins lack.
Three forms of collagen
FormTypesNotes
Fibril-formingI, II, IIII: bone, skin, tendon (most common). II: cartilage. III: blood vessels, skin, reticular fibres.
Network-formingIV, VIIIIV forms the basement membrane (basal lamina).
Fibril-associatedIX, XIIBind the surface of fibrils, linking fibrils to one another and to other ECM components.
Mnemonic: “Be So Totally Cool, Read Books”

Type I = Bone (and skin, tendon), II = cartilage (car-two-lage), III = Reticular / vessels, IV = Basement membrane (“under the floor”).

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Types of collagen (I, II, III, IV, and V) Watch from 3:47 to 7:01: how collagen is made and its types.

Collagen synthesis

  1. Synthesis (RER): α chains are translated as preprocollagen, mostly Gly-X-Y repeats (X and Y often proline or lysine).
  2. Hydroxylation (RER): specific proline and lysine residues are hydroxylated. Requires vitamin C. Hydroxyproline maximises interchain hydrogen bonds that stabilise the triple helix.
  3. Glycosylation: sugars are added to hydroxylysine residues; three pro-α chains form procollagen, a triple helix held by hydrogen and disulfide bonds.
  4. Exocytosis: procollagen is secreted into the extracellular space.
  5. Proteolytic processing: the disulfide-rich end pieces are cut off by procollagen peptidases → insoluble tropocollagen.
  6. Cross-linking: many staggered tropocollagen molecules are joined by covalent lysine–hydroxylysine cross-links made by copper-containing lysyl oxidase → collagen fibrils.
Where each disease hits

Triple-helix formation → osteogenesis imperfecta. Hydroxylation (vitamin C) → scurvy. Processing enzymes (lysyl hydroxylase, procollagen peptidase) → Ehlers–Danlos. Cross-linking (copper, lysyl oxidase) → Menkes.

Osteogenesis imperfecta

  • A genetic “brittle bone disease”, most often from defects in COL1A1 and COL1A2.
  • Most common form: autosomal dominant, with less production of otherwise normal type I collagen (altered triple-helix formation).
SignWhy
Multiple fractures and deformities after minimal traumaWeak bone collagen
Blue scleraeThin, translucent connective tissue lets the choroidal veins show through
Opalescent teeth that wear easily (dentinogenesis imperfecta)Lack of dentin
Conductive hearing lossAbnormal ossicles (middle-ear bones)

Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (EDS)

Caused by deficiency of collagen-processing enzymes (e.g. lysyl hydroxylase, procollagen peptidase) or mutations in collagen types I, III or V. Typical signs: stretchy skin and loose joints.

TypeFeaturesGene
HypermobilityJoint instability; the most common type—
ClassicalJoint and skin symptomsType V collagen (COL5A1, COL5A2)
VascularFragile vessels (e.g. aorta), muscles and organs prone to rupture (e.g. pregnant uterus)Type III procollagen (COL3A1)
