Scurvy and copper

Scurvy: vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency

Without vitamin C, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases cannot work, so the triple helix is unstable. Signs:

  • swollen, bleeding gums; easy bruising; petechiae (small red or purple skin spots);
  • hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints); perifollicular hemorrhages; “corkscrew” hair;
  • anemia, poor wound healing, weak immune response.

Copper

Copper is part of several key enzymes:

  • Lysyl oxidase (collagen and elastin cross-links).
  • Ferroxidases such as ceruloplasmin and hephaestin, which oxidise ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to ferric (Fe³⁺) for storage or transport in blood.
  • Ceruloplasmin is the major copper-carrying protein in the blood.
In the clinic: Menkes disease

Copper deficiency is mainly genetic, e.g. Menkes disease: a mutation in the Menkes P-type ATPase, encoded by ATP7A. Copper cannot be moved from enterocytes to the liver and other cells → low copper → weak cross-linking of collagen and elastin (plus brittle, kinky hair and nerve damage).

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Scurvy - Vitamin C Deficiency Watch from 0:00 to the end: why vitamin C deficiency weakens collagen.
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Menkes Disease - Menkes Kinky Hair Syndrome - Copper Watch from 0:00 to the end: Menkes disease and copper.

Alport syndrome

  • A genetic defect of type IV collagen (basement membrane).
  • Triad: glomerulonephritis, often sensorineural hearing loss, sometimes eye problems.
  • Infancy: intermittent gross hematuria. Adolescence: signs of chronic kidney disease (e.g. proteinuria), possibly hearing or (rarely) vision loss.
  • Mild forms may stay without symptoms and need only monitoring.
Memory hook

Alport: “can’t see, can’t pee, can’t hear a bee” (eye, kidney, ear).

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Alport Syndrome | Nephritic | 5-Minute Review Series Watch from 6:52 to 9:44: Alport syndrome.

Elastin and Marfan syndrome

Elastin is the elastic protein of elastic fibres, which are made of elastin plus microfibrils. Elastin is built from cross-linked monomers of tropoelastin.

Elastin composition
ComponentAmount / role
Glycine31%
Alanine22%
Proline11%, mostly not hydroxylated (unlike collagen)
Desmosine and isodesmosineCross-links that give elasticity

How elastin forms

  1. Cells make and secrete tropoelastin into the ECM.
  2. Fibrillin and other glycoproteins form microfibrils.
  3. Tropoelastin attaches to the microfibrils.
  4. Lysyl oxidase converts some lysines to allysine.
  5. Three allysines + one lysine form a desmosine cross-link.
  6. The cross-linked network = mature elastic fibre.
In the clinic: Marfan syndrome (defective fibrillin-1)
  • Tall, with long limbs; long, tapering fingers and toes (arachnodactyly); hypermobile joints.
  • Chest wall deformity: pectus carinatum (pigeon chest) or pectus excavatum (sunken chest).
  • Cystic medial necrosis of the aorta → aortic root aneurysm, rupture or dissection; mitral valve prolapse.
  • Lens dislocated upward and temporally (weak suspensory ligaments).

From the textbook: autosomal dominant, FBN1 gene on chromosome 15.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Marfan Syndrome - Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment Watch from 0:00 to 12:23: fibrillin, lens dislocation and the aorta in Marfan syndrome.

α1-Antitrypsin (AAT)

  • A plasma protein that inhibits proteases; its key job is to block neutrophil elastase, which digests the elastin of alveolar walls and other structural proteins.
  • Mostly made and secreted by the liver.
  • Alveoli are always exposed to low levels of neutrophil elastase from activated and dying neutrophils; AAT keeps this in check.
In the clinic: α1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Lungs: unchecked elastase destroys elastin → early-onset panacinar emphysema, uniform destruction of the whole acinus (respiratory bronchioles and alveolar sacs). Breathlessness, wheeze, mucus, chronic cough. Smoking makes it much worse.
  • Liver: misfolded AAT gets stuck in hepatocytes → damage → cirrhosis and higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Inherited Liver Diseases | Clinical Medicine Watch from 18:23 to 22:56: α1-antitrypsin deficiency in the lung and liver.

Laminin

  • After type IV collagen, the most abundant protein of basal laminae.
  • Binds type IV collagen and other ECM molecules, adding structural support.
  • A heterotrimer of α, β and γ subunits: 5 α (α1–α5), 3 β (β1–β3), 3 γ (γ1–γ3) → up to 45 combinations (5 × 3 × 3).
  • Typical example: laminin 111 = α1β1γ1.

Proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans

A proteoglycan is a core protein with one or more covalently attached glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains. They sit on the cell surface (signalling) or in the ECM, filling spaces and binding collagen, hyaluronan and other proteoglycans. They give the matrix its swelling and hydration.

Glycosaminoglycans

  • About 95% of a proteoglycan is GAG, so it is more polysaccharide than protein.
  • GAGs are unbranched chains of repeating disaccharides: a uronic acid (glucuronic or iduronic acid) + an amino sugar (N-acetylglucosamine or N-acetylgalactosamine).
  • Joined to a serine of the core protein through a tetrasaccharide linker: xylose–galactose–galactose–glucuronic acid.

Synthesis

  1. The core protein is made on the ER and enters its lumen, where glycosylation starts.
  2. UDP-sugars add sugars, first to the protein, then to the non-reducing end of the growing chain. Glycosylation continues in the Golgi.
  3. Sulfation in the Golgi makes the chains strongly negative.
  4. Negative charge attracts Na⁺, Na⁺ attracts water → a highly hydrated gel.

Degradation

Proteoglycans, glycoproteins and glycolipids are taken in by endocytosis and broken down by lysosomal glycosidases: endoglycosidases cut chains into shorter oligosaccharides; exoglycosidases remove sugars one by one from the non-reducing end.

Mucopolysaccharidoses

When a lysosomal glycosidase is missing, partly broken-down carbohydrates collect in vesicles inside cells (residual bodies). Organs enlarge and stop working properly. These are the mucopolysaccharidoses. The syllabus names two:

Hurler syndrome (MPS I)Hunter syndrome (MPS II)
Missing enzymeα-L-iduronidaseIduronate-2-sulfatase
InheritanceAutosomal recessiveX-linked recessive
Builds upDermatan and heparan sulfateDermatan and heparan sulfate
EyesCorneal cloudingNo corneal clouding
OtherCoarse facial features, skeletal deformity, developmental delay, hepatosplenomegalyMilder; aggressive behaviour
Memory hook

“Hunters need to see clearly to aim at the X”: Hunter has clear corneas and is X-linked.

Integrins and fibronectin

Integrins

  • Transmembrane receptors for cell–cell and cell–ECM adhesion.
  • Two main jobs: attach cells to the ECM and carry signals from the ECM into the cell.
  • Also involved in extravasation, cell migration, and as virus receptors (adenovirus, echovirus, hantavirus). They allow rapid, flexible responses at the cell surface.
  • Two subunits: α decides which ligand binds; β carries signals inside and binds the cytoskeleton.
  • Over 24 integrins are made from 18 α and 8 β subunits.
IntegrinRole
α5β1Binds fibronectin; development and wound healing
VLA-1Immune cell adhesion
αVβ3Angiogenesis

Adhesion proteins: fibronectin

Adhesion proteins in the ECM link integrins to other ECM parts. Fibronectin is the prime example: a large ECM glycoprotein that binds integrins, and also collagen, fibrin and heparan sulfate proteoglycans. It takes part in cell adhesion, growth, migration and differentiation. Losing adhesion can lead to normal or abnormal cell movement.

Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)

  • Calcium-dependent, zinc-containing endopeptidases that can degrade all kinds of ECM proteins.
  • Also cut cell-surface receptors, release apoptotic ligands and inactivate chemokines; involved in proliferation, migration, differentiation, angiogenesis, apoptosis and host defence.
  • Controlled by: gene transcription, proteolytic activation, the plasma protein α2-macroglobulin, and tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs).
  • MMPs and TIMPs must be regulated together; an imbalance contributes to some cancers and atherosclerosis.
  • Metastasis: tumour cells must degrade the ECM (collagen, elastin) to move out of their tissue and into blood or lymph; MMPs do this.

Watch out

Watch out: VLA-1

Slide 24 labels VLA-1 as “αLβ1”. VLA-1 is α1β1 (αL pairs with β2 to form LFA-1). Remember VLA-1 as an immune-cell adhesion integrin.

Watch out: Hurler and Hunter

The syllabus lists Hurler and Hunter, but the slides only define mucopolysaccharidoses in general. The table above follows Lippincott; learn the enzymes and the corneal difference.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Vitamin C is for hydroxylation; copper is for cross-linking (lysyl oxidase).
  • OI hearing loss is conductive; Alport hearing loss is sensorineural.
  • Vascular EDS is type III; classical EDS is type V.
  • AAT deficiency emphysema is panacinar and early; smoker’s emphysema is centriacinar.
  • MMPs need zinc and are calcium-dependent.
  • The α integrin subunit chooses the ligand, not the β.

GCT I · Biochemistry · Week 7

Globular Proteins: Hemoglobin and Myoglobin

How heme proteins bind oxygen, why hemoglobin’s curve is S-shaped and myoglobin’s is not, what shifts the curve, and the hemoglobin diseases: thalassemias, sickle cell, HbC, methemoglobinemia and CO poisoning.

Labobo topic: Biochem Wk 7: Globular Proteins (Hb and Mb)

In 60 seconds

  • Heme = protoporphyrin IX + Fe²⁺. Fe²⁺ has 6 bonds: 4 to porphyrin N, 1 to the proximal histidine, 1 for O₂.
  • Myoglobin: one chain, hyperbolic curve, P50 ≈ 1 mm Hg. Hemoglobin: α₂β₂, sigmoidal (cooperative) curve, P50 ≈ 26 mm Hg.
  • T form = deoxy, low affinity; R form = oxy, high affinity. The last O₂ binds ~300× more tightly than the first.
  • Right shift (release O₂): ↑ H⁺ (Bohr effect), ↑ CO₂, ↑ 2,3-BPG. HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly → higher affinity.
  • CO shifts the curve left; methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) can’t carry O₂ — treat with methylene blue.
  • α genes on chromosome 16 (4 copies in total), β gene on chromosome 11. 3 α genes lost = HbH (β₄); 4 lost = Hb Bart (γ₄), hydrops fetalis.
  • HbS: Glu6→Val in β; HbC: Glu6→Lys. Hydroxyurea raises HbF. HbA1c tracks average glucose over the RBC’s 120 days.

Learning objectives

Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 8th ed., Chapter 3, pages 87–132. By the end you can:

  • describe globular heme proteins and the structure of heme;
  • compare the structure and function of myoglobin and hemoglobin, and the types of hemoglobin;
  • explain the oxygen-dissociation curve, cooperativity, the Bohr effect, 2,3-BPG and CO;
  • describe the hemoglobinopathies and how electrophoresis separates hemoglobins.

Globular heme proteins

A globular protein is water-soluble and folds into a sphere-like shape. Hemeproteins are globular proteins with heme as a tightly bound prosthetic group. The protein’s 3-D structure decides what the heme does.

HemeproteinWhat the heme does
CytochromesIn the mitochondrial electron transport chain, the iron switches rapidly and reversibly between Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, passing electrons along
CatalaseHeme is part of the active site; breaks down hydrogen peroxide
HemoglobinProtein structure sets how Fe²⁺ sits in the heme plane, controlling O₂ binding between lungs and tissues

Hemoglobin and the heme group

  • Found only in red blood cells. Main job: carry O₂ from the lungs to tissue capillaries. It also carries H⁺ and CO₂ from tissues to the lungs.
  • Human HbA is a tetramer: two α-globin + two β-globin chains.
  • Hydrophobic residues are buried inside: they stabilise folding and form a pocket for the hydrophobic heme.

The heme group

  • Heme = protoporphyrin IX + ferrous iron (Fe²⁺).
  • Colour: purple when deoxygenated (venous blood), red when oxygenated (arterial blood).
  • The top of the heme is hydrophilic (charged propionate side chains); the bottom is hydrophobic.
The six bonds of heme iron
BondPartner
1–4The four nitrogens of the porphyrin ring (holds Fe in the centre)
5Proximal histidine of the globin (its imidazole ring); in myoglobin this is His93 (F8)
6Free to bind O₂ reversibly, on the other side of the ring

T and R forms

T (taut) formR (relaxed) form
StateDeoxyhemoglobinOxyhemoglobin
αβ dimersHeld by a network of ionic and hydrogen bonds that limits movementO₂ binding breaks some polar bonds between the dimers, allowing movement
O₂ affinityLowHigh
IronFe²⁺ sits slightly out of the heme plane, pulled by the proximal histidineO₂ binding pulls Fe²⁺ into the plane, dragging the proximal histidine (and the chain) with it

That small movement of the histidine is how binding at one heme is signalled to the other subunits.

Types of hemoglobin

HemoglobinChainsWhen / where
Hb Gower 1ζ₂ε₂ (α-like zeta, β-like epsilon)Early embryo, yolk sac, first month
HbFα₂γ₂Main fetal Hb, about 60% near the end of pregnancy. Production moves from yolk sac to liver at ~5 weeks, later to bone marrow

In the clinic: HbA1c

HbA is slowly and non-enzymatically glycated. In diabetes, red cells meet higher glucose during their 120-day life, so HbA1c rises. HbA1c is used to monitor average blood glucose over the past months.

Myoglobin

  • Found in heart and skeletal muscle; stores O₂ for the muscle.
  • A classic highly α-helical protein: over 70% of it is in eight α-helices, labelled A to H.
  • The helices fold into a compact sphere with a hydrophobic pocket where heme binds non-covalently.
  • The heme crevice is lined with nonpolar amino acids, except two histidines (basic):
    • Proximal histidine (His93, F8): bonds to Fe (5th bond), anchoring the heme.
    • Distal histidine (His64, E7): near, but not bonded to, the O₂-binding site.

Oxygen-binding curves

Both proteins bind O₂ reversibly through ferrous iron (Fe²⁺). If the iron is oxidised to Fe³⁺ (the met form), the protein can no longer carry O₂.

MyoglobinHemoglobin
Chains / O₂ bound1 chain, binds 1 O₂4 chains, binds up to 4 O₂
Curve shapeHyperbolic (simple equilibrium Mb + O₂ ⇌ MbO₂)Sigmoidal (S-shaped) = cooperative binding
P50≈ 1 mm Hg≈ 26 mm Hg
AffinityVery highLower, and changes with conditions
  • P50 = the pO₂ at which half the binding sites are filled. Higher affinity → lower P50.
  • Cooperativity: O₂ binding to one subunit raises the affinity of the others. The first O₂ binds with difficulty; later ones bind easily (steep part of the curve near 20–30 mm Hg).
  • Hb’s affinity for the last O₂ is about 300 times its affinity for the first.
  • Pulse oximetry estimates arterial O₂ saturation (SpO₂) non-invasively by comparing light absorbed by oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin.

Allosteric effectors and the Bohr effect

Hb’s O₂ binding is changed by pO₂, pH, pCO₂ and 2,3-BPG. They are allosteric (“other site”) effectors: binding at one site changes the shape and O₂ binding at other sites.

pO₂

  • Lungs (high pO₂): Hb almost fully saturated, R state, holds O₂.
  • Tissues (low pO₂): Hb shifts to the T state and releases much of its O₂.

The Bohr effect

  • Lower pH (more H⁺) or higher pCO₂ → Hb releases O₂ more easily → lower affinity → curve shifts right. Both stabilise the T form.
  • Why: the T form has a higher affinity for H⁺. Certain histidine side chains have a higher pKa in deoxy-Hb, so when H⁺ rises they become protonated (positive) and form ionic bonds that stabilise deoxy-Hb.
  • Histidine is basic: in acidosis it accepts H⁺; at normal pH it is mostly neutral. This also makes Hb an important blood buffer.
What shifts the Hb curve
Right shift (↓ affinity, more O₂ released)Left shift (↑ affinity, O₂ held)
↑ H⁺ (↓ pH)↓ H⁺ (↑ pH)
↑ pCO₂↓ pCO₂
↑ 2,3-BPG↓ 2,3-BPG (e.g. stored blood)
↑ temperatureHbF, carbon monoxide, methemoglobin
Mnemonic: “CADET, face Right”

CO₂, Acid, DPG (2,3-BPG), Exercise, Temperature: all shift the curve to the right.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Respiratory | Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve Watch from 16:06 to 20:44: the Bohr effect.

2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)

  • Made in red cells from an intermediate of glycolysis.
  • Binds deoxyhemoglobin but not oxyhemoglobin, stabilising the T form → lower O₂ affinity → curve shifts right. This lets Hb release O₂ well at tissue pO₂.
  • 2,3-BPG rises in chronic hypoxia, COPD, emphysema and at high altitude.

Fetal hemoglobin

HbF has γ chains instead of β. The γ chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly because a histidine is replaced by serine. So HbF has a higher O₂ affinity than HbA and pulls O₂ from the mother’s blood across the placenta.

In the clinic: stored blood

2,3-BPG falls during storage, so transfused Hb holds O₂ too tightly and delivers less to tissues. Red cells restore 2,3-BPG in 6–24 hours, which can be dangerous in critically ill patients. A rejuvenation solution regenerates 2,3-BPG and ATP, improving O₂ delivery right after transfusion.

Carbon monoxide (CO)

  • CO binds heme iron very tightly but reversibly, forming carboxyhemoglobin.
  • CO on one or more hemes shifts Hb to the R form, so the remaining hemes hold O₂ more tightly.
  • The curve shifts left: Hb cannot release O₂ to tissues → hypoxia.

Globin genes and thalassemias

Gene familyChromosomeCopies
α-globin162 genes on each chromosome 16 → 4 in total
β-globin111 gene on each chromosome 11 → 2 in total

β-Thalassemia

  • β-chain synthesis is reduced or absent, usually from point mutations that affect production of functional mRNA.
  • Extra α chains cannot form stable tetramers; they precipitate and kill red cell precursors early (ineffective erythropoiesis).
  • HbA2 (α₂δ₂) and HbF (α₂γ₂) increase.
  • β⁺ = reduced β synthesis; β⁰ = none.
  • β-thalassemia major babies look healthy at birth (still have HbF) but become severely anemic in the first or second year.
  • β⁰/β⁰ (Cooley’s anemia): severe anemia → erythroid hyperplasia and extramedullary hematopoiesis (blood made outside the marrow, e.g. liver, spleen).

α-Thalassemia

α genes defectiveConditionFeatures
1 of 4Silent carrierNo signs
2 of 4α-thalassemia traitMild
3 of 4HbH diseaseHbH = β₄; damages red cells → hemolysis
4 of 4Hb Bart diseaseHb Bart = γ₄; hydrops fetalis and fetal death (α chains are needed even for HbF)

  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Beta Thalassemia - Causes and Types Watch from 0:00 to the end: β⁰ and β⁺, thalassemia minor, intermedia and major.

Methemoglobinemia

  • Heme iron is oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺; Fe³⁺ cannot bind O₂ properly.
  • Causes: drugs such as nitrates, benzocaine and some other local anaesthetics; or congenital NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency.
  • “Chocolate cyanosis”: blue skin and mucous membranes with brown blood.
  • Symptoms depend on hypoxia: anxiety, headache, dyspnea; rarely coma and death.
  • Treatment: methylene blue, which is oxidised as it reduces Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺.
Watch: explains the section above

Sickle cell disease, HbC and HbSC

Sickle cell disease (HbS)

  • Autosomal recessive. One nucleotide change in the β-globin gene: glutamate at position 6 → valine.
  • Symptoms start only when enough HbF has been replaced by HbS (infants are protected by HbF, which does not sickle).
  • Red cell lifespan < 20 days (normal 120).
  • HbS gives some protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
  1. Deoxygenation (hypoxemia, dehydration, acidosis) makes HbS polymerise; more 2,3-BPG makes it worse.
  2. Rigid fibres bend the red cell into a sickle.
  3. At first sickling reverses with reoxygenation, but repeated sickling damages the membrane.
  4. Stiff cells are removed by splenic macrophages: extravascular hemolysis.

Clinical features: lifelong painful crises; chronic hemolytic anemia with hyperbilirubinemia; more infections from infancy; acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic and kidney damage; bone changes from marrow hyperplasia, seen on skull X-ray as a “crew-cut” pattern of radiating striations.

Treatment: hydroxyurea raises HbF, which dilutes HbS and reduces symptoms.

HbC and HbSC

  • HbC: also a change at position 6 of β-globin, but glutamate → lysine.
  • Homozygous HbC: mild chronic hemolytic anemia; no infarctive crises; no specific therapy.
  • HbSC: one HbS gene and one HbC gene (compound heterozygote). Hb levels higher than in sickle cell anemia (may be low-normal); fewer and milder crises, though variable.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Sickle Cell Disease “part 2” - Pathophysiology Watch from 1:46 to the end: oxygen cycling, HbS polymerisation and why HbF does not sickle.

Electrophoresis

  • Separates proteins (or DNA) by charge and size. Positive molecules move to the negative pole; negative molecules to the positive pole.
  • Replacing negative glutamate changes charge: valine (neutral) in HbS makes it less negative; lysine (positive) in HbC makes it even less negative.
HbChargeMovement towards + pole
HbAMost negativeFastest
HbSLess negativeSlower
HbCLeast negativeSlowest
Mnemonic: “A Slow Cat”

From fastest to slowest towards the positive pole: A, S, C.

Watch out

Watch out: how many α genes?

Slide 20 says the α cluster “contains two genes”. That is per chromosome 16. Everyone has two chromosome 16s, so four α genes in total, which is why α-thalassemia is counted 1 to 4 genes lost.

Watch out: HbC charge

Slide 27 says HbC “has a positive charge” and may move the opposite way. In the standard alkaline test all three are negative; HbC is just the least negative, so it moves slowest. The order A > S > C is what is examined.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Higher affinity means lower P50.
  • 2,3-BPG binds deoxy-Hb, not oxy-Hb.
  • CO shifts the curve left, not right.
  • HbF has higher O₂ affinity because it binds 2,3-BPG poorly.
  • Sickle hemolysis is mainly extravascular (spleen).
  • HbC homozygotes do not get infarctive crises.
  • Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, not CO poisoning.

Check yourself

  1. The fifth coordination bond of heme iron in hemoglobin is to:

    1. Oxygen
    2. The proximal histidine
    3. The distal histidine
    4. A propionate group
    Show answer

    B. The sixth position binds O₂; the distal histidine lies nearby without bonding Fe.

  2. Why is the hemoglobin O₂ curve sigmoidal?

    1. Hb binds only one O₂
    2. Subunits bind O₂ cooperatively
    3. Hb contains Fe³⁺
    4. Hb is found in muscle
    Show answer

    B. Binding at one subunit raises the affinity of the others.

  3. Which has the lowest P50?

    1. HbA
    2. HbA with high 2,3-BPG
    3. Myoglobin
    4. HbA at low pH
    Show answer

    C. Myoglobin’s P50 is about 1 mm Hg (highest affinity).

  4. Which shifts the Hb curve to the right?

    1. Carbon monoxide
    2. Low 2,3-BPG
    3. Increased H⁺
    4. HbF
    Show answer

    C. The Bohr effect: H⁺ and CO₂ stabilise the T form.

  5. The Bohr effect depends mainly on which residues?

    1. Glycine
    2. Histidine
    3. Proline
    4. Cysteine
    Show answer

    B. Histidines with higher pKa in deoxy-Hb become protonated and form ionic bonds.

  6. HbF has higher O₂ affinity than HbA because:

    1. It has more heme groups
    2. Its γ chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly
    3. It contains Fe³⁺
    4. It has no α chains
    Show answer

    B. A histidine is replaced by serine in γ chains.

  7. Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia because:

    1. It oxidises Fe²⁺
    2. It shifts the curve left so Hb won’t release O₂
    3. It destroys red cells
    4. It blocks 2,3-BPG synthesis
    Show answer

    B. CO pushes Hb into the R form.

  8. A newborn with hydrops fetalis and only γ₄ hemoglobin has:

    1. β-thalassemia major
    2. HbH disease
    3. Hb Bart disease (all four α genes lost)
    4. Sickle cell disease
    Show answer

    C. Without α chains even HbF cannot form.

  9. Which hemoglobins rise in β-thalassemia?

    1. HbA and HbS
    2. HbA2 and HbF
    3. HbH and Hb Bart
    4. HbA1c
    Show answer

    B. α₂δ₂ and α₂γ₂ increase because β is lacking.

  10. Brown blood with cyanosis after benzocaine is best treated with:

    1. Oxygen alone
    2. Methylene blue
    3. Hydroxyurea
    4. Vitamin C only
    Show answer

    B. Methemoglobinemia: methylene blue reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺.

  11. The sickle cell mutation is:

    1. Glu6→Lys in β-globin
    2. Glu6→Val in β-globin
    3. Val6→Glu in α-globin
    4. Deletion of α genes
    Show answer

    B. Glu6→Lys is HbC.

  12. Hydroxyurea helps in sickle cell disease because it:

    1. Raises HbF
    2. Lowers 2,3-BPG
    3. Removes the spleen
    4. Converts HbS to HbA
    Show answer

    A. HbF does not sickle and dilutes HbS.

  13. On electrophoresis towards the positive pole, the order from fastest is:

    1. C, S, A
    2. S, A, C
    3. A, S, C
    4. A, C, S
    Show answer

    C. HbA is the most negative.

gct/genetics/wk01-introduction-mendel:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 1

Introduction to Genetics and Mendel’s First Postulates

The words every later lecture uses (gene, allele, locus, genotype, phenotype…), the human genome in numbers, Mendel’s first three postulates, the sources and types of genetic variation, and sickle-cell anemia as the classic link from DNA to disease.

Labobo topic: MG Wk 1: Mendel & Inheritance Basics

In 60 seconds

  • Genetics = the science of heredity and variation. DNA → gene → RNA/protein → cell function.
  • Human genome: about 3.2 billion bp, 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs (22 autosome pairs + XX or XY), 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes = only 1–2% of DNA.
  • Allele = a version of a gene; locus = its position; genotype = alleles carried; phenotype = observable trait (genotype + environment).
  • Mendel’s postulates: (1) unit factors in pairs, (2) dominance/recessiveness, (3) segregation → monohybrid ratios 1 : 2 : 1 and 3 : 1.
  • Variation comes from mutation, recombination and independent assortment; types are SNPs, indels, STRs, CNVs.
  • Sickle cell: HBB gene, A→T, GAG (Glu) → GTG (Val) → HbS.
  • Germ-line mutations are inherited; somatic mutations are not (but can cause cancer).

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 1. By the end you can:

  • define the key terms of modern genetics;
  • describe the human genome and chromosomes;
  • state Mendel’s first three postulates and predict a monohybrid cross;
  • explain the sources and types of genetic variation;
  • link genotype to phenotype using sickle-cell anemia, and explain why model organisms are used.

Contents

  1. What genetics is
  2. A brief history
  3. Why genetics matters in medicine
  4. Core terminology
  5. The human genome and chromosomes
  6. Mendel’s first three postulates
  7. Genetic variation
  8. Genotype to phenotype: sickle-cell anemia
  9. Model organisms
  10. Numbers to remember

What genetics is

Genetics is the biological science of heredity and variation. It asks how traits pass from parents to offspring and why individuals of the same species differ.

  • It explains how information in DNA determines the structure, function and behaviour of living things: how it is stored, copied, expressed and changed.
  • It links molecules → cells → organisms → populations → health and disease.
  • Hereditary information is organised into genes: DNA sequences that code for proteins or functional RNAs. All of it together is the genome.
  • The cascade DNA → gene → RNA/protein → cell function is the framework for understanding traits, normal physiology and disease.

A brief history

  1. Ancient societies recognised heredity through plant and animal breeding.
  2. Greek philosophers proposed speculative theories (humors, the homunculus).
  3. Gregor Mendel (19th century; 1822–1884, an Augustinian monk, the “father of genetics”): pea-plant experiments showed discrete hereditary units.
  4. Early 20th century: chromosomes identified as the carriers of genes.
  5. 1953: the structure of DNA discovered → genetics becomes a molecular science.

Why genetics matters in medicine

Disease typeCauseExamples
Single-gene disordersA specific DNA change in one geneCystic fibrosis, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, sickle-cell anemia
Complex diseasesMany genes interacting with the environmentDiabetes, cardiovascular disease

Genetics supports diagnosis, risk prediction, screening and counselling, and personalised medicine (choosing a drug and dose by genetic profile). Genome sequencing, genetic testing and gene editing bring new treatments, along with ethical questions.

Core terminology

TermMeaningExample / note
GeneA defined DNA segment that makes a protein or functional RNAProducts are structural, enzymatic or regulatory
AlleleAn alternative sequence version of a geneNormal vs sickle hemoglobin allele
Polymorphic geneA gene with several common alleles in a populationABO blood group gene
LocusThe specific chromosomal position of a geneUsed in gene mapping
GenomeThe complete genetic material of an organismHumans ≈ 3 billion bp
ChromosomeOne continuous DNA double helix packaged with histonesVisible when condensed during cell division
Diploid (2n)Two copies of each autosome + sex chromosomesSomatic cells; divide by mitosis → identical daughter cells
Haploid (n)One set of chromosomesGametes (sperm, egg), made by meiosis; fertilisation restores diploidy
MutationHeritable change in DNA sequence; the source of variationSee germ-line vs somatic below
GenotypeThe combination of alleles at one or more lociPp
PhenotypeThe observable trait, from genotype + environmentPurple flowers; brown eyes
HomozygousIdentical alleles at a locusAA or aa
HeterozygousDifferent alleles at a locusAa
Dominant alleleExpressed even in a single copyAa shows A
Recessive alleleExpressed only when both copies are that alleleaa
Germ-line mutationSomatic mutation
Occurs inGametesBody cells after conception
Inherited?Yes; present in every cell of the offspringNo
Example consequenceInherited diseaseCancer
Dominant does not mean “normal” or “better”

Dominance only describes how two alleles interact in a heterozygote. Many disease alleles are dominant. Clinical outcome depends on the gene’s function, the type of mutation and the biological context.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · Inheritance and Punnett squares Watch from 0:00 to the end: genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant and recessive.

The human genome and chromosomes

  • About 3.2 billion DNA base pairs (one slide rounds to 3 billion).
  • Organised into 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs: 22 pairs of autosomes (same in both sexes) and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male).
  • One chromosome of each pair comes from each parent, so we inherit half our genetic material from the mother and half from the father.
  • About 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes, only 1–2% of the DNA. The rest: regulatory elements, non-coding RNAs, and DNA that organises and stabilises chromosomes.

Chromosomes carry heredity

  • A chromosome is one continuous DNA double helix wrapped around histones.
  • During cell division they condense into rod-like bodies visible under the microscope.
  • Each holds hundreds to thousands of genes, each at a fixed locus.
  • Because we are diploid, every somatic cell carries two copies of each autosomal gene, one from each parent.

Mendel’s first three postulates

PostulateWhat it saysPea example
1. Unit factors in pairsEach trait is controlled by unit factors (genes) that occur in pairs, one from each parent; the two may be the same (homozygous) or different (heterozygous)Flower colour: PP, pp or Pp
2. Dominance/recessivenessWhen two different alleles are present, one (dominant) masks the other (recessive)Tall is dominant over dwarf: tall and heterozygous plants are both tall; only homozygous recessive plants are dwarf
3. SegregationThe two alleles separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets one; fertilisation restores the pairPp makes P and p gametes in equal numbers

Postulate 2 explains why a recessive trait can disappear in one generation and reappear in the next.

The monohybrid cross Pp × Pp

Punnett square
Pp
PPP (purple)Pp (purple)
pPp (purple)pp (white)
  • Genotypic ratio: 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp.
  • Phenotypic ratio: 3 purple : 1 white.

This predictable pattern showed that hereditary units stay discrete across generations rather than blending.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · 1st & 2nd Mendelian Laws Watch from 1:00 to 3:57: Punnett squares and the law of segregation.
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Punnett Squares - Monohybrid Cross, Dihybrid Cross Watch from 2:23 to 5:36: monohybrid crosses and the test cross.

Genetic variation

Genetic variation = differences in DNA sequence between individuals of a species. Humans share more than 99% of their DNA, yet the small differences explain traits (height, eye colour, metabolism), disease risk, and why people respond differently to the same drug.

Sources

SourceHow
MutationPermanent change in DNA; may be neutral, harmful or helpful
RecombinationHomologous chromosomes swap segments in meiosis (crossing-over) → new allele combinations
Independent assortmentEach gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes

Together these make every person genetically unique, except identical twins.

Types

TypeWhat it isNote
SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism)Change in a single baseThe most common variation
Insertions and deletions (indels)Small additions or losses of basesMay affect gene function
STRs (short tandem repeats)Short sequences repeated in a rowHighly variable; used in forensics
CNVs (copy number variations)Large segments duplicated or deletedInfluence traits and disease risk
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Types of Mutations | Changes in the Gene Pool Watch from 0:00 to 6:44: how mutations create variation.

Genotype to phenotype: sickle-cell anemia

  1. Mutation in the HBB gene (β-globin): one base change A → T.
  2. Codon GAG (glutamic acid) becomes GTG (valine).
  3. Abnormal hemoglobin: HbS.
  4. At low oxygen HbS molecules stick together, distorting red cells into a sickle shape.
GenotypePhenotype
HbS/HbS (homozygote)Sickle-cell anemia: fragile cells → chronic anemia; blocked small vessels → severe pain, organ damage, stroke risk
HbA/HbS (heterozygote)Usually healthy (sickle-cell trait); mild symptoms under stress

One DNA change can therefore produce severe clinical disease.

Model organisms

Many discoveries come from non-human species, chosen because they:

  • grow and reproduce quickly;
  • are easy to manipulate in the laboratory;
  • share fundamental genetic processes with humans.

Example: genes involved in human retinitis pigmentosa (a complex retinal disease) are identical to Drosophila genes involved in retinal degeneration, so studying the fly helps explain the human disease. Other common models (from the textbook): E. coli, yeast (Saccharomyces), the worm C. elegans, the mouse and the plant Arabidopsis.

ValueWhat it is
≈ 3.2 billion bpHuman genome size
46 / 23Chromosomes / pairs
22 + 1Autosome pairs + sex chromosome pair
20,000–25,000Protein-coding genes
1–2%Share of DNA that codes for protein
> 99%DNA shared between any two humans
1 : 2 : 1 / 3 : 1Genotypic / phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross
1822–1884Mendel’s life
1953DNA structure discovered
GAG → GTGSickle-cell codon change (Glu → Val)

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
Gene vs alleleThe gene is the unit; alleles are its versions.
Locus vs geneLocus is the address; the gene is what sits there.
Genotype vs phenotypeAlleles carried vs the visible trait (genotype + environment).
Genotypic vs phenotypic ratio1 : 2 : 1 vs 3 : 1 in a monohybrid cross.
Germ-line vs somatic mutationInherited vs not inherited.
Recombination vs independent assortmentSwapping pieces between homologues vs random sorting of whole chromosomes.
STR vs SNPRepeat number varies (forensics) vs one base changes (most common).

Watch out

Watch out: “tall-flower allele”

Slide 10 calls tallness a “tall-flower allele (P)”. Mendel’s tall/dwarf trait is plant height (stem length), a different gene from flower colour (purple/white). The idea being tested, dominance, is the same; don’t mix the two traits in one cross.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Only 1–2% of the genome codes for protein.
  • Phenotype depends on genotype and environment.
  • Somatic mutations are not passed to children.
  • A heterozygote Pp makes P and p gametes in equal numbers (segregation).
  • The most common variation is the SNP; STRs are used in forensics.
  • Sickle cell is Glu → Val (GAG → GTG).

Check yourself

  1. An alternative version of a gene is called:

    1. A locus
    2. An allele
    3. A genome
    4. A chromosome
    Show answer

    B. The locus is the gene’s position.

  2. About what share of human DNA codes for protein?

    1. 1–2%
    2. 25%
    3. 50%
    4. 99%
    Show answer

    A. About 20,000–25,000 genes.

  3. How many pairs of autosomes do humans have?

    1. 21
    2. 22
    3. 23
    4. 46
    Show answer

    B. Plus one pair of sex chromosomes = 23 pairs.

  4. A mutation in a skin cell of an adult:

    1. Is passed to all children
    2. Is somatic and not inherited
    3. Is a germ-line mutation
    4. Cannot cause disease
    Show answer

    B. Somatic mutations can still cause cancer.

  5. Which postulate explains a 1 : 1 ratio of gametes from a heterozygote?

    1. Unit factors in pairs
    2. Dominance
    3. Segregation
    4. Independent assortment
    Show answer

    C. The two alleles separate into different gametes.

  6. Pp × Pp gives which genotypic ratio?

    1. 3 : 1
    2. 1 : 2 : 1
    3. 1 : 1
    4. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
    Show answer

    B. The phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1.

  7. Why can a recessive trait skip a generation?

    1. It is lost by mutation
    2. It is masked in heterozygotes
    3. It is only on the Y chromosome
    4. It blends with the dominant trait
    Show answer

    B. Dominance (postulate 2).

  8. Which type of variation is most common?

    1. CNV
    2. STR
    3. SNP
    4. Large deletion
    Show answer

    C. A single-base difference.

  9. Forensic DNA profiling mainly uses:

    1. SNPs
    2. Short tandem repeats
    3. Coding exons
    4. Mitochondrial genes only
    Show answer

    B. STRs are highly variable between individuals.

  10. Crossing-over during meiosis produces variation by:

    1. Mutation
    2. Recombination between homologues
    3. Doubling the genome

    Show answer

    B. Homologous chromosomes exchange segments.

  11. The sickle-cell mutation changes codon GAG to:

    1. GGG
    2. GTG
    3. AAG
    4. GAA
    Show answer

    B. Glutamic acid → valine in β-globin (HBB).

  12. A person with HbA/HbS is usually:

    1. Severely anemic
    2. Healthy, with mild symptoms under stress
    3. Unable to make hemoglobin

gct/genetics/wk02-dominance-abo:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 2

Incomplete Dominance, Codominance and the ABO System

When alleles don’t follow simple dominance: intermediate heterozygotes (pink flowers, Tay–Sachs carriers), both alleles expressed side by side (MN and ABO blood groups), and how a second gene can hide ABO completely (the Bombay phenotype).

Labobo topic: MG Wk 2: Dominance, Codominance & ABO

In 60 seconds

  • Incomplete dominance: heterozygote is intermediate (red × white → pink), because of gene dosage.
  • Codominance: heterozygote shows both products side by side (MN, AB blood types). Ratio 1 : 2 : 1 for genotype and phenotype.
  • Tay–Sachs: HEXA (chromosome 15q23–q24), Hex A degrades GM2. Carriers have ~50% activity: biochemically intermediate but clinically normal (threshold effect).
  • ABO gene on 9q34; alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ (codominant) and i (null, recessive) = multiple alleles.
  • A antigen = H substance + GalNAc; B antigen = H + galactose; O = H only.
  • Bombay (hh): no FUT1 → no H substance → no A or B; has anti-A, anti-B and anti-H; can receive only Bombay blood. An example of epistasis.

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 4, pages 62–68. By the end you can:

  • define incomplete dominance and contrast it with complete dominance;
  • describe Tay–Sachs disease as biochemical incomplete dominance;
  • define codominance and distinguish it from incomplete dominance;
  • explain the ABO system as codominance and multiple alleles, and the biochemistry of the A and B antigens;
  • explain the Bombay phenotype (FUT1, no H substance) and its transfusion consequences.

Contents

  1. Incomplete dominance
  2. Tay–Sachs disease
  3. Codominance and the MN system
  4. The ABO system
  5. How A and B antigens are made
  6. The Bombay phenotype
  7. Numbers to remember
  8. Commonly confused
  9. Exam traps
  10. Check yourself

Incomplete (partial) dominance

In Mendel’s crosses one allele was fully dominant. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote has a phenotype between the two homozygotes, not like either parent.

Molecular explanation: gene dosage

GenotypeEnzyme for red pigment (anthocyanin)Flower
R¹R¹Two working copies → high pigmentRed
R¹R²One working copy → about half the pigmentPink
R²R²R² is loss-of-function → no pigmentWhite

So the heterozygote’s phenotype is proportional to the amount of working enzyme. Crossing two pink plants gives red : pink : white = 1 : 2 : 1 (phenotype matches genotype).

Tay–Sachs disease: incomplete dominance at the biochemical level

FeatureDetails
InheritanceAutosomal recessive: both alleles must be mutated for disease
GeneHEXA, chromosome 15q23–q24
ProteinThe α-subunit of β-hexosaminidase A (Hex A)
Normal jobHex A degrades GM2 ganglioside in lysosomes, especially in neurons
MutationsFrameshift, nonsense, splice-site or missense: abolish or greatly reduce Hex A

Enzyme activity by genotype

GenotypeHex A activityResult
HEXA⁺/HEXA⁺100%Normal; GM2 degraded
HEXA⁺/HEXA⁻ (carrier)~50%Biochemically intermediate, clinically normal
HEXA⁻/HEXA⁻~0%GM2 builds up in neurons → lysosomal swelling, cell dysfunction
The threshold effect

Many enzyme processes need only part of full activity. For Tay–Sachs the threshold for normal nerve function is below 50%, so carriers have no symptoms. So the disease is recessive clinically but shows incomplete dominance biochemically. In other disorders the threshold may be higher, and carriers may have mild symptoms.

Clinical forms

FormOnsetFeaturesDeath
Infantile (classic, most common)Normal at birth; slowing from 3–6 monthsLoss of motor skills, hypotonia, then spasticity and paralysis; blindness and deafness; cherry-red spot (ganglion cells degenerate, fovea spared); seizures, cognitive declineBy 2–3 years
JuvenileAbout 2–5 yearsSlower progressionBy adolescence
Late-onset / adultAdulthood (rare)Progressive weakness, psychiatric symptoms, variable neurodegenerationMay survive into adulthood
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Tay-Sachs, Fabry, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick Disease Watch from 17:59 to 28:11: Tay–Sachs disease and Hex A.

Codominance and the MN system

In codominance, both alleles of a gene are expressed independently and at the same time in the heterozygote. Both products are made and can be detected. There is no blending.

PatternHeterozygote
Complete dominanceLooks like the dominant homozygote
Incomplete dominanceIntermediate, blended (pink)
CodominanceShows both traits fully, side by side (MN, AB)

The MN blood group

  • Discovered by Karl Landsteiner and Philip Levine; based on two forms of a glycoprotein antigen on red cells.
  • Locus on chromosome 4; two alleles Lᴹ and Lᴺ.
  • MN × MN gives M : MN : N = 1 : 2 : 1 for both genotype and phenotype.
  • Both M and N glycoproteins are detected on MN red cells: an unambiguous example of codominance.

Codominance features: equal, parallel expression of both alleles; each product separately detectable; genotype and phenotype ratios both 1 : 2 : 1.

The ABO system

ABO blood groups are carbohydrate antigens on the red cell surface; they decide transfusion and transplant compatibility.

  • ABO gene on chromosome 9 (9q34), with three main alleles:
    • Iᴬ → A antigen
    • Iᴮ → B antigen
    • i → no antigen (null allele)
  • Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant; each is dominant over i. So ABO shows codominance and multiple alleles.
GenotypeAntigen on RBCBlood typeAntibodies in plasma
IᴬIᴬ or IᴬiAAAnti-B
IᴮIᴮ or IᴮiBBAnti-A
IᴬIᴮA and BABNone
iiNone (H substance only)OAnti-A and anti-B
In the clinic: transfusion

Plasma naturally contains antibodies against any ABO antigen missing from your own red cells. A mismatched transfusion causes agglutination and hemolysis. Example: a type A patient (anti-B) cannot receive B or AB blood. ABO typing is also used in organ transplantation and forensic identification.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · ABO Blood Types Made Easy! Watch from 0:00 to the end: antigens and antibodies of each blood type.
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Blood Types (ABO system) - Blood Groups Watch from 0:29 to the end: the ABO system, antibodies and blood typing.

How A and B antigens are made

A and B antigens are terminal sugars on glycolipids and glycoproteins sticking out of the red cell membrane. They are added to a common precursor, the H substance.

  • H substance: an oligosaccharide chain containing galactose, N-acetylglucosamine and fucose. The fucose is added by a fucosyltransferase encoded by FUT1 (the H gene).
AlleleEnzymeAdds to HResult
IᴬN-acetylgalactosaminyltransferaseGalNAcA antigen
IᴮGalactosyltransferaseGalactoseB antigen
iNone (usually loss-of-function)NothingH stays unmodified → O

In an IᴬIᴮ person both enzymes act independently on the many H sites, so some molecules get GalNAc (A) and others galactose (B): codominance at the molecular level.

Memory hook

A gets the Amino sugar (N-acetylgalactosamine); B gets plain galactose.

The Bombay phenotype

First identified in Mumbai (Bombay) in 1952; an example of epistasis (one gene masking another).

  1. Normal people have at least one working FUT1 (H) allele → H substance made.
  2. People homozygous for non-working FUT1 (hh) make no H substance.
  3. With no H, the Iᴬ and Iᴮ enzymes have no substrate to add sugars to.
  4. No A or B antigens appear, even if the person carries Iᴬ or Iᴮ: they type as O, though their genotype may be IᴬIᴬ, IᴮIᴮ or IᴬIᴮ.
In the clinic
  • Plasma contains anti-A, anti-B and anti-H.
  • They cannot receive any normal blood, even type O, because all normal types carry H antigen.
  • They can receive blood only from another Bombay donor.
  • Frequency: about 1 in 10,000 in India and 1 in a million elsewhere.

ValueWhat it is

~50%Hex A activity in carriers

2–5 yearsJuvenile Tay–Sachs onset
Chromosome 4MN locus
9q34ABO gene
3Main ABO alleles

1 in 10,000 / 1 in a millionBombay frequency in India / elsewhere

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
Incomplete dominance vs codominanceBlended intermediate (pink) vs both shown separately (AB).
Multiple alleles vs polygenicMore than two alleles of one gene (ABO) vs many genes for one trait.
Type O vs BombayO has H antigen and only anti-A/anti-B; Bombay lacks H and also has anti-H.
A vs B transferaseAdds GalNAc vs galactose.
FUT1 vs ABO geneMakes H substance (chromosome 19) vs modifies it (chromosome 9).

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Tay–Sachs is autosomal recessive clinically; “incomplete dominance” refers only to enzyme levels.
  • Type AB has no ABO antibodies; type O has both.
  • A Bombay person can’t receive O blood.
  • Bombay is epistasis, not codominance.
  • Hex A’s gene HEXA codes the α-subunit.
  • In codominance the phenotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1, not 3 : 1.

Check yourself

  1. Red × white snapdragons give pink offspring. This is:

    1. Codominance
    2. Incomplete dominance
    3. Epistasis

    3. GM2 ganglioside

    1. 6 months
    2. 2–3 years
    3. Adolescence
    4. Adulthood
    Show answer

    B. Symptoms begin at 3–6 months.

    1. Only M
    2. Only N
    3. Both M and N
    4. A blended MN antigen
    Show answer

    C. Codominance.

    1. IᴬIᴮ
    2. Iᴬi
    3. ii
    4. Iᴮi
    Show answer

    B. IᴬIᴬ also gives type A.

    2. Anti-A only
    3. Anti-A and anti-B

    2. A
    3. O (Bombay)

    2. Type AB

gct/genetics/wk03-gene-interaction-x-lin:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 3

Gene Interaction, X-Linkage, Penetrance and Imprinting

How two genes shape one trait (epistasis and its modified ratios), how one gene shapes many traits (pleiotropy), X-linked and sex-dependent inheritance, why the same genotype can look different (penetrance, expressivity), and parent-of-origin effects (Prader–Willi and Angelman).

Labobo topic: MG Wk 3: Gene Interaction & X-Linkage

In 60 seconds

  • Mendel’s 4th postulate: independent assortment → dihybrid ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
  • Epistasis ratios: recessive 9 : 3 : 4, dominant 12 : 3 : 1, complementary 9 : 7, duplicate 15 : 1.
  • Pleiotropy: one gene, many traits (Marfan: FBN1 → eye, heart, skeleton).
  • X-linked recessive (colour blindness, hemophilia, DMD): mostly males, no father→son. X-linked dominant (vitamin D-resistant rickets, Rett): affected father → all daughters.
  • Sex-limited = expressed in one sex only (milk, beard). Sex-influenced = dominance differs by sex (pattern baldness).
  • Penetrance = does it show (%); expressivity = how strongly (NF1).
  • Imprinting at 15q11–q13: lose paternal → Prader–Willi; lose maternal (UBE3A) → Angelman.

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 4, pages 70–85. By the end you can:

  • explain gene interaction and how it modifies the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio;
  • describe recessive, dominant, complementary and duplicate epistasis;
  • explain pleiotropy with Marfan syndrome (and PKU);
  • describe X-linked recessive and dominant inheritance;
  • distinguish sex-limited and sex-influenced traits;
  • define penetrance and expressivity;
  • explain genomic imprinting, Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes.

Contents

  1. Independent assortment
  2. Gene interaction
  3. Epistasis and its ratios
  4. Pleiotropy
  5. X-linked inheritance
  6. Sex-limited and sex-influenced traits
  7. Penetrance and expressivity
  8. Genomic imprinting
  9. Prader–Willi and Angelman
  10. Numbers to remember
  11. Commonly confused
  12. Watch out
  13. Exam traps
  14. Check yourself
  15. Key terms

Mendel’s fourth postulate: independent assortment

During gamete formation, allele pairs for different traits sort into gametes independently. In peas, inheriting seed colour (yellow/green) does not affect inheriting seed shape (round/wrinkled).

A dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb therefore gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb), from 16 equal combinations.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · 1st & 2nd Mendelian Laws Watch from 2:59 to 5:05: independent assortment and meiosis.
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Punnett Squares - Monohybrid Cross, Dihybrid Cross Watch from 5:36 to the end: the dihybrid cross and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Gene interaction

Gene interaction: two or more different genes (not alleles of one gene) influence one trait. The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio then often changes, because the genes’ effects depend on each other.

Picture a factory line: each worker (gene) does one step. Gene A makes a colourless substance; gene B turns it into red pigment. If either fails, there is no colour. Both are needed.

Mendel’s laws still hold

With gene interaction the genes still segregate and assort independently. Only the phenotypes are grouped differently, so the 16 parts are shared out in a new way (9 : 7, 12 : 3 : 1…). The total is always 16.

Epistasis and its ratios

Epistasis (Greek epi = upon, stasis = standing/stopping): one gene masks the effect of another gene at a different locus. The masking gene is epistatic; the hidden gene is hypostatic.

TypeWhat hidesRatioExample and logic
Recessive epistasisHomozygous recessive aa9 : 3 : 4Mouse coat: A = makes pigment, a = albino; B = black, b = brown. 9 A_B_ black : 3 A_bb brown : 4 aa__ albino (no pigment for B to colour)
Dominant epistasisA dominant allele A12 : 3 : 1Summer squash: A blocks pigment → white. 12 A___ white : 3 aaB_ yellow : 1 aabb green
Complementary gene actionEither gene homozygous recessive9 : 7Sweet pea: both C and P needed for purple. 9 C_P_ purple : 7 white (C_pp, ccP_, ccpp)
Duplicate dominantEither dominant gene is enough15 : 1A or B both give a triangular flower/fruit; only aabb is ovoid. 15 triangular : 1 ovoid
How to rebuild each ratio from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
  • 9 : 3 : (3 + 1) = 9 : 3 : 4 → recessive
  • (9 + 3) : 3 : 1 = 12 : 3 : 1 → dominant
  • 9 : (3 + 3 + 1) = 9 : 7 → complementary
  • (9 + 3 + 3) : 1 = 15 : 1 → duplicate

Pleiotropy

Pleiotropy: one gene affects two or more different traits. The same protein is used in several organs, so one mutation gives many symptoms.

Gene interactionPleiotropy
Two or more genes → one traitOne gene → several traits
Sweet-pea flower colourMarfan syndrome

Marfan syndrome

  • Gene FBN1 → fibrillin-1, which builds connective tissue throughout the body.
  • Mutation weakens connective tissue everywhere:
    • skeleton: long arms and fingers;
    • eye: lens dislocation;
    • cardiovascular: weak aorta → aneurysm.

The objectives also name PKU (phenylketonuria): one enzyme defect (phenylalanine hydroxylase) causes intellectual disability, light skin and hair, and a musty odour.

X-linked inheritance

Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). A trait whose gene is on the X chromosome is X-linked.

X-linked recessive

  • Females need two mutant copies; males need only one (they have one X, they are hemizygous). So males are affected far more often.
  • Crisscross pattern: an affected man passes the allele to all his daughters (carriers), who pass it to half their sons.
  • Examples: red–green colour blindness, hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Colour blindness (Xᴺ normal, Xᶜ colour-blind)
GenotypeSexPhenotype
XᴺXᴺFemaleNormal
XᴺXᶜFemaleCarrier (normal vision, can pass it on)
XᶜXᶜFemaleColour-blind
XᴺYMaleNormal
XᶜYMaleColour-blind

X-linked dominant

  • Both sexes affected, often more females (two X chromosomes = two chances).
  • Affected father → all daughters affected, no sons (sons get his Y).
  • Affected mother (heterozygous) → 50% of sons and daughters affected.
  • Examples: vitamin D-resistant rickets, Rett syndrome; fragile X shows dominant-like inheritance in some forms.
PatternIn malesIn femalesFather → sonFather → daughter
X-linked recessiveOftenRareNeverAlways (as carrier)
X-linked dominantOftenOftenNeverAll daughters affected
Watch: explains the section above

  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · Genetic inheritance of disease Watch from 15:30 to the end: autosomal dominant and sex-linked disease patterns.

Sex-limited and sex-influenced traits

Some autosomal genes behave differently in males and females because of sex hormones and physiology.

Sex-limitedSex-influenced
MeaningGene in both sexes, trait shown in only one sex (the other lacks the hormonal environment)Trait in both sexes, but dominance differs between sexes: same genotype, different phenotype
ExamplesMilk yield in cows (bulls carry and pass on the genes); beard growth (testosterone; women with excess androgens may show some); tail feathers of roostersPattern baldness: allele B causes hair loss
Pattern baldness
GenotypeMaleFemale
BBBaldBald
BbBald (B dominant in males)Not bald or slightly thin (B recessive in females)
bbNot baldNot bald

Penetrance and expressivity

PenetranceExpressivity
Question“Does it show?” (yes/no)“How much does it show?”
Definition% of people with the genotype who show the phenotype. All = complete (100%); some = incomplete (reduced)The degree or severity of the phenotype among those who show it
ExamplesPolydactyly (dominant P): some Pp people have extra digits, some don’t; 8 of 10 → 80% penetrance. BRCA1: not every carrier gets breast/ovarian cancerNF1: 100% penetrant, but from a few café-au-lait spots to many tumours and bone deformities. Drosophila eyeless: eyes slightly smaller to absent

Both are shaped by other genes and the environment.

Genomic imprinting

  • Expression of a gene depends on which parent it came from.
  • An epigenetic process: one parental allele is expressed, the other silenced, by DNA methylation at CpG islands and histone modification. The DNA sequence does not change.
  • Some genes are expressed only from the father, others only from the mother.
  • Set during gametogenesis (before fertilisation), then maintained through mitosis after conception.
  • Imprinted genes: one allele expressed. Non-imprinted genes: both expressed.

Why it matters

  • Growth and development: fetal growth, placenta, brain development.
  • Disease: Prader–Willi, Angelman, Beckwith–Wiedemann, Silver–Russell.
  • Cancer: loss of imprinting (LOI) in Wilms tumour and colorectal cancer.
  • It shows how epigenetics links inheritance, environment and disease.

Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes

Both involve chromosome 15q11–q13, the most studied imprinted region.

Prader–Willi (PWS)Angelman (AS)
What is lostPaternal 15q11–q13 expressionMaternal 15q11–q13 expression: UBE3A
Causes70–75% paternal deletion (mostly sporadic); 20–25% maternal uniparental disomy; < 5% imprinting defectMostly maternal deletions; only about 3–5% uniparental disomy (paternal)
FeaturesNeonatal hypotonia, poor suck, feeding problems, delayed milestones; hyperphagia and obesity from early childhood; mild intellectual disability; hypogonadism, delayed pubertySevere intellectual disability; ataxia, seizures; frequent laughter (“happy puppet”)
Memory hook

Prader–Willi = Paternal missing. Angelman = mAternal missing (“Angel” is mum’s little angel).

Numbers to remember

ValueWhat it is
9 : 3 : 3 : 1Dihybrid cross
9 : 3 : 4Recessive epistasis
12 : 3 : 1Dominant epistasis
9 : 7Complementary genes
15 : 1Duplicate dominant genes
80%Penetrance if 8 of 10 carriers show the trait
15q11–q13Prader–Willi / Angelman region
70–75% / 20–25% / < 5%PWS: deletion / maternal UPD / imprinting defect
3–5%Angelman from uniparental disomy

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
Epistasis vs dominanceEpistasis: between different genes. Dominance: between alleles of one gene.
Epistatic vs hypostaticThe masking gene vs the masked gene.
Gene interaction vs pleiotropyMany genes → one trait vs one gene → many traits.
Sex-linked vs sex-limited vs sex-influencedGene on X vs autosomal, shown in one sex vs autosomal, dominance differs by sex.
Penetrance vs expressivityWhether vs how strongly.
PWS vs ASPaternal loss, obesity, mild ID vs maternal loss (UBE3A), seizures, severe ID, laughter.

Watch out

Watch out: uniparental disomy in Angelman

Slide 27 says “paternal disomy much less common than maternal”. In Angelman, the disomy that causes disease is paternal (two paternal copies, no maternal UBE3A); in Prader–Willi it is maternal. Uniparental disomy is a minor cause in Angelman (3–5%) but a major one in Prader–Willi (20–25%). Learn the rule: the missing parent’s copy causes the syndrome.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Epistasis does not break Mendel’s laws; it only changes phenotype ratios.
  • X-linked inheritance never goes father → son.
  • An affected father with an X-linked dominant trait has all daughters affected.
  • Pattern baldness is autosomal (sex-influenced), not X-linked.
  • NF1 shows variable expressivity with 100% penetrance.
  • Imprinting changes methylation, not the DNA sequence.

Check yourself

  1. AaBb × AaBb in mice gives 9 black : 3 brown : 4 albino. This is:

    1. Dominant epistasis
    2. Recessive epistasis
    3. Complementary genes
    4. Duplicate genes
    Show answer

    B. aa blocks pigment whatever B is.

  2. The ratio 12 : 3 : 1 indicates:

    1. Recessive epistasis
    2. Dominant epistasis
    3. Complementary genes
    4. Codominance
    Show answer

    B. Summer squash colour.

  3. Two white sweet-pea lines give purple F1; F2 is 9 purple : 7 white. The genes show:

    1. Complementary gene action
    2. Dominant epistasis
    3. Pleiotropy
    4. Duplicate dominance
    Show answer

    A. Both C and P are needed.

  4. Marfan syndrome affecting the eye, aorta and skeleton is an example of:

    1. Epistasis
    2. Pleiotropy
    3. Incomplete penetrance

    Show answer

    B. One gene (FBN1), many traits.

  5. A colour-blind man and a homozygous normal woman have children. Their daughters will be:

    1. All colour-blind
    2. All carriers
    3. Half carriers
    4. All normal non-carriers
    Show answer

    B. Each daughter gets his X; sons get his Y and are normal.

  6. An affected father with vitamin D-resistant rickets will have:

    1. All sons affected
    2. All daughters affected, no sons
    3. 50% of all children affected
    4. No affected children
    Show answer

    B. X-linked dominant.

  7. A Bb man is bald but a Bb woman is not. This is:

    1. Sex-limited
    2. Sex-influenced
    3. X-linked
    4. Imprinting
    Show answer

    B. Dominance differs between sexes.

  8. Milk yield genes carried by bulls but expressed only in cows show:

    1. Sex-limited inheritance
    2. Sex-influenced inheritance
    3. Y-linkage
    4. Pleiotropy
    Show answer

    A. The trait appears in only one sex.

  9. Only 7 of 10 people with a dominant allele show the trait. The penetrance is:

    1. 30%
    2. 70%
    3. 100%
    4. Variable expressivity
    Show answer

    B. Incomplete penetrance.

  10. NF1 patients range from a few café-au-lait spots to many tumours. This is:

    1. Incomplete penetrance
    2. Variable expressivity
    3. Epistasis
    4. Anticipation
    Show answer

    B. All show it, with different severity.

  11. Genomic imprinting is mainly caused by:

    1. Point mutations
    2. DNA methylation at CpG islands
    3. Crossing-over
    4. Nondisjunction
    Show answer

    B. An epigenetic mark set in gametogenesis.

  12. A child with neonatal hypotonia, later hyperphagia, obesity and hypogonadism most likely lacks:

    2. Paternal 15q11–q13
    3. UBE3A only
    4. An X chromosome
    Show answer

    B. Prader–Willi syndrome.

Independent assortment
Alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently.
Dihybrid cross
Cross following two genes.
Gene interaction
Several genes affecting one trait.
Epistasis
One gene masking another gene’s effect.

Masking / masked gene.
Pleiotropy

gct/genetics/wk04-chromosome-mapping:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 4

Chromosome Mapping and Linkage

How geneticists find where genes sit on a chromosome without looking at it: crossing over, map units, the three-point test cross, DNA markers and genome databases, plus sister chromatid exchange and Bloom syndrome.

Labobo topic: MG Wk 4: Chromosome Mapping & Linkage

In 60 seconds

  • Genes on the same chromosome are linked: they tend to be inherited together.
  • Crossing over in prophase I makes recombinant gametes; the farther apart two genes, the more often it happens.
  • 1 map unit (m.u.) = 1 centiMorgan (cM) = 1% recombination.
  • Three-point test cross: the gene that switches between the parental and double-crossover classes is the middle gene.
  • DNA markers: RFLPs, STRs (microsatellites), SNPs; databases: NCBI, Ensembl, UCSC (and OMIM).
  • Sister chromatid exchange (S/G2, seen with BrdU) changes no information; very high SCE = Bloom syndrome (BLM helicase, chromosome 15).

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 5. By the end you can:

  • explain chromosome mapping and why crossing over measures gene distance;
  • work out gene order from recombination data;
  • describe DNA markers and genome databases;
  • explain sister chromatid exchanges and their significance.

Contents

  1. Linked genes and mapping
  2. Crossing over and map units
  3. Gene order: the three-point test cross
  4. DNA markers and databases
  5. Sister chromatid exchange and Bloom syndrome
  6. Numbers to remember
  7. Commonly confused
  8. Exam traps
  9. Check yourself
  10. Key terms

Linked genes and mapping

  • A chromosome is like a long necklace with genes as beads in a line. Some are close together, some far apart.
  • Genes on the same chromosome are linked: they tend to be inherited together, so they do not assort independently.
  • Chromosome mapping = finding where genes are on a chromosome and how far apart they are.
  • It is done not with a microscope, but by measuring how often genes are separated during meiosis.

Crossing over and map units

  1. In prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair up.
  2. They can swap segments of DNA: crossing over.
  3. Gametes with new combinations of alleles are recombinant; those with the original combinations are parental (non-recombinant).
Genes areCrossing over between themInherited
Very closeRareUsually together
Far apartFrequentOften separated

So the frequency of recombination measures distance, in map units (m.u.) or centiMorgans (cM): 1 m.u. = 1 cM = 1% recombinant gametes.

Worked example

  • 10% of gametes are recombinant for genes A and B → A and B are 10 cM apart.
  • B and C show 20% recombination → 20 cM apart, farther than A and B.

From the textbook: recombination between two genes can never exceed 50%; genes that far apart (or on different chromosomes) behave as if unlinked.

Recombination frequency formula

RF (%) = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring × 100. The answer in % is the distance in cM.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Sex-linked Crosses and Gene maps Watch from 4:12 to 9:01: linked genes, crossing over and chromosome mapping.

Gene order: the three-point test cross

To find the order of three genes (A, B, C), geneticists use a three-point test cross: a triple heterozygote crossed with a triple homozygous recessive, so each offspring’s phenotype shows exactly which alleles came from the heterozygous parent.

  1. Sort the 8 offspring classes into 4 pairs of reciprocal types.
  2. The most frequent pair = parental (non-crossover).
  3. The least frequent pair = double crossovers.
  4. Compare parental and double-crossover types: the gene whose allele has switched is the middle gene.
  5. Distance between each pair = (single crossovers in that region + double crossovers) ÷ total × 100.

Example

Parental types: A B C and a b c. Double crossovers: A b C and a B c. Only B has swapped relative to its neighbours → B is in the middle: order A–B–C.

The slide links a video (watch on YouTube, slide 9) that walks through a full three-point cross.

DNA markers and genome databases

In the past, mapping relied on visible traits (eye colour, body colour). Today DNA itself is used.

  • A DNA marker is a known, short DNA sequence that varies between people: a “signpost” in the genome. It usually doesn’t cause a trait; it shows where you are.
MarkerWhat it is
RFLPRestriction fragment length polymorphism: different fragment sizes when DNA is cut by a restriction enzyme
STR / microsatelliteShort repeated sequences; repeat number varies
SNPOne base differs (e.g. A → G)

Compare markers in people with and without a disease: a marker that is always inherited with the disease lies near the disease gene. This is how the genes for cystic fibrosis and Huntington disease were found.

Annotated computer databases

  • Examples: NCBI Genome Data Viewer, Ensembl, UCSC Genome Browser (and OMIM for diseases).
  • They show a gene’s exact position (in base pairs), its function, known variants, and links to diseases and studies.
  • Used to locate genes, compare species and study how variants cause disease.

Sister chromatid exchange and Bloom syndrome

  • Before mitosis each chromosome is copied into two identical sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.
  • Sister chromatids can still swap pieces: sister chromatid exchange (SCE).
  • SCEs happen in S and G2 phase (during copying or repair) and are seen in mitosis, especially metaphase.
  • Detected by staining the two chromatids differently with BrdU (bromodeoxyuridine) (“harlequin” chromosomes).

Why SCEs matter

  • Sister chromatids are identical, so SCEs don’t change genetic information.
  • But they show how busy DNA repair is. Many SCEs suggest unstable DNA or faulty repair.
In the clinic: Bloom syndrome

Mutation in the BLM gene on chromosome 15, which encodes a DNA helicase (best known for its role in DNA replication). Cells show very high SCE rates → chromosomal instability → higher cancer risk and developmental problems.

Numbers to remember

ValueWhat it is
1% = 1 cM = 1 m.u.Recombination and map distance
50%Maximum recombination (unlinked behaviour)
8 classesOffspring types in a three-point test cross
Chromosome 15BLM gene (Bloom syndrome)
S, G2Phases when SCEs occur

Commonly confused

TheseThe difference
Crossing over vs SCEBetween homologous chromosomes in meiosis (new combinations) vs between sister chromatids in mitosis (no new information).
Parental vs recombinantOriginal allele combinations vs new combinations.
Most vs least frequent classesParental vs double crossovers.
Linked vs unlinked genesSame chromosome, close (RF < 50%) vs different chromosomes or far apart (RF = 50%).
Marker vs disease geneA signpost near the gene vs the gene that causes the disease.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Crossing over happens in prophase I of meiosis.
  • The middle gene is found by comparing parental with double-crossover classes.
  • SCEs do not create new allele combinations.
  • BLM encodes a helicase.
  • A marker linked to a disease need not cause the disease.

Check yourself

    1. Alleles
    2. Linked genes
    3. Epistatic genes
    4. Imprinted genes
    Show answer

    B. Crossing over can separate them.

  2. Crossing over occurs during:

    2. Prophase I of meiosis
    3. Anaphase II
    4. S phase only
    Show answer

    B. When homologues pair.

  3. 15 of 100 offspring are recombinant for genes D and E. The map distance is:

    1. 1.5 cM
    2. 15 cM
    3. 85 cM
    4. 150 cM
    Show answer

    B. 15% recombination = 15 cM.

  4. In a three-point test cross, the least frequent offspring classes are:

    1. Parental types
    2. Single crossovers
    3. Double crossovers
    4. Non-recombinants
    Show answer

    C. They need two crossovers at once.

  5. Parental types are A B C / a b c; double crossovers are A b C / a B c. Which gene is in the middle?

    1. A
    2. B
    3. C
    4. Cannot tell
    Show answer

    B. B is the allele that switched.

  6. Which is a DNA marker based on short repeated sequences?

    1. SNP
    2. RFLP
    3. Microsatellite (STR)
    4. Exon
    Show answer

    C. SNPs are single-base changes.

  7. A marker is always inherited with a disease in families. This means:

    1. The marker causes the disease
    2. The disease gene lies near the marker
    3. The marker is on another chromosome
    4. The disease is imprinted
    Show answer

    B. This is how CF and Huntington genes were found.

  8. Sister chromatid exchanges are made visible with:

    1. Giemsa banding only
    2. BrdU differential staining

gct/genetics/wk05-sex-determination:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 5

Sex Determination and Differentiation in Humans

How the father’s sperm decides genetic sex, what the X and Y chromosomes carry, how SRY switches on the testis pathway, how hormones then build male or female anatomy, the Y genes needed for sperm (AZF), and the three human sex ratios.

Labobo topic: MG Wk 5: Sex Determination

In 60 seconds

  • Sex determination = the genetic decision at fertilisation; sex differentiation = the anatomy that follows.
  • Every egg carries X; sperm carry X or Y → the father decides sex. Primary sex ratio ≈ 1 : 1.
  • X: large, > 1000 genes. Y: small, < 200 genes. PAR1/PAR2 let X and Y pair; MSY (~95% of Y) doesn’t recombine.
  • SRY (Yp11.3, HMG transcription factor) at ~6 weeks activates SOX9 → Sertoli cells → testis. SRY is necessary and sufficient.
  • Sertoli → AMH (Müllerian ducts regress). Leydig → testosterone (Wolffian ducts). 5α-reductase → DHT (penis, scrotum, prostate).
  • No SRY → ovaries; Müllerian ducts persist; Wolffian ducts regress: the default pathway.
  • AZF regions on Yq: a (Sertoli-cell-only), b (maturation arrest), c (DAZ; oligo- to azoospermia). Secondary sex ratio ≈ 105 : 100.

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 7, pages 151–159. By the end you can:

  • explain the chromosomal basis of sex and the father’s role;
  • describe the X and Y chromosomes, PARs and the MSY;
  • explain SRY, SOX9 and testis formation;
  • describe male and female differentiation (SRY, AMH, testosterone, DHT);
  • explain AZF genes and male infertility;
  • compare primary, secondary and tertiary sex ratios.

Contents

  1. Determination vs differentiation
  2. Chromosomal basis of sex
  3. The X and Y chromosomes
  4. The indifferent stage
  5. SRY and testis formation
  6. Male differentiation
  7. Female differentiation
  8. Y genes and spermatogenesis
  9. Sex ratios
  10. Numbers to remember
  11. Commonly confused
  12. Exam traps
  13. Check yourself
  14. Key terms

Sex determination vs sexual differentiation

Sex determinationSexual differentiation
WhatThe genetic mechanism deciding male or femaleThe physical development of gonads and genitals
WhenAt fertilisation (chromosomal decision)Afterwards (from about week 6)

Chromosomal basis of sex

  • 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes. Female XX, male XY.
  • Meiosis makes haploid gametes with 23 chromosomes:
    • every egg carries one X;
    • sperm are of two types: half carry X, half carry Y.
  • X sperm + egg → XX (female). Y sperm + egg → XY (male).
  • So the father determines the child’s sex. Equal numbers of X and Y sperm give a primary sex ratio of about 1 : 1.

The X and Y chromosomes

X chromosomeY chromosome
SizeLarge, gene-richSmall, gene-poor
Genes> 1000; mostly metabolism, growth, nerve development (not sex determination)< 200 functional; many for male development and reproduction
  • Pseudoautosomal regions (PAR1 and PAR2): small matching regions at the tips of X and Y. They let X and Y pair and recombine in meiosis and behave like autosomal genes; essential for correct segregation.
  • Male-specific region of the Y (MSY): between the PARs, about 95% of Y. It does not recombine with X and passes almost unchanged from father to son. It carries testis-formation and spermatogenesis genes.
Three sequence classes in the MSY
ClassWhat it is
X-transposedRecent copies of genes from the X
X-degenerateDecayed remains of the ancestral autosome that became the Y
AmpliconicLarge palindromes with multiple copies of testis-specific genes expressed only in the male germ line

The indifferent stage

Genetic sex is fixed at fertilisation, but for the first weeks XX and XY embryos look identical. The reproductive system is bipotential; genes, hormones and receptors begin acting around week 6.

At about 4–5 weeks, every embryo has:

  • Gonadal ridges: bulges on the mesonephros (primitive kidney) that become testes or ovaries.
  • Two pairs of ducts: Wolffian (mesonephric) and Müllerian (paramesonephric).
  • External genitalia: the genital tubercle, urogenital folds and labioscrotal swellings.

SRY and testis formation

  • SRY (sex-determining region of the Y) is on the short arm of Y, Yp11.3: the master switch for testis formation.
  • SRY protein is an HMG (high-mobility-group) transcription factor: it binds and bends DNA, changing chromatin to switch on downstream genes, especially SOX9.
  • SOX9 drives Sertoli cell differentiation and testis cord formation, and keeps itself on by positive feedback, so the male pathway continues after SRY switches off. It also suppresses the ovarian pathway.
  • SRY acts briefly, around week 6 (6–7), but decisively.
  • No working SRY → the bipotential gonad becomes an ovary, even with a Y present.
Evidence that SRY is necessary and sufficient
KaryotypeSRYPhenotype
46,XYDeleted or mutatedFemale
46,XXTranslocated onto an XMale

Male differentiation

CellMakesEffect
Sertoli cellsAnti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) = Müllerian inhibiting substance (MIS)Müllerian ducts degenerate: no uterus or fallopian tubes
Leydig cells (between testis cords)TestosteroneWolffian ducts grow into the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles
Genital skin, urogenital sinusDHT (dihydrotestosterone), made from testosterone by 5α-reductase; stronger than testosteronePenis, scrotum, prostate
  1. SRY → testis
  2. Sertoli (AMH) and Leydig (testosterone)
  3. DHT → external virilisation; organs well defined by about 12 weeks

Male differentiation is an active process that needs each hormonal step.

In the clinic (textbook)

5α-reductase deficiency: XY with testes and male internal ducts, but female-looking or ambiguous external genitalia at birth (no DHT). Androgen insensitivity: XY with testes and AMH (no uterus), but no response to testosterone → female external appearance.

Female differentiation

  • XX: no Y, no SRY → gonads become ovaries; supporting cells → granulosa cells, interstitial cells → theca cells.
  • No Sertoli cells → no AMH → Müllerian ducts stay and form the fallopian tubes, uterus and upper vagina.
  • No testosterone → Wolffian ducts regress.
  • No DHT → external genitalia take the female form.
Same starting structures, different outcomes
Indifferent structureMale (with DHT)Female
Genital tuberclePenis (glans)Clitoris
Urogenital foldsShaft of penis (penile urethra)Labia minora
Labioscrotal swellingsScrotumLabia majora
Wolffian ductsEpididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesiclesRegress
Müllerian ductsRegress (AMH)Fallopian tubes, uterus, upper vagina

Because female development happens when male signals are absent, it is called the default pathway.

Y genes and spermatogenesis

Beyond SRY, the long arm (Yq) carries the azoospermia factor (AZF) regions needed for sperm production. Deletions here are a major genetic cause of male infertility.

RegionGenesDeletion causes
AZFaUSP9Y, DDX3Y (germ-cell survival)Sertoli-cell-only syndrome (no germ cells)
AZFb—Maturation arrest at the spermatocyte stage
AZFcDAZ (deleted in azoospermia) family: RNA-binding proteins for germ-cell maturationVariable: oligospermia to complete azoospermia
  • Other testis-expressed Y genes: RBMY, PRY, HSFY, TSPY (spermatid differentiation and meiosis).
  • Many lie in multiple copies inside large palindromes, which allow limited recombination within the Y to correct mutations.
  • The same repeats make the Y unstable, prone to microdeletions that impair fertility.

Sex ratios

RatioWhenValueWhy
PrimaryAt fertilisationAbout 1 : 1Half the sperm carry X, half Y; IVF embryos confirm equal XX and XY zygotes
SecondaryAt birthAbout 105 males : 100 females (1.05 : 1)Female embryos are lost slightly more often in the earliest weeks; males are more fragile later but still slightly ahead at birth. Very stable worldwide and over time
TertiaryIn adultsBecomes balanced, then women outnumber men in old ageMales have higher mortality at almost every age: birth complications, accidents, cardiovascular and lifestyle disease. Women are the majority over 60

Commonly confused

Sertoli vs LeydigAMH (removes Müllerian ducts) vs testosterone (keeps Wolffian ducts).
Testosterone vs DHTInternal male ducts vs external genitalia and prostate.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • The father, not the mother, decides the baby’s sex.
  • SRY is on the short arm (Yp); AZF regions are on the long arm (Yq).
  • 46,XX with SRY → male; 46,XY without SRY → female.
  • AMH comes from Sertoli cells, not Leydig.
  • The secondary sex ratio favours males slightly; older adults are mostly female.
