gct/genetics/wk06-x-inactivation:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 6

Dosage Compensation, X-Inactivation and Barr Bodies

Why females switch off one X chromosome in every cell, how to count Barr bodies, why some genes escape and still matter in Turner and Klinefelter syndromes, the Lyon hypothesis and mosaicism, and the molecular switch (XIST, TSIX, XITE).

Labobo topic: MG Wk 6: X-Inactivation & Barr Bodies

In 60 seconds

  • Dosage compensation: one X is inactivated in every female somatic cell so both sexes express one active X.
  • Happens around the blastocyst stage; choice is random but then permanent in all daughter cells (Lyon, 1961).
  • Barr bodies = number of X chromosomes − 1 (XX → 1, XY → 0, 45,X → 0, XXY → 1, XXX → 2).
  • Barr body = condensed heterochromatin (histone deacetylation, promoter DNA methylation) at the nuclear membrane; found by Barr and Bertram, 1949.
  • About 15% of X genes escape inactivation and 10% vary → explains symptoms in Turner, Klinefelter and triple X.
  • Females are mosaics: calico/tortoiseshell cats, patchy colour vision in carriers.
  • XIST lncRNA coats the X to be silenced (recruits PRC1/PRC2); TSIX (antisense) blocks XIST on the active X; XITE boosts TSIX.

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 7, pages 159–163. By the end you can:

  • explain dosage compensation and X-chromosome inactivation;
  • count Barr bodies in normal and abnormal karyotypes;
  • explain genes that escape inactivation and their clinical meaning;
  • state the Lyon hypothesis and give examples of mosaicism;
  • describe the X-inactivation centre and the roles of XIST, TSIX and XITE.

Contents

  1. Dosage compensation
  2. Barr bodies
  3. Counting Barr bodies
  4. Genes that escape inactivation
  5. The Lyon hypothesis and mosaicism
  6. The X-inactivation centre: XIST, TSIX, XITE
  7. Numbers to remember
  8. Commonly confused
  9. Watch out
  10. Exam traps
  11. Check yourself
  12. Key terms

Dosage compensation

  • The X carries hundreds of essential genes unrelated to sex (metabolism, development, cell function), needed in both sexes.
  • If both Xs worked in females, every X gene would be expressed at double dose compared with males, upsetting the balance with autosomes and causing developmental problems.
  • Dosage compensation equalises X gene products: one X is inactivated in every female somatic cell.
  • This X-chromosome inactivation (XCI), also called Lyonization, happens early, around the blastocyst stage. The inactive X condenses into the Barr body.

Barr bodies

  • Discovered in 1949 by Canadian researchers Murray L. Barr and Ewart G. Bertram: a small dark body at the edge of the nucleus in nerve cells of female cats, not males.
  • Later found in many female tissues, including human buccal (cheek) epithelial cells. Also called the sex chromatin body.
  • A Barr body is an inactivated X: highly condensed, transcriptionally silent, usually pressed against the inner nuclear membrane.

How it is kept silent

  • Histone deacetylation → chromatin compacts.
  • DNA methylation of promoters → transcription is permanently suppressed.

The Barr body is the visible evidence of dosage compensation; it is facultative heterochromatin (heterochromatin that is silent in one cell type or chromosome copy but not the other).

Counting Barr bodies

Number of Barr bodies = total number of X chromosomes − 1. Only one X per cell stays active, whatever the karyotype.

KaryotypeConditionBarr bodies
46,XXNormal female1
46,XYNormal male0
45,XTurner syndrome0
47,XXYKlinefelter syndrome1
47,XXXTriple X2

Counting Barr bodies helps in cytogenetic sex determination and in diagnosing sex chromosome abnormalities.

Genes that escape inactivation

  • Not every gene on the inactive X is switched off: about 15% stay active and about 10% show variable inactivation.
  • Most escape genes are in the pseudoautosomal regions (PARs) at the tips of the X.

This explains why an abnormal number of X chromosomes still causes symptoms even though extra Xs are inactivated:

ConditionWhy symptoms appear
Turner (45,X)Missing active copies of escape genes → growth and ovarian defects
Klinefelter (47,XXY), triple X (47,XXX)Extra active copies of escape genes → mild cognitive or physical abnormalities

The Lyon hypothesis and mosaicism

Proposed in 1961 by British geneticist Mary F. Lyon, from mouse coat patterns and human X-linked traits:

  1. One X is inactivated early in development (around the blastocyst stage).
  2. Which X (maternal or paternal) is chosen at random in each cell.
  3. Once chosen, the same X stays inactive in all descendant cells (a clonal pattern).

So every female is a mosaic: some cells express the maternal X, others the paternal X.

Evidence

  • Mouse coat colour: a heterozygous female XᴮXᴼ (black/orange alleles on X). Cells that silence Xᴮ show orange; cells that silence Xᴼ show black. Clones of cells form patches → a variegated, mottled coat, as in calico and tortoiseshell cats.
  • Males have one X, so only one colour: no patches.
  • Humans: women heterozygous for red–green colour blindness have retinal cells with the normal allele and others with the mutant allele. Vision seems normal, but careful testing shows a patchwork of colour perception.
In the clinic

Because inactivation is random, a female carrier of an X-linked disease (e.g. hemophilia) may occasionally show symptoms if, by chance, most of her cells silenced the normal X (“skewed” inactivation).

The X-inactivation centre: XIST, TSIX, XITE

Each X has an X-inactivation centre (Xic), a region with regulatory genes and non-coding RNAs (no proteins). It works like a switchboard: it counts the X chromosomes and makes sure only one stays active, inactivating all others (as in normal females or Klinefelter males).

ElementWhat it isRole
XIST (X-inactive specific transcript)Long non-coding RNA (not translated)Expressed only from the X to be silenced; spreads along that same chromosome (in cis) like a blanket; recruits Polycomb complexes PRC1 and PRC2, which modify histones, condense chromatin and silence almost all its genes
TSIXGene transcribed in the opposite (antisense) direction to XISTNegative regulator of XIST: its RNA binds the XIST locus and blocks it, so the X expressing TSIX stays active
XITE (X-inactivation intergenic transcription elements)Regulatory DNA near XIST and TSIXEnhances TSIX, stabilising the choice of the active X
Tug of war

The X that wins XIST expression is inactivated; the X that keeps TSIX stays active. TSIX is XIST spelled backwards, because it is read backwards.

Numbers to remember

ValueWhat it is

1961Lyon hypothesis
X − 1Number of Barr bodies

BlastocystStage of inactivation

Turner vs Klinefelter Barr bodies45,X → 0; 47,XXY → 1.

Watch out

Watch out: where is the Xic?

Slide 10 places the X-inactivation centre on the short arm “close to the centromere”. The human Xic (with XIST) is on the long arm, Xq13, near the centromere. If asked, choose Xq13.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • A Klinefelter male has a Barr body.
  • Inactivation is random, not always the paternal X.
  • XIST RNA acts in cis (on its own chromosome).
  • XIST is not translated; it works as RNA.
  • Escape genes explain why X aneuploidies still cause symptoms.

  2. How many Barr bodies does a 47,XXY cell have?

  3. How many Barr bodies does a 45,X cell have?

    3. 2

    A. There is only one X.

  4. Which modification helps keep the Barr body silent?

  5. Why do women with 47,XXX have mild abnormalities despite inactivating two Xs?

  6. The Lyon hypothesis states that X inactivation is:

    2. Random, then clonally maintained

  7. Tortoiseshell coat colour is seen almost only in female cats because:

  8. XIST RNA silences the X chromosome by:

    2. Coating the chromosome in cis and recruiting Polycomb complexes
    3. Degrading mRNA from the other X

  9. The X that expresses TSIX will:

    2. Remain active
    3. Be lost

  10. XITE acts by:

    2. Enhancing XIST
    3. Coding a protein
    4. Methylating DNA

gct/genetics/wk07-sex-chromosome-aneuplo:
GCT I · Medical Genetics · Week 7

Nondisjunction and Sex Chromosome Aneuploidies

What goes wrong when chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis, and the four main results for the sex chromosomes: Klinefelter (47,XXY), Turner (45,X), triple X (47,XXX) and 47,XYY, plus how FISH confirms them.

Labobo topic: MG Wk 7: Sex Chromosome Aneuploidies

In 60 seconds

  • Nondisjunction = homologues (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) fail to separate → trisomy (2n+1) or monosomy (2n−1).
  • Risk rises with maternal age (weak cohesin, poorer spindle checkpoint in long-arrested oocytes).
  • Klinefelter 47,XXY: ~1 in 650 males; commonest cause of primary testicular failure; tall (extra SHOX), low testosterone, infertile.
  • Turner 45,X: ~1 in 2000 females; mostly paternal nondisjunction; only ~1% of 45,X conceptuses survive; short (SHOX loss), streak gonads, webbed neck, coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve.
  • Triple X 47,XXX: ~1 in 1000 females; usually mild; 2 Barr bodies.
  • 47,XYY: ~1 in 1000 males; paternal meiosis II; tall, usually normal; no link to criminality.
  • Diagnosis: karyotype, confirmed by FISH.

Learning objectives

Course textbook, Chapter 7, pages 153–155. By the end you can:

  • explain nondisjunction in meiosis I and II and the maternal age effect;
  • describe the origin, mechanism and features of Klinefelter, Turner, triple X and XYY;
  • explain why escape genes (e.g. SHOX) produce symptoms;
  • describe how karyotype and FISH are used for diagnosis.

Contents

  1. Nondisjunction
  2. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
  3. Turner syndrome (45,X)
  4. Triple X (47,XXX)
  5. 47,XYY
  6. FISH

  8. Numbers to remember

Nondisjunction

Normal meiosis

  • Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes (XX or XY) pair and separate; each cell gets one of each pair.
  • Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate → haploid gametes with one copy of each chromosome (X or Y in sperm, X in eggs).

When it fails

Error inWhat fails to separateGametes
Meiosis IHomologous chromosomesOne cell gets both members of the pair, the other gets none
Meiosis IISister chromatidsGametes with two copies or no copy

An abnormal gamete + a normal gamete → an aneuploid zygote: trisomic (2n+1) or monosomic (2n−1).

  • Klinefelter usually from maternal meiosis I (per the slides); XYY from paternal meiosis II.
  • Maternal age effect: oocytes are arrested in prophase I for decades; their cohesin proteins weaken and spindle checkpoint control drops, so errors rise with age.
  • Mosaics (e.g. 46,XY/47,XXY) come from mitotic nondisjunction after fertilisation and are usually milder.

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)

  • Male phenotype with one or more extra X chromosomes; most commonly 47,XXY.
  • About 1 in 650 male births: the most frequent cause of primary testicular failure.
  • Origin: mainly maternal meiosis I nondisjunction (XX egg + Y sperm); less often paternal meiosis I or II. Mosaic 46,XY/47,XXY is milder.

Mechanism

  • One X is inactivated (one Barr body), but ~15% of genes escape, especially in PAR1/PAR2.
  • Extra dose of the escape gene SHOX → tall stature and long limbs.
  • Seminiferous tubules degenerate → Leydig cell function falls → low testosterone.

Clinical picture (slide 6 is an image; from the textbook): tall with long legs, small firm testes, infertility (azoospermia), gynecomastia, sparse body hair, raised FSH and LH, sometimes learning or language difficulties. Treated with testosterone.

Turner syndrome (45,X)

  • Complete or partial monosomy X: female with one X (45,X) or mosaic 45,X/46,XX.
  • About 1 in 2000 live female births.
  • Usually from paternal nondisjunction: a sperm with no sex chromosome.
  • Only about 1% of 45,X conceptuses survive to birth.

Mechanism

  • Haploinsufficiency of genes that normally escape inactivation, especially SHOX in PAR1 → short stature and skeletal abnormalities.
  • Too little X gene expression → defective ovaries → streak gonads.
AreaFeatures
BodyShort stature, webbed neck, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, lymphedema at birth (hands and feet)
ReproductivePrimary amenorrhea from ovarian dysgenesis (streak ovaries)
HeartCoarctation of the aorta, bicuspid aortic valve (major causes of illness); risk of aortic dilation and dissection
IntelligenceUsually normal; spatial and mathematical reasoning may be affected

Management: growth hormone for height; estrogen–progestin to induce puberty and protect bone; lifelong cardiovascular monitoring.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Cardiovascular complications in Turner syndrome Watch from 0:00 to the end: the heart and aorta in Turner syndrome.

Triple X (47,XXX)

  • Females with three X chromosomes; about 1 in 1000 live female births; often undiagnosed because signs are mild.
  • Usually maternal meiosis I nondisjunction (XX egg + X sperm); mosaics 46,XX/47,XXX from post-zygotic errors.
  • Two Xs are inactivated (2 Barr bodies), but escape genes give subtle effects.
AreaFeatures
PhysicalUsually normal; sometimes tall, mild epicanthal folds
DevelopmentMore speech/language delay, mild learning difficulty, subtle executive-function problems; IQ usually normal
ReproductionPuberty and fertility usually normal; some premature ovarian failure
BehaviourSlightly more anxiety and attention problems

Diagnosis by karyotype or FISH, often found incidentally in prenatal screening. Prognosis is excellent.

47,XYY

  • Males with an extra Y; about 1 in 1000 live male births; often found by chance.
  • Origin: paternal meiosis II: Y sister chromatids fail to separate → YY sperm + X egg → 47,XYY. Mosaics are milder.
  • There is no inactivation mechanism for the Y, but the Y has few active genes, so the dose effect is small.
AreaFeatures
PhysicalTall; normal sexual development and fertility
DevelopmentSlightly more learning and speech delay; IQ normal
BehaviourModern studies refute the old idea of aggression or criminality
HealthMildly higher risk of autism features, attention problems, infertility

Life expectancy is normal; support with education and speech if needed.

FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridisation)

  1. Cells (e.g. blood, amniotic fluid) are spread on a slide.
  2. A fluorescent DNA probe, made to bind (hybridise) only to a specific gene or chromosome region, is added.
  3. Under a fluorescence microscope the probe glows, showing where (and how many copies of) that sequence are present.

Sex chromosome abnormalities are found by karyotype and confirmed by FISH with X- and Y-specific probes.

The slides say Klinefelter arises “primarily” from maternal meiosis I. Many textbooks report that roughly half of 47,XXY cases are paternal (meiosis I, an XY sperm).   • Turner intelligence is usually normal.
  • XYY is not linked to criminality.
  • Klinefelter males have one Barr body; XYY males have none.

gct/histology/lec01-methods-of-study:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 1

Histology and Its Methods of Study

What histology studies, how a piece of tissue becomes a stained slide (fixation to sectioning), how H&E staining works, and the special methods that find specific molecules: autoradiography, cell culture, enzyme histochemistry, immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation.

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 1: Methods of Study

In 60 seconds

  • Histology = the study of tissues and how they are arranged into organs. A tissue = cells + extracellular matrix (ECM).
  • Tissue is too thick for light, so we cut thin sections. Steps, in order: Fixation → Dehydration → Clearing → Infiltration → Embedding → Trimming (then cut on a microtome).
  • Fixative: formaldehyde (cross-links proteins, stops enzymes). Dehydration: rising alcohol. Embedding medium: paraffin.
  • Basophilic parts (DNA, RNA) take basic dyes such as hematoxylin (blue-purple). Acidophilic parts (most proteins, collagen) take acidic dyes such as eosin (pink). H&E is the commonest stain.
  • Autoradiography: radioactive precursors → black silver grains show where new molecules are (³H-thymidine = DNA-replicating cells).
  • Enzyme histochemistry: unfixed tissue, cryostat, substrate → insoluble coloured product (phosphatases, dehydrogenases, peroxidase).
  • Immunohistochemistry: labelled antibodies find proteins; indirect (secondary antibody) is more sensitive. In situ hybridisation: labelled probes find DNA/RNA sequences.

Learning objectives

Source: Junqueira’s Basic Histology, Text and Atlas. By the end you can:

  • define histology, tissue and ECM;
  • list the steps of tissue preparation in order and say what each one does;
  • explain basophilia, acidophilia and H&E staining;
  • describe autoradiography, cell culture and enzyme histochemistry;
  • compare direct and indirect immunohistochemistry, and polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies;
  • outline the steps and uses of in situ hybridisation.

Contents

  1. Tissues and the ECM
  2. Preparing tissue for study
  3. Staining
  4. Autoradiography
  5. Cell and tissue culture
  6. Enzyme histochemistry
  7. Immunohistochemistry
  8. Hybridisation and in situ hybridisation
  9. Commonly confused
  10. Watch out
  11. Exam traps
  12. Check yourself
  13. Key terms

Tissues and the ECM

  • Histology is the study of the body’s tissues and how they are arranged to form organs.
  • Every tissue has two interacting parts: cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM).
  • The ECM is made of many macromolecules, most forming complex structures such as collagen fibrils. It:
    • supports the cells;
    • holds the fluid that brings nutrients to cells and carries away wastes and secretions.
  • During development, cells and their matrix become specialised, giving the basic tissue types. Organs are orderly combinations of these tissues; the precise arrangement lets each organ (and the whole body) work.
  • Cells and matrix are tiny, so histology depends on microscopes and molecular methods.

Preparing tissue for study

The commonest procedure is to make sections (thin slices) that can be examined with transmitted light (light that passes through the tissue). Most tissues are too thick for light to pass through, so thin, translucent sections are cut and put on glass slides. The ideal slide is preserved so it looks exactly as the tissue did in the body.

  1. Fixation. Small pieces go into chemicals that cross-link proteins and inactivate degradative enzymes, so the cells do not digest themselves. A common fixative is formaldehyde (the slide says 37%).
  2. Dehydration. The tissue passes through increasingly concentrated alcohol (e.g. 70% → 95% → 100%) to remove all water. Paraffin and water do not mix, so water must go.
  3. Clearing. Alcohol is replaced by an organic solvent (e.g. xylene) that mixes with both alcohol and paraffin. It is called clearing because the tissue turns translucent.
  4. Infiltration. The tissue sits in melted paraffin (in an oven, ~56–60 °C) until paraffin fills it completely.
  5. Embedding. The infiltrated tissue is put in a small mould of paraffin and allowed to harden into a block.
  6. Trimming. The block is trimmed to expose the tissue, then sliced on a microtome (sections of a few micrometres, ~3–10 μm).
Mnemonic: order of the steps

Fix, Dehydrate, Clear, Infiltrate, Embed, Trim: “Find Dad’s Car In Every Town.”

Staining

  • Most cells and ECM are colourless, so sections must be stained. Stains make components both visible and distinguishable.
  • Many stains work by charge:
    • Basophilic (“base-loving”) components are acidic, negatively charged (e.g. nucleic acids, with their phosphate groups). They attract basic dyes.
    • Acidophilic (“acid-loving”) components are basic (many proteins). They attract acidic dyes.
DyeTypeStainsColour
HematoxylinBehaves as a basic dyeDNA and RNA: nucleus, RNA-rich cytoplasmDark blue/purple
EosinAcidic dyeOther cytoplasmic structures and collagenPink
  • H&E (hematoxylin and eosin) is the most widely used stain.
  • Special stains give extra contrast: trichrome stains (e.g. separate collagen from muscle) and the periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) reaction (magenta for carbohydrate-rich molecules such as glycogen and glycoproteins).

Autoradiography

Finds where newly made macromolecules are in cells.

  1. Give living cells radioactively labelled building blocks (metabolites).
  2. They are built into DNA, RNA or protein.
  3. Sections are coated with photographic emulsion; the weak radiation exposes it.
  4. After developing, small black grains of metallic silver sit over the labelled molecules.
  • ³H-thymidine (tritiated thymidine) is only used to make DNA, so labelled nuclei = cells replicating DNA.
  • Inject radioactive amino acids and take samples over time to track protein production and secretion (e.g. ER → Golgi → secretory granules).

Cell and tissue culture

  • Live cells are kept in vitro (outside the body) so we can watch them directly and do experiments impossible in vivo.
  • Cells grow in complex nutrient solutions, often with serum or growth factors.
  • They are separated from tissue mechanically and enzymatically and grown in sterile dishes: these are primary cultures.
  • Most normal cells have a finite lifespan; some become immortalised by transformation, changes like those in early cancer cells.
  • Histology on cultured cells taught us much about the cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments).

Enzyme histochemistry

  • Localises structures by a specific enzyme activity.
  • To keep enzymes working, tissue is unfixed or only mildly fixed and cut on a cryostat (a microtome in a freezer). Paraffin processing would destroy the enzymes.
  1. Put the section in the enzyme’s substrate.
  2. The enzyme acts on it.
  3. Add a marker compound that reacts with the product.
  4. An insoluble, coloured or dense precipitate forms exactly where the enzyme is, visible by light or electron microscopy.
EnzymeWhat it doesWhat it marks
PhosphatasesRemove phosphate groupse.g. acid phosphatase in lysosomes
DehydrogenasesCitric acid cycle enzymesMitochondria
PeroxidaseOxidises substrates using H2O2e.g. peroxisomes, some blood cells; also used as a label in immunohistochemistry

Visualising specific molecules: immunohistochemistry

  • A tagged compound that binds one target molecule is added. The tag must be visible: fluorescent label, radioactive atom, enzyme (e.g. peroxidase) or metal particle (e.g. gold for electron microscopy). This can detect sugars, proteins and nucleic acids.
  • Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses labelled antibodies to find a specific protein.
  • Antibodies are made by injecting a purified protein into another species (e.g. human protein into a rabbit); its immune system makes antibodies against it.
PolyclonalMonoclonal
SourceMany different lymphocyte clonesOne cell line (one clone)
BindsSeveral sites on the proteinOne site only
Direct IHCIndirect IHC
HowThe primary antibody itself carries the labelAn unlabelled primary binds the protein; a labelled secondary antibody binds the primary
SensitivityLowerHigher: several secondaries bind each primary, amplifying the signal
PracticalEach antibody must be labelledOne labelled secondary works with many primaries; includes the biotin–avidin method; widely used in research and diagnosis

Hybridisation and in situ hybridisation (ISH)

  • Hybridisation = binding of two complementary nucleic acid strands (DNA or RNA) by base pairing. Used to detect, identify or quantify specific sequences.
  • In situ hybridisation finds specific DNA or RNA sequences inside fixed cells or tissue sections (“in situ” = in place).
  1. Sample preparation: fix (usually formaldehyde) and section.
  2. Hybridisation: incubate with labelled probes under conditions favouring specific binding.
  3. Washing: remove unbound probe.
  4. Detection: see the probe by microscopy, using fluorescence (FISH) or autoradiography.
UseExample
Gene expressionWhere a gene’s mRNA is made in a tissue
Developmental biologyTracking expression through stages of development
PathologyViral infections, genetic abnormalities, tumour markers
Comparative genomicsWhere a gene lies in different species

Commonly confused

PairDifference
Basophilic vs basic dyeA basophilic structure is acidic and binds a basic dye (hematoxylin).
Dehydration vs clearingDehydration removes water (alcohol); clearing removes alcohol (solvent).
Infiltration vs embeddingInfiltration fills the tissue with paraffin; embedding sets it in a hardened block.
Microtome vs cryostatCryostat = microtome in a cold chamber for frozen, unfixed tissue (enzymes survive).
IHC vs ISHIHC finds proteins (antibodies); ISH finds nucleic acids (probes).

Watch out

Watch out: “37% formaldehyde”

37% formaldehyde is the stock solution (formalin). For fixing tissue it is diluted: the usual fixative is 10% buffered formalin, about 4% formaldehyde. If an exam asks for the fixative, answer “formaldehyde/formalin”.

Watch out: hematoxylin “basic”

Strictly, hematoxylin needs a metal mordant to act as a basic dye. For exams treat it as the basic dye that stains nucleic acids.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Dehydration comes before clearing; clearing before infiltration.
  • Nucleic acids are basophilic; collagen is acidophilic (eosin).
  • ³H-thymidine labels DNA (not RNA: RNA uses uridine).
  • Enzyme histochemistry uses unfixed / lightly fixed, frozen tissue.
  • Indirect IHC is the more sensitive one.
  • Monoclonal = one clone.

  2. The main purpose of fixation is to:

  3. In clearing, the tissue is placed in a solvent that is miscible with:

    2. Alcohol and paraffin

  4. Hematoxylin stains mainly:

gct/histology/lec02-microscopy:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 2

Microscopy

The five kinds of light microscope (bright-field, fluorescence, phase-contrast, confocal, polarizing), resolving power, the two electron microscopes (TEM and SEM), and how to interpret sections and their artifacts.

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 2: Microscopy

In 60 seconds

  • Light microscopes: bright-field, fluorescence, phase-contrast, confocal, polarizing. All use light interacting with tissue.
  • Resolving power = smallest distance at which two objects are still seen as separate. Light microscope: 0.2 μm, useful magnification 1000–1500×. A ribosome or microfilament is too small to see.
  • Fluorescence: light in, longer wavelength out (e.g. acridine orange for DNA and RNA).
  • Phase-contrast: turns invisible phase shifts (refractive index differences) into brightness differences: living, unstained cells.
  • Confocal: laser point + pinhole removes out-of-focus light → sharp optical slices, 3-D.
  • Polarizing: polarized light shows ordered, birefringent structures (crystals, collagen, muscle).
  • Electron microscopes: electron wavelength is much shorter → ~1000× better resolution. TEM = through ultra-thin sections (inside); SEM = scans the surface (3-D look).
  • Artifacts (e.g. shrinkage spaces, wrinkles, stain precipitate) are not in living tissue. A section is a 2-D slice of a 3-D structure.

Learning objectives

  • name the light microscope types and the principle of each;
  • define resolving power and give the limit of the light microscope;
  • explain why phase-contrast is used for living cells;
  • compare TEM and SEM;
  • recognise common artifacts and the limits of a 2-D section.

Contents

  1. Types of light microscope
  2. Bright-field and resolving power
  3. Fluorescence
  4. Phase-contrast
  5. Confocal
  6. Polarizing
  7. Electron microscopy: TEM and SEM
  8. Interpreting sections
  9. Numbers to remember
  10. Exam traps
  11. Check yourself
  12. Key terms

Types of light microscope

MicroscopePrincipleBest for
Bright-fieldLight passes through the specimen; dark sample on a bright backgroundStained or naturally pigmented sections (routine H&E)
FluorescenceSpecimen absorbs one wavelength and emits a longer oneSpecific molecules tagged with fluorescent dyes
Phase-contrastConverts phase shifts into brightnessLiving, unstained cells
ConfocalLaser point + pinhole removes out-of-focus lightSharp optical sections, 3-D reconstruction
PolarizingPolarized light; ordered molecules rotate it (birefringence)Crystals, collagen, muscle fibres

Bright-field microscopy and resolving power

  • The most common light microscope: light is transmitted through the specimen, seen against a bright background. Works because of contrast between the specimen and its surroundings, so it suits stained or pigmented samples.
  • The key to a crisp image is resolving power (resolution): the smallest distance between two structures at which they are still seen as two separate objects.
  • Maximum resolving power of the light microscope ≈ 0.2 μm, giving clear images magnified 1000–1500 times. Magnifying more just makes a bigger blur (“empty magnification”).
  • Anything smaller than 0.2 μm (a single ribosome, a microfilament) cannot be distinguished.
  • Virtual microscopy: a stained slide is scanned into high-resolution digital images, studied on a computer without a microscope or the glass slide.
Key idea: resolution vs magnification

Magnification makes things bigger; resolution makes them clearer (separate). Better resolution = a smaller resolvable distance.

Fluorescence microscopy

  • The specimen is lit with a specific wavelength (often ultraviolet or blue); fluorescent molecules absorb it and emit light of a longer wavelength, which is what we see (bright on a dark background).
  • Fluorescent dyes or tags (e.g. fluorescent antibodies) make specific structures or molecules glow.
  • Example: acridine orange binds both DNA and RNA; they fluoresce slightly different colours, so they can be located separately.
  • Used in cell biology, pathology and biochemistry.

Phase-contrast microscopy

The problem

  • Cells are mostly water and very transparent. In bright-field, light passes through with little absorption: poor contrast, a faint image.
  • But light slows down slightly as it passes structures with different refractive indices (nucleus, organelles, cytoplasm). This causes a phase shift in the light waves.
  • Our eyes cannot see phase shifts, only differences in intensity (brightness).

The solution

  • The phase-contrast system converts phase shifts into brightness differences, so structures look lighter or darker than each other.
  • No staining is needed, so it is ideal for living cells, tissue culture and microorganisms, and for watching dynamic processes.

Confocal microscopy

  • A laser lights one small point of the sample at a time.
  • The emitted fluorescence or reflected light passes through a pinhole that blocks out-of-focus light from above and below the focal plane.
  • Result: better contrast and resolution; a series of thin “optical sections” can be stacked into a 3-D image.
  • Used for cellular structures, tissues and real-time processes.

Polarizing microscopy

  • Filters make polarized light (waves vibrating in one plane) that passes through the sample.
  • Structures with highly ordered, repeating molecules rotate polarized light: birefringence. They shine brightly on a dark background.
  • Reveals orientation, birefringence and texture: crystals, collagen bundles, skeletal muscle striations, also used in geology and materials science.

Electron microscopy: TEM and SEM

  • Both use a beam of electrons interacting with tissue.
  • The wavelength of electrons is much shorter than light’s → about 1000-fold better resolution than the light microscope.
TEM (transmission)SEM (scanning)
ElectronsPass through an ultra-thin sectionScan across the surface
Image2-D, internal fine structure (organelles, membranes)3-D-looking surface topography
SampleVery thin sectionsWhole surfaces (no sectioning needed)
SpecialCryofracture and freeze etching: study cells without fixation or embedding; especially useful for membrane structureShows surface shape and composition at many magnifications

Interpreting structures in sections

  • Artifacts are structural changes caused by preparation that do not exist in living tissue:
    • shrinkage from fixatives, ethanol or the heat of paraffin embedding → artificial spaces between cells;
    • wrinkles (folds) in sections;
    • stain precipitates that can look like cell structures.
  • No single stain shows all components, so several preparations must be studied.
  • TEM gives great detail but only of tiny samples.
  • A section is two-dimensional: one cut through a 3-D structure. A tube may look like a ring, an oval or a strip depending on the angle of the cut, so think in 3-D.

Numbers to remember

ValueWhat it is
0.2 μmResolving power of the light microscope
1000–1500×Useful light microscope magnification
~1000×Resolution gain of the electron microscope over light
5Types of light microscope in this lecture
2Types of electron microscope (TEM, SEM)

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Fluorescence emits a longer wavelength than it absorbs.
  • Phase-contrast needs no stain: living cells.
  • The pinhole is the confocal microscope.
  • SEM = surface, 3-D; TEM = inside, thin sections.
  • Freeze fracture/etching is a TEM technique for membranes.
  • Spaces between cells after paraffin processing are usually shrinkage artifacts.

gct/histology/lec03-plasma-membrane-tran:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 3

The Plasma Membrane, Transport and Signalling

Cell differentiation, the structure of the plasma membrane (lipids, proteins, glycocalyx, lipid rafts), how molecules cross it (diffusion, channels, carriers, pumps), endocytosis and exocytosis, and how cells receive signals.

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 3: Plasma Membrane & Transport

In 60 seconds

  • Cells are the smallest living units. All come from the zygote → blastomeres → inner cell mass (embryonic stem cells) → differentiated cells.
  • Plasma membrane: phospholipids, cholesterol, proteins + oligosaccharides; 7.5–10 nm thick, seen only by EM as three layers (dark–light–dark: trilaminar).
  • Proteins ≈ 50% of membrane weight: integral (in the bilayer; multipass if they cross many times) and peripheral. Sugars outside = glycocalyx. Fluid mosaic model; lipid rafts are cholesterol-rich, less fluid.
  • Passive: diffusion (small nonpolar), channels (pores), carriers (change shape). Active: pumps (ATPases) use ATP against gradients.
  • Endocytosis: phagocytosis (large particles, phagosome), pinocytosis (fluid, ~80 nm vesicles, transcytosis), receptor-mediated (e.g. LDL).
  • Exocytosis: vesicle fuses with the membrane, often triggered by Ca²⁺. Constitutive (continuous) vs regulated (on a signal).
  • Signalling: endocrine, paracrine, synaptic, autocrine, juxtacrine. ~25 receptor families. Membrane receptors: channel-linked, enzymatic, G protein-coupled.

Learning objectives

  • describe how cells differentiate from the zygote;
  • describe the structure of the plasma membrane and the fluid mosaic model;
  • distinguish passive and active transport;
  • compare the three kinds of endocytosis and the two kinds of exocytosis;
  • classify signalling by distance and receptors by mechanism.

Contents

  1. Cells and differentiation
  2. The plasma membrane
  3. Membrane proteins and the fluid mosaic
  4. Membrane transport
  5. Endocytosis
  6. Exocytosis
  7. Signal reception
  8. Receptor types
  9. Numbers to remember
  10. Watch out
  11. Exam traps
  12. Check yourself
  13. Key terms

Cells and differentiation

  • Cells + extracellular material make up all tissues. Cells are the basic structural and functional units: the smallest living parts of the body.
  • Animal cells are eukaryotic: a membrane-bound nucleus surrounded by cytoplasm.
  1. Zygote: sperm + egg.
  2. Early divisions → blastomeres.
  3. Blastomeres → inner cell mass, which gives rise to all fetal tissues (grown in culture, these are embryonic stem cells).
  4. Differentiation: cells switch on specific genes for special functions, often changing shape.

Example: muscle precursors become long fibres full of actin and myosin, turning chemical energy into contraction.

The plasma membrane

  • Made of phospholipids, cholesterol and proteins, with oligosaccharide chains attached to many of them.
  • Jobs:
    • selective barrier: controls what enters and leaves; keeps the cytoplasm’s ion balance different from extracellular fluid;
    • recognition and signalling with the environment;
    • integrins link the inner cytoskeleton to the ECM.
  • Very thin: 7.5–10 nm, visible only with the electron microscope.
  • Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails, forming a bilayer.
  • The two layers have different phospholipids (asymmetry). Some outer lipids carry sugar chains that form a protective coat, the glycocalyx.
  • In TEM the membrane looks trilaminar: two dark lines (the heads) with a light layer between (the tails).
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Membrane Structure & Function Watch from 0:34 to 8:20: the lipid bilayer and its lipids.

Membrane proteins and the fluid mosaic

  • Proteins are about 50% of the membrane’s weight.
  • Integral proteins are embedded in the bilayer. Those crossing it many times are multipass proteins.
  • Peripheral proteins sit on the surface, usually the cytoplasmic side.
  • Glycoproteins carry carbohydrate chains that add to the glycocalyx; they help in cell interactions, recognition and hormone responses.
  • Fluid mosaic model: proteins are not fixed; they drift sideways in the fluid bilayer.
  • Proteins in large enzyme complexes (especially for signal transduction) move less. They gather in lipid rafts: areas rich in cholesterol and saturated fatty acids, which are less fluid.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Membrane Structure & Function Watch from 8:20 to 17:47: integral and peripheral proteins and the glycocalyx.

Membrane transport

MechanismHowEnergy
DiffusionSmall, nonpolar molecules (O2, CO2) pass straight through the lipid bilayerPassive
ChannelsMultipass proteins forming a pore; ions or small molecules pass selectivelyPassive
CarriersBind a molecule and move it across by a change of shape (conformation)Passive
PumpsEnzymes (ATPases) that hydrolyse ATP to move ions/solutes against steep gradients (e.g. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase)Active

Passive transport moves substances down their concentration gradient, driven by their own kinetic energy.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Passive & Active Transport | Endocytosis & Exocytosis Watch from 0:31 to 57:09: simple and facilitated diffusion, and primary and secondary active transport.

Endocytosis

Large molecules enter mainly by endocytosis: the membrane folds inward (often after binding receptors) and pinches off a vesicle.

TypeWhat is taken inDetails
Phagocytosis (“cell eating”)Large particles: bacteria, dead cellsBy macrophages and neutrophils. Membrane extends around the particle → phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome
Pinocytosis (“cell drinking”)Extracellular fluid and dissolved substancesSmall invaginations → pinocytotic vesicles (~80 nm). Fuse with lysosomes, or cross to the opposite surface and release contents: transcytosis
Receptor-mediatedSpecific ligands (e.g. LDL)Ligand binds receptor; receptors cluster in a region that invaginates. Selective
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Passive & Active Transport | Endocytosis & Exocytosis Watch from 57:09 to 1:15:29: pinocytosis, phagocytosis and receptor-mediated endocytosis.

Exocytosis

  • A vesicle carrying large molecules fuses with the plasma membrane and releases them outside, without breaking the membrane.
  • Fusion is often triggered by a brief rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺ and controlled by specific membrane proteins.
Constitutive secretionRegulated secretion
WhenContinuously, right after synthesisOnly after a specific signal
ExampleCollagen subunits for the ECMDigestive enzymes from pancreatic cells
NoteNo storageProducts stored in granules; usually at the apical surface of epithelial (gland) cells
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Cell Biology | Passive & Active Transport | Endocytosis & Exocytosis Watch from 1:15:29 to 1:22:47: exocytosis.

Signal reception and transduction

  • Cells communicate to guide development, control growth and division, and coordinate function.
  • They may share ions and small molecules directly through gap junctions.
  • They use about 25 families of receptors for extracellular signals. Signal molecules = ligands; cells with the matching receptor = target cells.
SignallingRouteExample
EndocrineHormones carried in the blood to target cells anywhereInsulin
ParacrineDiffuses in extracellular fluid but is quickly broken down, so acts only locallyLocal growth factors
SynapticSpecial paracrine: neurotransmitters act on the next cell across a synapseAcetylcholine
AutocrineBinds receptors on the same cell that made itSome growth factors
JuxtacrineContact: a ligand on one cell surface binds a receptor on the neighbourImmune cell contacts

Receptor types

Hydrophilic signals (polypeptide hormones, neurotransmitters) cannot cross the membrane, so their receptors are transmembrane proteins in the plasma membrane. Three classes:

ReceptorWhat ligand binding does
Channel-linkedOpens a channel for ions or molecules
EnzymaticSwitches on catalytic activity in associated peripheral proteins
G protein-coupledActivates a G protein, which binds GTP and is released to activate other cytoplasmic proteins

(Hydrophobic signals such as steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell.)

ValueWhat it is

~50%Protein share of membrane weight
~80 nmPinocytotic vesicle diameter
~25Receptor families

Watch out

Watch out: missing unit

The slide gives the membrane thickness as “7,5 to 10” with no unit. It is 7.5–10 nm (nanometres).

Exam trap
  • Channels and carriers are passive; only pumps use ATP.
  • Lipid rafts are less fluid (more cholesterol and saturated fats).
  • Transcytosis = vesicle crosses the cell to the opposite surface.
  • LDL enters by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  • Synaptic signalling is a special kind of paracrine.
  • Juxtacrine needs cell contact; autocrine acts on the same cell.

gct/histology/lec04-ribosomes-er-golgi:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 4

Ribosomes, Endoplasmic Reticulum and Golgi Apparatus

The cytoplasm, ribosomes and polysomes, rough ER (signal sequence, SRP, ERAD), smooth ER (lipids, detoxification, calcium) and the Golgi apparatus (cis and trans faces, COP coats, processing).

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 4: Ribosomes, ER & Golgi

In 60 seconds

  • Cytoplasm holds organelles (membranous, e.g. mitochondria, and non-membranous, e.g. ribosomes), organised by the cytoskeleton. The cytosol has enzymes such as those of glycolysis.
  • Ribosomes: small + large subunit of rRNA + protein; rRNA catalyses peptide bonds. Assembled in the nucleus; several on one mRNA = polysome. RNA makes them basophilic.
  • Free polysomes → proteins for the cytosol and imported organelles. ER-bound → proteins for the ER, Golgi, membrane, lysosomes, secretion.
  • RER: flat cisternae with ribosomes, basophilic; big in pancreas, fibroblasts, plasma cells. Signal sequence + SRP bring the ribosome to the ER. ERAD: misfolded → ubiquitin → proteasome.
  • SER: no ribosomes, tubular; lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification (cytochrome P450, liver), Ca²⁺ storage (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle).
  • Golgi: near the nucleus; cis face receives from RER, trans face ships out. COPII forward, COPI backward (retrograde), Rab proteins target vesicles. Glycosylation, sulfation, phosphorylation, limited proteolysis.

Learning objectives

  • describe the cytoplasm and the structure and assembly of ribosomes;
  • explain why protein-making cells are basophilic;
  • describe RER structure, the signal hypothesis and ERAD;
  • list SER functions with examples;
  • describe Golgi structure, vesicle traffic and processing.

Contents

  1. Cytoplasm
  2. Ribosomes
  3. The endoplasmic reticulum
  4. Rough ER
  5. Signal sequence and SRP
  6. Quality control (ERAD)
  7. Smooth ER
  8. Golgi apparatus
  9. Golgi traffic and processing
  10. Commonly confused
  11. Exam traps
  12. Check yourself
  13. Key terms

Cytoplasm

  • Inside the cell membrane, the cytoplasm (cytosol) surrounds and supports the organelles.
  • Organelles are either membranous (e.g. mitochondria) or non-membranous protein complexes (e.g. ribosomes).
  • The cytoskeleton organises organelles and controls cell shape and movement.
  • The cytosol contains many enzymes, including those of glycolysis; O2, CO2, ions and metabolites diffuse through it to the organelles that use or make them.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · The Cell and Organelles Watch from 0:00 to the end: a 7-minute tour of the organelles.

Ribosomes

  • Molecular machines that join amino acids into polypeptides, reading mRNA with the help of tRNA.
  • Two subunits, each of rRNA + proteins: a small subunit and a large one (more rRNA and protein).
  • rRNA gives structure, positions tRNA, and catalyses the peptide bond (a ribozyme). Proteins stabilise the catalytic core.
  1. Ribosomal proteins are made in the cytoplasm.
  2. They are imported into the nucleus (nucleolus) and combined with rRNA into subunits.
  3. Subunits return to the cytoplasm to make proteins.
  4. Several ribosomes on one mRNA = a polyribosome (polysome).
  • RNA’s phosphate groups make ribosome-rich cytoplasm stain intensely basophilic (blue with hematoxylin).
  • Free polysomes make proteins for the cytosol or for import into organelles (nucleus, mitochondria, peroxisomes).
  • ER-bound ribosomes make proteins for the ER, Golgi, plasma membrane, lysosomes and secretory vesicles.
  • Folding is helped by chaperones; misfolded proteins are destroyed by proteasomes.

The endoplasmic reticulum

  • A network of membranes extending from the nuclear envelope, forming connected channels and sacs called cisternae.
  • Its membrane area is much larger than the plasma membrane’s.
  • Central to making proteins and lipids.
  • Two types, distinguished by whether polyribosomes are attached.

Rough ER (RER)

  • Prominent in cells that secrete protein: pancreatic acinar cells, fibroblasts (collagen), plasma cells (antibodies).
  • Flattened sacs in stacks of cisternae, with polyribosomes on the cytosolic surface → basophilic.
  • Makes membrane proteins, secreted proteins and proteins for membranous organelles.
  • Starts glycosylation of glycoproteins and other post-translational modifications.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Endoplasmic Reticulum Structure & Function Watch from 0:36 to 14:01: ER structure and what the rough ER does.

Signal sequence and SRP

  1. Translation starts in the cytosol.
  2. Proteins for the ER begin with a signal sequence.
  3. The signal-recognition particle (SRP) binds it and pauses translation.
  4. The complex docks on the ER membrane; translation resumes and the protein enters the RER lumen.
  5. The signal sequence is cut off; the protein folds with chaperones and is modified.

Quality control: ERAD

  • ER-associated degradation (ERAD) makes sure only correctly folded proteins move on.
  • Misfolded proteins are tagged with ubiquitin and destroyed by proteasomes.
  • RER products go to lysosomes, secretory vesicles (exocytosis) or become integral membrane proteins. These destinations give cell types their histological look (e.g. granules in secretory cells).

Smooth ER (SER)

  • No ribosomes; continuous with the RER but usually less abundant and less basophilic (paler).
  • Cisternae are tubular or saclike and interconnected (RER cisternae are flattened).
FunctionDetailsWhere it is big
Lipid and steroid synthesisMakes phospholipids and steroids; sends lipids to other membranes by diffusion or vesiclesSteroid hormone cells (adrenal cortex, gonads)
DetoxificationEnzymes such as cytochrome P450 inactivate drugs and alcoholLiver cells
Ca²⁺ storage and releaseSequesters calcium for cell responsesMuscle: called the sarcoplasmic reticulum, controls contraction
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Endoplasmic Reticulum Structure & Function Watch from 14:01 to 29:33: what the smooth ER does.

Golgi apparatus

  • Also called the Golgi complex: a dynamic organelle that modifies, packages and sorts proteins from the RER.
  • Made of smooth membrane saccules (flattened or vesicular), usually near the nucleus.
  • Two faces:
    • cis face (entry, toward the ER): receives transport vesicles from the RER;
    • trans face (exit): packs modified proteins into larger vesicles for other organelles or exocytosis.

Golgi traffic and processing

ProteinRole
COPIIForward (anterograde) movement, ER → cis Golgi
COPIBackward (retrograde) movement, Golgi → ER and between cisternae
Rab proteins, receptors, fusion proteinsGuide vesicles to the correct destination and make them fuse
  • Enzymes in the cis, medial and trans cisternae modify proteins by:
    • glycosylation (adding/trimming sugars);
    • sulfation;
    • phosphorylation (e.g. mannose-6-phosphate on lysosomal enzymes);
    • limited proteolysis (cutting precursors to active forms).
  • The Golgi also concentrates, stores and packages secretory products, sorting them to lysosomes or secretory vesicles.
Key idea: the secretory path

Ribosome → RER lumen → (COPII vesicle) → cis Golgi → medial → trans Golgi → lysosome, membrane or secretory granule → exocytosis.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Golgi Apparatus Structure & Function Watch from 0:36 to 24:53: Golgi faces and how proteins are modified and sorted.

RERSER
RibosomesYesNo
ShapeFlattened sacsTubules
StainingBasophilicPale, less basophilic
MakesProteins (secreted, membrane, lysosomal)Lipids, steroids; detox; Ca²⁺
Rich inPancreas, fibroblasts, plasma cellsLiver, steroid cells, muscle

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • The catalyst for the peptide bond is rRNA, not protein.
  • Ribosomal proteins are made in the cytoplasm but assembled in the nucleus.
  • SRP pauses translation; it does not end it.
  • ERAD destroys proteins with ubiquitin + proteasome, not lysosomes.
  • Sarcoplasmic reticulum = SER of muscle.
  • COPII forward, COPI backward (“two goes to, one comes back”).

gct/histology/lec05-lysosomes-proteasome:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 5

Lysosomes, Proteasomes and Peroxisomes

The cell’s three clean-up and detox systems: lysosomes (acid hydrolases, M6P, heterolysosomes, residual bodies, autophagy), proteasomes (ubiquitin, ATP) and peroxisomes (H2O2, catalase, β-oxidation). Mitochondria from the same deck are in the Lecture 6 guide.

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 5: Lysosomes & Peroxisomes

In 60 seconds

  • Lysosomes: single-membrane spheres, 0.05–0.5 μm, ~40 acid hydrolases, work best at pH ~5 (cytosol 7.2 keeps leaked enzymes inactive). Abundant in macrophages and neutrophils.
  • Enzymes made in RER → Golgi adds mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) → M6P receptors send them to lysosomes.
  • Phagosome/pinocytotic vesicle + lysosome = secondary lysosome (heterolysosome) → undigested remains = residual body → lipofuscin in long-lived cells (neurons, muscle).
  • Autophagy: SER membrane wraps old organelles → autophagosome → fuses with lysosome. Increases in starvation.
  • Proteasomes: cylinders of protease rings with regulatory caps; destroy single ubiquitin-tagged proteins using ATP.
  • Peroxisomes: single membrane; oxidases make H2O2, catalase breaks it down; detox (liver, kidney), β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, bile acids, cholesterol. Proteins imported from the cytosol.

Learning objectives

  • describe lysosome structure, enzymes and why they need acid pH;
  • explain how M6P targets enzymes to lysosomes;
  • trace heterophagy and autophagy to the residual body;
  • contrast lysosomes and proteasomes;
  • list peroxisome enzymes and functions.

Contents

  1. Lysosomes
  2. Making lysosomes: M6P
  3. Digestion of endocytosed material
  4. Autophagy
  5. Proteasomes
  6. Peroxisomes
  7. Commonly confused
  8. Exam traps
  9. Check yourself
  10. Key terms

Lysosomes

  • Small membrane-bound organelles that break down cell waste and components: the cell’s digestive system.
  • About 40 enzymes, mainly acid hydrolases (proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases, phosphatases) that digest proteins, nucleic acids, lipids and sugars.
  • Especially abundant in phagocytic cells: macrophages and neutrophils.
  • Usually spherical, 0.05–0.5 μm; dense and granular in the electron microscope. In macrophages they can be large enough to see by light microscopy with special stains.

Why the cell does not digest itself

  • The lysosomal membrane keeps the enzymes apart from the cytosol.
  • The enzymes work best at acidic pH ≈ 5.0. The cytosol is neutral, ≈ 7.2, so any leaked enzymes are inactive.

Making lysosomes: mannose-6-phosphate

  1. Lysosomal enzymes are made in the rough ER.
  2. They travel to the Golgi, where a marker, mannose-6-phosphate (M6P), is added.
  3. M6P receptors in the Golgi recognise the enzymes and send them into lysosomes rather than the secretory pathway.

Digestion of endocytosed material

  1. Material enters by endocytosis in a phagosome or pinocytotic vesicle.
  2. It fuses with a lysosome → secondary lysosome (heterolysosome); contents are mixed with enzymes and acidified.
  3. Digested nutrients pass into the cytosol.
  4. Undigested material stays in a residual body.
  5. In long-lived cells (neurons, heart and skeletal muscle) residual bodies accumulate as the brown pigment lipofuscin (“age pigment”).
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Lysosomes Structure & Function Watch from 0:40 to 25:57: how lysosomes are made and what they digest.

Autophagy

  • “Self-eating”: lysosomes remove damaged or excess organelles.
  • A membrane from the smooth ER surrounds the material → an autophagosome → fuses with a lysosome for digestion.
  • Increases under stress such as starvation; the products are recycled.

Proteasomes

  • Small, abundant protein complexes (no membrane) that destroy damaged, misfolded or unneeded proteins.
  • Lysosomes digest whole organelles and endocytosed material; proteasomes destroy individual proteins.
  • Structure: a cylinder of stacked rings containing proteases, with a regulatory particle at each end that recognises ubiquitin.
  1. An unwanted protein is tagged with a chain of ubiquitin molecules.
  2. The cap recognises it; the protein is unfolded using ATP and fed into the cylinder.
  3. It is cut into peptides inside; ubiquitin is recycled.
  4. Peptides are broken down further, or used by the immune system (antigen presentation).

Peroxisomes

  • Spherical organelles with a single membrane.
  • Contain enzymes that make and destroy hydrogen peroxide (H2O2):
    • oxidases remove hydrogen atoms from substrates and pass them to O2 → H2O2;
    • peroxidases such as catalase break H2O2 down (to water and O2) so it cannot damage the cell.
  • Detoxify harmful substances and some drugs, especially in liver and kidney cells.
  • Lipid metabolism: β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids; help make bile acids and cholesterol.
  • Formed by budding from the ER or by division of existing peroxisomes.
  • Their proteins are made on free ribosomes in the cytoplasm and carry targeting sequences for import.

LysosomeProteasomePeroxisome

DestroysOrganelles, endocytosed materialSingle ubiquitinated proteinsH2O2, toxins, long fatty acids
Key enzymesAcid hydrolasesProteasesOxidases, catalase
Proteins come fromRER → Golgi (M6P)CytosolCytosol (targeting sequence)

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Lysosomal enzymes are inactive at pH 7.2; that protects the cell.
  • M6P is added in the Golgi, not the ER.
  • Lipofuscin = residual bodies in long-lived cells.
  • The autophagosome membrane comes from the SER.
  • Proteasomes need ATP and ubiquitin; ubiquitin is recycled.
  • Peroxisomes both make (oxidases) and destroy (catalase) H2O2.

gct/histology/lec06-mitochondria-inclusi:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 6

Mitochondria and Cytoplasmic Inclusions

Mitochondrial structure and ATP synthesis, their role in apoptosis, how they divide and why they look like bacteria; then the inclusions you see in electron micrographs: glycogen granules, lipid droplets, pigments and secretory granules. Built from the mitochondria slides of the Lecture 5 deck and the “Organelles” image set.

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 6: Mitochondria & Inclusions

In 60 seconds

  • Mitochondria make most ATP. Glucose → pyruvate in the cytoplasm; pyruvate is oxidised in the mitochondrion.
  • Two membranes: outer with pores (lets pyruvate in); inner folded into cristae (more surface) with the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
  • Electron transport pumps protons into the intermembrane space; protons flow back through ATP synthase, which rotates and makes ATP (> 100 ATP/s): oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Release of cytochrome c triggers apoptosis.
  • They grow and divide by fission; have their own DNA and ribosomes, but most proteins come from nuclear genes → endosymbiont (aerobic bacterium) origin.
  • Inclusions = stored, non-living material: glycogen (dense granules/rosettes, liver and muscle), lipid droplets (round, no membrane), pigments (lipofuscin, melanin), secretory granules.

Learning objectives

  • describe the membranes and compartments of a mitochondrion;
  • explain how the proton gradient drives ATP synthase;
  • state the role of mitochondria in apoptosis and the evidence for endosymbiosis;
  • recognise the main cytoplasmic inclusions in electron micrographs.

Contents

  1. Mitochondrial structure
  2. Oxidative phosphorylation
  3. ATP synthase
  4. Apoptosis, division and origin
  5. Cytoplasmic inclusions
  6. Recognising organelles in EM images
  7. Watch out
  8. Exam traps
  9. Check yourself
  10. Key terms

Mitochondrial structure

  • Membrane-bound organelles that make ATP, the cell’s main energy currency, by aerobic respiration.
  • Glucose is split to pyruvate in the cytoplasm (glycolysis); pyruvate is oxidised further in the mitochondria.
  • In TEM there are two membranes:
    • outer membrane: has pores (porins) that let small molecules such as pyruvate through;
    • inner membrane: folded into cristae, which greatly increase its surface area.
  • Compartments: intermembrane space (between the membranes) and matrix (inside the inner membrane; holds DNA, ribosomes and citric acid cycle enzymes).
  • Cells with high energy needs (heart muscle, kidney tubules) have many mitochondria with many cristae.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Mitochondria Structure & Function Watch from 0:33 to 5:52: the membranes, cristae and matrix.

Oxidative phosphorylation

  • The inner membrane is specialised for energy production. It holds the electron transport chain; the citric acid cycle supplies its electrons (NADH, FADH2).
  • Electrons pass along a chain of enzyme complexes, which pump protons (H⁺) from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
  • This builds an electrochemical gradient across the inner membrane, which powers ATP synthesis.
  • This process makes most of the cell’s ATP.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Ninja Nerd · Mitochondria Structure & Function Watch from 13:03 to 19:03: the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

ATP synthase

  1. ATP synthase complexes sit in the inner membrane with a proton channel.
  2. Protons flow back down their gradient into the matrix through the channel.
  3. The flow makes part of the enzyme rotate: electrical energy → mechanical motion.
  4. The rotation drives ADP + Pi → ATP.

Very efficient: each synthase makes more than 100 ATP per second.

Apoptosis, division and origin

  • Under stress, mitochondria release cytochrome c (an electron carrier) into the cytosol, which triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death).
  • Mitochondria grow and divide (fission). At cell division each daughter cell gets about half of them.
  • They are partly autonomous: own DNA (circular), ribosomes and protein-making machinery.
  • But most mitochondrial proteins are coded by nuclear DNA, made in the cytoplasm and imported.
  • These bacteria-like features support the endosymbiotic theory: mitochondria came from an aerobic prokaryote living inside an ancestral eukaryotic cell.

Cytoplasmic inclusions

Inclusions are stored or accumulated materials, not organelles with a working machinery. Many have no membrane.

Lipid dropletsStored triglycerides (and cholesterol esters)Round, no limiting membrane; empty-looking holes in paraffin sections (lipid dissolved by solvents)Adipocytes, liver, steroid-making cells
PigmentsLipofuscin (residual bodies), melanin, hemosiderin (iron)Brown granulesNeurons and muscle (lipofuscin); skin (melanin)
Secretory granulesPackaged products waiting for regulated exocytosisMembrane-bound, often dense, near the apical surfacePancreatic acinar cells, endocrine cells

The slide says the inner membrane houses enzymes of the citric acid cycle. Most citric acid cycle enzymes are in the matrix; only succinate dehydrogenase sits in the inner membrane (it is also Complex II). The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner membrane.

Exam traps

  • Protons are pumped into the intermembrane space, then flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
  • Cristae belong to the inner membrane.
  • Cytochrome c release → apoptosis.
  • Most mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded.
  • Lipid droplets and glycogen have no membrane.

gct/histology/lec07-cytoskeleton:
GCT I · Histology · Lecture 7

The Cytoskeleton

The three protein filament systems of the cell: microtubules (tubulin, MTOC, kinesin and dynein), microfilaments (actin, treadmilling, cortex) and intermediate filaments (keratins, vimentin family, neurofilaments, lamins).

Labobo topic: Histo Lec 7: Cytoskeleton

In 60 seconds

  • Three filaments: microtubules (thickest, ~25 nm), intermediate filaments (~10 nm), microfilaments (thinnest, 5–7 nm). Together: cell shape, organelle and vesicle movement, whole-cell movement.
  • Microtubules: α/β-tubulin heterodimers → 13 protofilaments form the wall. Organised by the MTOC (centrosome with centrioles).
  • Motors use ATP: kinesin → toward the + end (away from the nucleus, anterograde); dynein → toward the − end (toward the nucleus, retrograde).
  • Microfilaments: G-actin → F-actin double helix (needs K⁺, Mg²⁺). Nucleated by formin and Arp2/3 (branches). Treadmilling: add at +, lose at −. Form the cell cortex.
  • Intermediate filaments: stable, give mechanical strength; dimers → antiparallel tetramers → bundles. Types: keratins (epithelia; tonofibrils), vimentin, desmin (muscle), GFAP (glia), neurofilaments (neurons), lamins (nuclear lamina).

Learning objectives

  • compare the three cytoskeletal filaments by subunit, size, stability and function;
  • describe microtubule structure, MTOCs and motor proteins;
  • describe actin assembly, treadmilling and the cortex;
  • name the intermediate filament proteins and the cells that contain them.

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Microtubules
  3. MTOCs and motor proteins
  4. Microfilaments (actin)
  5. Intermediate filaments
  6. Intermediate filament proteins
  7. The three compared
  8. Watch out
  9. Exam traps
  10. Check yourself
  11. Key terms

Overview

  • The cytoskeleton is a complex array of microtubules, microfilaments (actin filaments) and intermediate filaments.
  • These protein polymers:
    • determine cell shape;
    • move organelles and vesicles;
    • allow whole cells to move.

Microtubules

  • Fine, dynamic, hollow tubes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells (~25 nm across).
  • Functions: structural support, cell shape, cell division (the mitotic spindle) and intracellular transport. Also the core of cilia and flagella.
  • Subunit: a heterodimer of α- and β-tubulin.
  • Dimers line up end to end as protofilaments; 13 parallel protofilaments form the wall.
  • They have polarity: a fast-growing plus (+) end and a minus (−) end anchored at the MTOC.

MTOCs and motor proteins

  • Microtubules grow from microtubule-organising centres (MTOCs). The commonest MTOC is the centrosome, near the nucleus, which contains a pair of centrioles and organises microtubules during cell division.
  • Microtubules act as tracks. Motor proteins use ATP to carry vesicles and organelles along them, in opposite directions:
MotorDirectionName of transport
KinesinAway from the MTOC/nucleus toward the + end (cell periphery)Anterograde
Cytoplasmic dyneinToward the − end, generally toward the nucleusRetrograde

Needed, for example, to extend the ER and move material between the Golgi and other parts of the cell.

Mnemonic

Kinesin Kicks things out (+ end); Dynein Drags them back home (− end).

Microfilaments (actin filaments)

  • Thin (5–7 nm) filaments of actin: cell movement and contraction.
  • G-actin (globular monomers) assemble into F-actin (filamentous), a double-stranded helix, in the presence of K⁺ and Mg²⁺.
  • New filaments are started (nucleated) by formin (straight filaments) and the Arp2/3 complex (which also makes branching networks).
  • Dynamic: monomers are added quickly at the + end and removed from the − end = treadmilling. This allows fast changes in structure.
  • Abundant just under the plasma membrane, forming the cell cortex, which supports endocytosis and cell movement. Also in microvilli and, with myosin, in muscle.

Intermediate filaments

  • Unlike the other two, they are stable (not constantly assembled and disassembled) and give mechanical strength.
  • Size ~10 nm: “intermediate” between microfilaments and microtubules.
  • Made of different proteins in different cell types.
  1. Subunits are coiled rod-like dimers.
  2. Two dimers join antiparallel → a tetramer (so the filament has no polarity).
  3. Tetramers assemble into large, stable bundles (protofibrils) → filament.

There are more than a dozen kinds; defects cause specific diseases. Because each cell type has its own kind, pathologists stain for them to identify the origin of a tumour.

ProteinFound inNotes

VimentinCells from embryonic mesenchyme (e.g. fibroblasts)Related proteins: desmin in muscle, GFAP in glial cells (astrocytes)
NeurofilamentsNeurons onlySupport axons
LaminsNucleus of all cellsForm the nuclear lamina just inside the nuclear envelope

Diameter~25 nm (thickest)5–7 nm (thinnest)~10 nm
Subunitα/β-tubulin dimerG-actinCell-type-specific (keratin, vimentin…)
StructureHollow tube, 13 protofilamentsDouble helixRope of antiparallel tetramers
Polarity+ and −+ and −None
Dynamic?YesYes (treadmilling)No, stable
MotorsKinesin, dyneinMyosinNone
Main jobTracks, spindle, ciliaMovement, contraction, cortexMechanical strength

  • Keratin = epithelium; desmin = muscle; GFAP = glia.

gct/molecular-biology/lec01-cells-prokar:
GCT I · Molecular Biology · Lecture 1

Basic Properties of Cells: Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes

How cells were discovered, the cell theory, how big cells and their parts are, the basic properties every cell shares, and the fundamental split between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

Labobo topic: MB Lec 1: Cells, Prokaryote vs Eukaryote

In 60 seconds

  • Hooke named “cells” (cork); Leeuwenhoek saw protists (“animalcules”) and bacteria from his teeth.
  • Cell theory (1838, Schleiden and Schwann; Virchow added that cells come only from pre-existing cells).
  • 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m; 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m; 1 Å = 0.1 nm = 10⁻¹⁰ m.
  • DNA ≈ 2 nm wide; ribosomes, microtubules, microfilaments 5–25 nm; nucleus 5–10 μm; mitochondrion ≈ 2 μm; prokaryote 1–5 μm; eukaryote 10–30 μm.
  • Cells are organised, have a genetic program, reproduce, use energy, run enzyme reactions, move, respond, self-regulate and evolve.
  • DNA replication: fewer than 1 error per 10 million nucleotides.
  • Eukaryotes have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotes don’t.

Learning objectives

Karp’s Cell and Molecular Biology (8th ed., 2016) and Alberts’ Essential Cell Biology (5th ed., 2019). By the end you can:

  • describe the discovery of cells and the cell theory;
  • use the units of cell measurement and the sizes of cell parts;
  • list and explain the basic properties of cells;
  • compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

Contents

  1. Discovery and cell theory
  2. Cells vary in shape
  3. Units and sizes
  4. What makes something alive
  5. Basic properties of cells
  6. Two basic types of cells
  7. Prokaryotes vs eukaryotes
  8. Numbers to remember
  9. Watch out
  10. Exam traps
  11. Check yourself
  12. Key terms

Discovery and cell theory

ScientistContribution
Robert HookeExamined a slice of cork and introduced the term “cells”
Anton van LeeuwenhoekBuilt powerful microscopes; saw a microscopic world of “animalcules” (protists) in pond water, and bacteria in scrapings from his teeth
Matthias Schleiden (botanist) and Theodor Schwann (zoologist)Cell theory, 1838
Rudolf VirchowAdded: cells arise only by division of a pre-existing cell

The cell theory

  1. All organisms are made of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the structural unit of life.
  3. Cells arise only by division of a pre-existing cell.

Cells vary in shape

CellShape and why
Brain nerve cellHugely extended: an axon 10,000 times longer than it is thick sends signals; branching extensions receive them
Paramecium (pond protist)Submarine-shaped, covered with thousands of cilia whose beating drives it forward, rotating
Plant surface cellSquat, immobile, in a rigid cellulose box with a waterproof wax coat
MacrophageCrawls through tissues, constantly changing shape, engulfing debris, microbes and dying cells
Fission yeastRod-shaped

Shape follows function.

Units and sizes

UnitValueUsed for
Micrometre (μm)10⁻⁶ mCells and organelles
Nanometre (nm)10⁻⁹ mMacromolecules and complexes
Ångström (Å)0.1 nm = 10⁻¹⁰ mAtomic dimensions
Typical sizes
StructureSize
DNA (width)~2.0 nm
Ribosomes, microtubules, microfilaments5–25 nm diameter
Long proteins (collagen, myosin)> 100 nm long
Mitochondrion~2 μm long
Nucleus5–10 μm diameter
Prokaryotic cell1–5 μm long
Eukaryotic cell10–30 μm

What makes something alive

Life is easy to recognise but hard to define. Living things:

  1. are highly organised compared with non-living objects;
  2. show homeostasis (a stable internal environment);
  3. reproduce;
  4. grow and develop from simple beginnings;
  5. take energy and matter from the environment and transform them;
  6. respond to stimuli;
  7. show adaptation to their environment.

Basic properties of cells

PropertyWhat it means
Complex and organisedRemarkably precise: DNA replication makes fewer than 1 error in 10 million nucleotides, and most are repaired. Levels: atoms → molecules → polymers → organelles → cells. Organelles have consistent shapes and positions; proteins fold into exact 3-D shapes
Genetic programInformation is packaged in chromosomes; genes hold the recipes for structures and activities. Changes (mutations) create variation and drive evolution
Reproduce themselvesBy division: a mother cell gives two daughter cells with complete, equal genetic information
Acquire and use energyPhotosynthesis turns light into chemical energy (sucrose, starch). In humans, glucose in the blood is the main fuel; its energy is captured as ATP, the ready-to-use energy currency
Carry out chemical reactionsAll need enzymes; metabolism = the sum of all these reactions
Mechanical activitiesTransport, contraction, assembly of structures, cell movement, driven by motor proteins: myosin, dyneins (cilia, flagella), kinesins (mitosis, meiosis)
Respond to stimuliObvious in protists; in multicellular organisms through surface receptors for hormones, growth factors and extracellular materials
Self-regulateRobust: feedback circuits return the cell to its proper state after disturbance
EvolveThe first cell’s origin is unknown, but living cells share a genetic code, plasma membrane and ribosomes. Evolution continues: drug resistance in bacteria, new COVID-19 variants

Two basic types of cells

  • All organisms fall into two groups by cell structure; the key is the nucleus (and membrane-bound organelles).
  • Eukaryotes: cells with a nucleus.
  • Prokaryotes: cells without a nucleus.

The slide groups living things into six kingdoms: bacteria, protists, fungi, plants, animals, and (with question marks) viruses, which are non-cellular.

Prokaryotes vs eukaryotes

A bacterial (prokaryotic) cell often has a tough cell wall around its plasma membrane, enclosing a single compartment with the cytoplasm and a circular DNA. The fuller comparison (Karp):

Watch out

Watch out: viruses are not a kingdom

Slide 20 lists viruses as a sixth kingdom with question marks. Viruses are not cells and are not placed in any kingdom. The usual six kingdoms are archaebacteria, eubacteria, protists, fungi, plants and animals.

Watch out: ATP is not a store

Slide 15 says glucose energy is “stored in the form of ATP”. ATP is the immediate energy currency, used within seconds. Energy is stored as glycogen and fat.

Watch out: “first microscope”

Leeuwenhoek made the best simple (single-lens) microscopes of his time; compound microscopes existed earlier (Hooke used one). The exam point is what he saw: protists and bacteria.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Hooke named cells; Leeuwenhoek saw bacteria.
  • “Cells only from cells” is Virchow, not Schleiden or Schwann.
  • 1 Å = 0.1 nm, not 10 nm.
  • Kinesins and dyneins move on microtubules; myosin on actin.
  • The defining difference is the nucleus.
