GCT I · Molecular Biology · Lecture 2

Types of Cells, Viruses, Viroids and Model Organisms

The two prokaryotic domains (Archaea, Bacteria), the kinds of eukaryotic cells and how they specialise, what viruses are and how they replicate (lytic and lysogenic), viroids, and the six model organisms of research.

Labobo topic: MB Lec 2: Cell Types, Viruses & Model Organisms

In 60 seconds

  • Prokaryotes: Archaea (extremophiles: methanogens, halophiles, acidophiles, thermophiles) and Bacteria.
  • Mycoplasma: smallest bacterium (0.2 μm), no cell wall, ~500 genes. Cyanobacteria: most complex, chlorophyll a, release O₂; ancestors of chloroplasts.
  • A fertilised human egg gives about 250 differentiated cell types.
  • Ivanovsky (1892): tobacco mosaic disease passes through bacteria-proof filters → viruses. TMV ≈ 300 nm × 18 nm.
  • Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: DNA or RNA, single or double, 3–4 to several hundred genes, inside a capsid (often an icosahedron), sometimes an envelope.
  • HIV gp120 binds CD4. Lytic cycle bursts the cell; lysogenic integrates as a provirus.
  • Models: E. coli, yeast, Arabidopsis (120 Mbp), C. elegans (~1000 cells), Drosophila, mouse.

Learning objectives

Karp’s Cell and Molecular Biology, 8th ed. By the end you can:

  • describe the types of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells;
  • explain cell differentiation;
  • describe the discovery, structure, host binding and replication of viruses, and what viroids are;
  • name the six model organisms and why each is used.

Contents

  1. Types of prokaryotic cells
  2. Types of eukaryotic cells
  3. Cell differentiation
  4. Discovery of viruses
  5. Structure of viruses
  6. Lytic and lysogenic cycles
  7. Viruses as tools; viroids
  8. Model organisms
  9. Numbers to remember
  10. Watch out
  11. Exam traps
  12. Check yourself
  13. Key terms

Types of prokaryotic cells

Two domains: Archaea (archaebacteria, “extremophiles”, most living in very harsh places) and Bacteria (including cyanobacteria).

Archaea
GroupLives / does
MethanogensConvert CO₂ + H₂ → methane (CH₄)
HalophilesExtremely salty places: Dead Sea, deep-sea brine pools (as salty as 5 M MgCl₂)
AcidophilesAcid-loving; drainage fluid of mine shafts
ThermophilesVery high temperatures; “strain 121” is a hyperthermophile

Many archaea also live in ordinary soil and ocean conditions.

Bacteria
GroupFeatures
MycoplasmaSmallest bacteria (0.2 μm); no cell wall; only ~500 genes; Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes pneumonia
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)Most complex bacteria; chlorophyll a; folded internal membranes for photosynthesis (like chloroplast thylakoids); split water and release O₂ like plants. Chloroplasts evolved from a symbiotic cyanobacterium. They even grow in polar bear hairs, colouring them green
Nitrogen-fixing bacteriaConvert atmospheric N₂ → ammonia (NH₃), used to make amino acids and nucleotides. Examples: symbiotic Rhizobium, free-living bacteria, and some cyanobacteria

Types of eukaryotic cells

  • Unicellular: protists. One cell does everything: senses the environment, traps food, escapes predators, expels excess water. Example: Vorticella, a complex ciliated protist.
  • Multicellular: fungi (some unicellular, e.g. yeasts), plants, animals.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Dr Matt & Dr Mike · The Cell and Organelles Watch from 0:00 to the end: a 7-minute tour of the eukaryotic cell and its organelles.

Cell differentiation

  • In multicellular organisms, different jobs are done by specialised cells, formed by differentiation.
  • A fertilised human egg develops into about 250 distinct differentiated cell types (gland, muscle, bone…).
  • Differentiated cells look different, contain unique materials and have distinct functions:
    • skeletal muscle cells: precisely aligned filaments of contractile proteins;
    • red blood cells: disc-shaped sacs filled with one protein, hemoglobin;
    • cartilage cells, etc.
  • Despite their differences, all are built from similar organelles.

Discovery of viruses

  1. Tobacco mosaic disease (plants) and hoof-and-mouth disease (cattle) suggested an infectious agent other than bacteria.
  2. Dmitri Ivanovsky forced sap from a diseased tobacco plant through filters with pores too small for the smallest known bacterium.
  3. The filtrate was still infective. In 1892 he concluded the pathogen was smaller and simpler than bacteria: a virus.

Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV): identical protein subunits wrap a single helical RNA molecule in a rod about 300 nm long and 18 nm wide.

Structure of viruses

  • Cause many human diseases: AIDS, polio, influenza, common cold, Ebola, measles, and some cancers.
  • All viruses are obligate intracellular parasites; hosts can be plant, animal or bacterial cells.
  • Outside a cell, a virus is a virion: a macromolecular package that cannot reproduce or metabolise on its own. Whether viruses are alive is still debated.
  • Genetic material: DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded; from 3–4 genes to several hundred.
  • Surrounded by a protein coat, the capsid.
VirusStructure
Adenovirus (respiratory infections)Icosahedral capsid (20 flat faces; a common polyhedral shape)
HIV (AIDS)Capsid inside a lipid envelope taken from the host’s plasma membrane as it buds out
T bacteriophageAmong the most complex viruses (and the most abundant biological entities on Earth): polyhedral head with DNA, cylindrical stalk that injects DNA, tail fibres; looks like a landing module

Binding to the host

Each virus has a surface protein that binds a specific component of its host cell. HIV’s gp120 (glycoprotein, 120,000 daltons) binds CD4 on certain white blood cells, letting the virus enter.

Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · An Introduction To Virology Watch from 0:00 to the end: what a virus is and how it is built.

Lytic and lysogenic cycles

LyticLysogenic
What happensVirus takes over the cell, stops its normal synthesis, makes viral nucleic acids and proteins, assembles virionsViral DNA integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus and waits
Host cellLyses (bursts), releasing new virionsSurvives (for now)

What a provirus can do

  • Bacteria: behave normally until a stimulus such as UV light activates the provirus → lysis and release of progeny.
  • Some animal cells (HIV): keep producing virions that bud from the surface without lysing the cell, which acts as a virus factory for a while.
  • Some animal cells: lose control of growth and division and become malignant (tumour viruses).

Viruses as tools; viroids

  • Research tools for studying DNA replication and gene expression.
  • Viral vectors deliver genes into human cells: the basis of gene therapy (in vivo or in vitro). Vectors include adenoviruses, herpes simplex viruses, retroviruses, and bacteriophages (hybrid vectors). Main uses: research, vaccines, gene therapy.
  • Insect- and bacteria-killing viruses may help fight pests and bacterial infections. Phage therapy has been used for decades in eastern Europe and Russia; the West relied on antibiotics.

Viroids

Listed in the topics; from Karp: viroids are even simpler infectious agents, small circular RNA molecules with no protein coat and no protein-coding genes. They cause diseases in plants.

Model organisms

OrganismWhy it is used
E. coli (the one prokaryote)Rod-shaped bacterium of the mammalian gut
Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiaeLeast complex common eukaryote; ideal for finding genes with mutants
Flowering plant, Arabidopsis thalianaUnusually small genome (120 million bp), fast generation, many seeds
Nematode, Caenorhabditis elegansA fixed number of cells (~1000), each from a precise division pattern; easy to culture, can be frozen, transparent, short generation
Fruit fly, Drosophila melanogasterEgg to adult in days; classic for genetics and developmental biology
Mouse, Mus musculusEasily bred; thousands of strains (often stored as frozen embryos). The nude mouse has no thymus, so it accepts human tissue grafts

Watch out

Watch out: Rhizobium is not a cyanobacterium

Slide 5 says nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium “belong to cyanobacteria”. Rhizobium is a separate group of soil bacteria living in legume root nodules. Some cyanobacteria also fix nitrogen, but nitrogen fixers are not all cyanobacteria.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Mycoplasma has no cell wall.
  • Cyanobacteria release oxygen; chloroplasts came from them.
  • HIV buds out without lysing its host cell.
  • The lysogenic provirus is integrated DNA.
  • The nude mouse lacks a thymus.
  • Yeast is the least complex model eukaryote.

  3. Chloroplasts are thought to have evolved from:

  4. About how many differentiated cell types arise from a fertilised human egg?

GCT I · Molecular Biology · Lecture 3

The Chemical Basis of Life: Macromolecules

The four kinds of organic molecules in a cell, functional groups, and the four macromolecules (carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids, proteins), with a close look at DNA architecture, base pairing, DNA vs RNA, ribozymes and ATP.

Labobo topic: MB Lec 3: Chemical Basis & Macromolecules

In 60 seconds

  • Cell organic molecules: macromolecules, their building blocks, metabolic intermediates, and miscellaneous molecules (vitamins, steroids, ATP, cAMP).
  • Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are polymers (made by polymerisation); lipids are not.
  • Sugars: (CH₂O)ₙ; glycosidic bond = C1 of one sugar to an –OH of another (C–O–C).
  • Glycogen (most branched), starch (helical), cellulose (unbranched, extended): all glucose. Glycogen/starch store energy; cellulose/chitin are structural.
  • Fat = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (ester bonds); phospholipid = 2 fatty acids + phosphate + polar group; steroids = 4 rings (cholesterol).
  • DNA: sugar–phosphate backbone outside, bases inside; phosphodiester bonds; 5′ phosphate end, 3′ OH end; antiparallel.
  • A=T (2 H bonds), G≡C (3 H bonds); G-C-rich DNA is more stable. RNA: single, short, unstable, has U and ribose. Ribozymes catalyse.

Learning objectives

Karp’s Cell and Molecular Biology, 8th ed. By the end you can:

  • classify the organic molecules of the cell and describe functional groups;
  • describe carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and proteins and their building blocks;
  • explain the architecture of DNA, chemical polarity and complementarity;
  • compare DNA and RNA and describe ribozymes and ATP.

  2. Functional groups
  3. Macromolecules and building blocks

Categories of organic molecules

CategoryExamples
MacromoleculesProteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, lipids
Building blocksSugars, amino acids, nucleotides, fatty acids
Metabolic intermediates (metabolites)Molecules formed along chemical pathways
Miscellaneous functionVitamins, steroids, amino acid hormones, ATP, cyclic AMP

Understanding cell function requires knowing the structure and properties of these molecules.

Functional groups

  • Most functional groups contain electronegative atoms (N, P, O, S).
  • They make organic molecules more polar, more water-soluble and more reactive.
  • Several can ionise and become positively or negatively charged (e.g. –COO⁻, –NH₃⁺, phosphate).

Macromolecules and building blocks

  • Proteins, nucleic acids and carbohydrates are polymers: many low-molecular-weight monomers joined by polymerisation.
  • Lipids are macromolecule-like but are not polymers of repeating units.
Building blockMakes
SugarsPolysaccharides
Amino acidsProteins
NucleotidesNucleic acids
Fatty acidsLipids

Carbohydrates

  • Simple sugars (monosaccharides) and everything built from them.
  • Main roles: stores of chemical energy and durable building materials (e.g. plant cell walls).
  • General formula (CH₂O)ₙ. By carbons: triose (3), tetrose (4), pentose (5), hexose (6), heptose (7).
  • Monosaccharides: glucose, fructose, galactose (hexoses), ribose, deoxyribose (pentoses).

Disaccharides and the glycosidic bond

Sugars join by covalent glycosidic bonds: C1 of one sugar reacts with a hydroxyl of another, forming a C–O–C link.

Polysaccharides

PolysaccharideMade ofShapeRole
GlycogenGlucoseMost highly branchedEnergy store (animals)
StarchGlucoseHelicalEnergy store (plants)
CelluloseGlucoseUnbranched, extendedStructural (plant cell walls)
ChitinN-acetylglucosamineUnbranchedStructural (insect skeletons, fungal walls)

Glycogen, starch and cellulose are all glucose, yet differ greatly because their monomers are linked differently.

Lipids

Important lipids: fats, steroids, phospholipids.

Fats (triacylglycerols)

  • A glycerol linked by ester bonds to three fatty acids: a triacylglycerol (triglyceride, neutral fat).
  • A fatty acid has a hydrophobic hydrocarbon chain and a hydrophilic carboxyl group (–COO⁻ at body pH). Molecules with both kinds of region are amphipathic.
  • Cell fatty acids are typically 14–20 carbons. Stearic acid is an 18-carbon saturated fatty acid common in animal fat.
  • Saturated: no double bonds. Unsaturated: double bonds, naturally in the cis configuration (which kinks the chain).

Phospholipids

  • Like a fat but with only two fatty acids (a diacylglycerol); the third glycerol –OH carries a phosphate bonded to a small polar group such as choline.
  • Example: phosphatidylcholine: negative phosphate + positive choline = hydrophilic head; fatty acid tails = hydrophobic.
  • Two ends with opposite properties make them ideal for cell membranes.

Steroids

  • Built on a four-ring hydrocarbon skeleton.
  • Cholesterol: part of animal cell membranes; precursor of testosterone, progesterone, estrogen, vitamin D and bile acids.
  • Largely absent from plant cells (so vegetable oils are “cholesterol-free”), though plants have related sterols.

Nucleic acids: nucleotides

  • Nucleic acids are long chains of nucleotides.
  • Nucleotide = sugar + nitrogenous base + phosphate. Sugar + base alone = nucleoside.
  • Bases: purines (two rings: A, G) and pyrimidines (one ring: C, T, U).
  • DNA: A, G, C, T; RNA: A, G, C, U.
  • DNA also has minor bases (methylated and oxidised forms).

DNA architecture

  • DNA is a long, unbranched, double-stranded polymer wound into a helix: the Watson–Crick model, which explained storage, replication and repair.
  • DNA sugar = deoxyribose, a five-carbon single-ring pentose.
  • Adjacent sugars are joined through one phosphate by a phosphodiester bond (really two covalent bonds, one on each side of the phosphate).
  • Phosphodiester bonds are the only links along a strand. Sugars + phosphates form the backbone, key to stability.
  • The backbone is outside the helix; the bases are inside.

Chemical polarity

  • Each phosphate joins the 5′ carbon of one sugar to the 3′ carbon of the next. This gives each strand direction, an asymmetric backbone, and makes the two strands antiparallel.
  • The 5′ end has a free phosphate; the 3′ end has a free –OH.
  • Polarity lets information be read in a consistent order, like reading English left to right: 5′ → 3′.

Base pairing and complementarity

  • Hydrogen bonds link bases on opposite strands (H with O or N). Each is weaker than a covalent phosphodiester bond, but thousands together give great stability.
  • A pairs only with T (2 H bonds); G only with C (3 H bonds). So G-C-rich DNA is more stable.
  • Pairs are always purine + pyrimidine, keeping the helix the same width all along.
  • Complementarity: one strand’s sequence predicts the other’s exactly.

Example: 5′-ATGC-3′ pairs with 3′-TACG-5′.

DNA vs RNA, ribozymes, ATP

FeatureDNARNA
Strands21
LengthLong (hundreds of millions of nucleotides)Short (thousands)
StabilityStableUnstable
FunctionStores hereditary informationReads and carries out hereditary information
Location (eukaryote)NucleusNucleus and cytoplasm
BasesA, G, C, TA, G, C, U
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
  • RNA is single-stranded but often folds back on itself, forming double-stranded segments and complex 3-D shapes (e.g. ribosomal RNA).
  • Ribozymes (RNA enzymes): an rRNA of the large ribosomal subunit catalyses peptide bond formation; the hammerhead ribozyme (from a viroid) cuts its own strand.
  • ATP: the main energy source of living things, and a building block for RNA (with energy) in transcription. GTP is also hugely important.

Numbers to remember

ValueWhat it is
4Categories of organic molecules; macromolecule types; rings in steroids

Watch out

Watch out: amphipathic fats?

Slide 15 describes the hydrophilic carboxyl group while talking about fats. That describes a free fatty acid, which is amphipathic. In a triacylglycerol all three carboxyl groups are tied up in ester bonds, so a fat is almost entirely hydrophobic (“neutral fat”). Phospholipids are the classic amphipathic membrane lipids.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Lipids are not true polymers.
  • Glycogen is more branched than starch.
  • Natural unsaturated fatty acids are cis.
  • Cholesterol makes vitamin D and bile acids, not insulin.
  • A–T has two H bonds, G–C three.
  • Bases are inside the helix; the backbone is outside.

gct/molecular-biology/lec04-protein-stru:
GCT I · Molecular Biology · Lecture 4

Proteins: Structure, Folding and Misfolding

Amino acids and peptide bonds, the four levels of protein structure (with myoglobin, domains and hemoglobin as examples), Anfinsen’s self-assembly experiment, chaperones and chaperonins, and diseases of protein structure.

Labobo topic: MB Lec 4: Protein Structure & Misfolding

In 60 seconds

  • 20 amino acids; α-carbon carries –COO⁻ and –NH₃⁺ at neutral pH; peptide bonds form by condensation (water released).
  • N-terminus = free α-amino; C-terminus = free α-carboxyl. Side chains: polar charged, polar uncharged, nonpolar, unique (Cys disulfides).
  • Possible sequences = 20ⁿ. Sickle cell: one change, Glu → Val in β-globin.
  • Secondary (α-helix, β-sheet) = backbone H bonds; tertiary = side-chain non-covalent bonds. Silk (β-sheet) is ~5× stronger than steel by weight.
  • Myoglobin: 153 aa, ~75% α-helix, no β-sheet, no disulfides. Phospholipase C has 4 domains. TGF-β2 = homodimer; hemoglobin = heterotetramer (α₂β₂).
  • Anfinsen (1956): ribonuclease A (124 aa, 4 S–S) refolds after urea + mercaptoethanol are removed → sequence decides shape.
  • Hsp70 binds chains as they leave the ribosome; Hsp60 chaperonins fold inside chambers (TRiC folds up to 15% of proteins).

Learning objectives

Karp’s Cell and Molecular Biology, 8th ed. By the end you can:

  • describe amino acids, peptide bonds and side-chain classes;
  • explain primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, domains, fibrous and globular proteins;
  • describe denaturation, Anfinsen’s experiment and protein folding;
  • explain the role of chaperones and chaperonins;
  • link protein structure to disease (sickle cell, PKU, Huntington, DMD, CJD).

Amino acids and peptide bonds

  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids; each protein has a unique sequence that gives it its properties.
  • 20 amino acids build proteins in every organism, from viruses to humans.
  • Every amino acid has a carboxyl and an amino group separated by one carbon, the α-carbon.
  • In neutral water the α-carboxyl loses a proton (–COO⁻) and the α-amino gains one (–NH₃⁺).
  • In protein synthesis each amino acid joins two neighbours, forming a long, unbranched polypeptide chain.
  • A peptide bond links the carboxyl of one amino acid to the amino group of the next, releasing water: a condensation reaction.
  • The N-terminus has a free α-amino group; the C-terminus a free α-carboxyl.

Primary structure and sickle cell

  • Primary structure = the linear amino acid sequence.
  • With 20 building blocks, the number of possible chains of length n is 20ⁿ. Most chains have well over 100 residues, so the variety is practically unlimited.
  • The sequence is encoded in the genome and determines the 3-D shape and so the function. Changes from mutation are often not tolerated.
In the clinic: sickle cell anemia

A single change in β-globin: nonpolar valine replaces charged glutamic acid. Red cells change from discs to sickles, block small vessels and lyse → pain crises, organ ischemia, hypoxia and life-threatening complications.

Secondary structure

α-helixβ-sheet
ShapeCylindrical twisting spiral; backbone inside, side chains outwardSeveral segments (β-strands) side by side, each pleated
H bondsBetween peptide bonds just above and below along the spiralPerpendicular to the chain, from one strand to the next
Arrangement—Parallel or antiparallel strands
Property—Highly extended → resists pulling (tensile) forces

Silk is rich in β-sheet. A spider silk fibre, a tenth the thickness of a hair, is about 5 times stronger than a steel fibre of the same weight.

Tertiary structure and myoglobin

SecondaryTertiary
Stabilised byH bonds between backbone peptide atomsNon-covalent bonds between side chains: H bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals forces
VarietyA few conformationsVirtually unlimited

Fibrous vs globular

  • Fibrous: elongated; mostly structural outside cells (collagen, elastin, keratin, silk); resist pulling and shearing.
  • Globular: compact; most enzymes and transport proteins.

Myoglobin

  • Stores oxygen in muscle; O₂ binds the iron of a heme group.
  • About 75% of its 153 amino acids are α-helix; no β-sheet.
  • Heme sits in a pocket of hydrophobic side chains, which lets O₂ bind without oxidising the iron.
  • No disulfide bonds: held entirely by non-covalent interactions.
  • Unlike myoglobin, most globular proteins have both α-helices and β-sheets. Each protein’s unique tertiary structure matches its sequence and function.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Protein Structure - Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary Watch from 14:30 to 18:50: the bonds that hold tertiary structure.

Domains

  • Most eukaryotic proteins have two or more domains: spatially distinct modules that fold independently.
  • Phospholipase C has 4 domains (one catalytic); each is found in other proteins too.
  • Domains often work semi-independently: binding a coenzyme vs a substrate, DNA vs another protein, or moving separately.
  • Examples: a PH domain lets a protein bind membranes containing a specific phospholipid; steroid hormone receptors have a ligand-binding domain and a DNA-binding domain.

Quaternary structure

  • Proteins with more than one chain; each chain is a subunit.
  • Subunits may be linked by disulfide bonds but most often by non-covalent bonds.
  • Homodimer: two identical subunits, e.g. TGF-β2. Heterodimer: two different subunits.
  • Hemoglobin: a heterotetramer of 2 α + 2 β globins held non-covalently (structure solved by Max Perutz, Cambridge, 1959). O₂ binding to one chain changes the shape and affinity of the others, so the assembled molecule behaves differently from separate chains.
Watch: explains the section above
  • Medicosis Perfectionalis · Protein Structure - Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary Watch from 18:50 to 21:27: quaternary structure and a review of all four levels.

Denaturation and Anfinsen’s experiment

  • Denaturation = unfolding of a protein, by detergents, organic solvents, radiation, heat, urea, guanidine chloride.
  1. 1956, Christian Anfinsen (NIH) studied ribonuclease A: one chain of 124 amino acids with 4 disulfide bonds.
  2. Mercaptoethanol (a reducing agent) breaks disulfides into –SH pairs, but the protein must first be partly unfolded by urea.
  3. With urea + mercaptoethanol, the enzyme lost all activity (fully unfolded).
  4. When both were removed, the enzyme regained its activity (renaturation) and was identical to the native protein.
  5. Conclusion: the amino acid sequence contains all the information for the 3-D shape: proteins can self-assemble.

Folding pathways

  • After myoglobin’s structure was solved (late 1950s), the question became: how does such a complex shape arise?
  • Once α-helices and β-sheets form, folding is driven by hydrophobic interactions that bury nonpolar residues in the core.
  • Simulations: proteins first explore many shapes, then funnel into fewer and fewer.
  • Most fold by a middle route where secondary structure and compaction happen together.
  • Because sequence decides folding, mutations can cause abnormal folding; many inherited disorders work this way, and misfolding can be fatal.

Chaperones and chaperonins

Molecular chaperones help unfolded or misfolded proteins reach their proper shape. They bind short hydrophobic stretches that are exposed in non-native proteins but buried in folded ones. They also help import proteins into organelles and prevent or reverse aggregation.

  1. Chains are made one amino acid at a time from the N-terminus.
  2. Hsp70 chaperones bind the growing chain as it leaves the exit channel of the large ribosomal subunit, stopping it binding other proteins and aggregating.
  3. After synthesis, many proteins are released and fold spontaneously; others are bound and released repeatedly until folded.
  4. Many larger proteins pass to chaperonins (Hsp60 family): cylinders with chambers where proteins fold undisturbed.

Group IIEukaryotic cytosol and archaea. TRiC: two rings of 8 different subunits; folds up to 15% of mammalian proteins (first known for actin and tubulin, now dozens of substrates)

gct/molecular-biology/lec05-mitochondria:
GCT I · Molecular Biology · Mitochondria

Mitochondria and Cellular Respiration

Why oxygen changed life, the structure of the mitochondrion (two membranes, cristae, matrix, its own DNA), the three stages of respiration, how the electron transport chain and ATP synthase make ATP, uncouplers and brown fat, and three mitochondrial diseases.

Labobo topic: MB Lec 5: Mitochondria & Cellular Respiration

In 60 seconds

  • O₂ is toxic but, once used, lets cells oxidise food fully to CO₂ and H₂O and extract far more energy.
  • Mitochondria fill 15–20% of a liver cell, with > 1000 proteins. Heart/skeletal muscle ~5000 per cell; liver 1000–2000; mature RBCs none.
  • Outer membrane: ~50% lipid, porins (2–3 nm), freely permeable. Inner: protein:lipid > 3:1, > 100 polypeptides, no cholesterol, rich in cardiolipin, impermeable.
  • Matrix: proteins up to 500 mg/ml, ribosomes, circular mtDNA with 37 genes (13 polypeptides, 2 rRNAs, 22 tRNAs).
  • Respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm, 10 enzymes) → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → TCA (8 steps) → oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Proton pumps: Complexes I, III, IV; mobile carriers ubiquinone (in bilayer) and cytochrome c (intermembrane space). Mitchell (1961): chemiosmosis.
  • NADH ≈ 3 ATP, FADH₂ ≈ 2 ATP, ~36 ATP per glucose. DNP uncouples; brown fat makes heat. Diseases: MERRF, KSS, LHON.

Learning objectives

Karp’s Cell and Molecular Biology, 8th ed. By the end you can:

  • describe the structure of mitochondria and their membranes and compartments;
  • outline glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and the TCA cycle;
  • explain the electron transport chain, chemiosmosis and ATP synthase;
  • explain uncouplers and brown fat;
  • describe MERRF, Kearns–Sayre syndrome and LHON.

Oxygen and evolution

  • Molecular oxygen is toxic: it takes extra electrons and reacts with biological molecules. Its appearance in the atmosphere was a powerful force of natural selection.
  • Species evolved that were protected from O₂ and then used it.
  • Without O₂, organisms extract only a little energy and excrete energy-rich products (lactic acid, ethanol).
  • With O₂, they oxidise these completely to CO₂ + H₂O, extracting much more energy. These first aerobes gave rise to all oxygen-using life.

Structure of mitochondria

  • In eukaryotes, oxygen is used in the mitochondrion: a bean-shaped, double-membrane organelle, the cell’s “energy transformer”.
  • It occupies 15–20% of a mammalian liver cell’s volume and has more than 1000 different proteins.
  • Main job: turn nutrient energy (e.g. glucose) into ATP. Cells use ATP constantly, so mitochondria always work, and need O₂ (which is why we breathe constantly).

The inner membrane’s two domains

  • Inner boundary membrane: just inside the outer membrane (forming a double envelope); rich in protein-import machinery.
  • Cristae: folded sheets reaching into the interior; huge surface area holding the machinery of aerobic respiration and ATP synthesis.
  • The two are joined by narrow tubes: cristae junctions.

Mitochondrial DNA

  • Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and machinery to make their own RNAs and proteins.
  • Human mtDNA has 37 genes: 13 polypeptides (all inner-membrane respiratory proteins), 2 rRNAs and 22 tRNAs.
  • The rest of the mitochondrial proteins are coded in the nucleus and imported.

Cellular respiration: the stages

Cellular respiration converts energy in nutrients (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids) into ATP; the usual electron acceptor is O₂, so it is aerobic. ATP then powers biosynthesis, movement and transport. Overall: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ATP).

  1. Glycolysis (cytoplasm, 10 enzymes): glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C); 2 ATP (net) and NADH.
  2. Pyruvate oxidation (matrix): each pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (2C), releasing CO₂ and making NADH.
  3. TCA (Krebs) cycle (matrix): acetyl-CoA joins a 4C molecule; the cycle regenerates it, making ATP (GTP), NADH, FADH₂ and CO₂.
  4. Oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane): NADH and FADH₂ give electrons to the ETC; protons are pumped out; they flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP; O₂ accepts the electrons to form water.

Glycolysis, NAD and pyruvate

  • NAD (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide): two nucleotides joined through their phosphates; carries electrons and H⁺ in redox reactions.
  • NAD⁺ is the oxidising form (accepts electrons); NADH is the reducing form (donates them).
  • Pyruvate (anion of pyruvic acid), the end product of glycolysis, stands at the junction of anaerobic and aerobic pathways:
    • no O₂: fermentation → ethanol (yeast) or lactate (bacteria, and sometimes our muscles);
    • with O₂: into the mitochondria → acetyl-CoA → TCA cycle.

TCA cycle, acetyl-CoA and ATP

  • 8 steps, 8 enzymes. Most of the energy is captured by NAD⁺ and FAD.
  • Each turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (GTP), and CO₂ as waste. Double this per glucose (2 pyruvates).
  • Hans Krebs won the Nobel Prize in 1953 for discovering the cycle.
  • Acetyl-CoA takes part in protein, carbohydrate and lipid metabolism; its main job is delivering acetyl groups to the cycle for oxidation.
  • ATP = adenine + ribose + three phosphates (α, β, γ); used up to ADP or AMP and regenerated repeatedly. Made mainly by glycolysis, the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation.

Electron transport chain

ComponentRole
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase)Takes electrons from NADH; pumps H⁺; passes electrons to CoQ
Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase)Takes electrons from FADH₂ (TCA cycle); passes them to CoQ; no pumping
Ubiquinone (CoQ)Mobile pool dissolved in the lipid bilayer; carries electrons to Complex III
Complex III (cytochrome bc₁)Pumps many H⁺; passes electrons to cytochrome c
Cytochrome cSmall soluble protein in the intermembrane space; carries electrons to Complex IV
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)Gives electrons to O₂, which binds H⁺ → water; the first ETC part shown to be a redox-driven proton pump
  • The three proton pumps are Complexes I, III and IV: they move H⁺ from the matrix to the intermembrane space.
  • Ubiquinone and cytochrome c are not part of any complex; they shuttle electrons between the large, fairly immobile complexes.
  • Oxygen, one of the most electronegative elements, accepts the electrons and drives the whole process.

Chemiosmosis and ATP synthase

  1. Substrates (e.g. isocitrate, succinate) are oxidised; electrons go to NAD⁺ or FAD → NADH, FADH₂.
  2. Electrons pass along the chain; energy pumps protons out → a proton electrochemical gradient (the proton-motive force).
  3. Protons flow back down the gradient through ATP synthase (Complex V), which uses the energy to make ATP from ADP + Pi.

Proposed in 1961 by Peter Mitchell (University of Edinburgh): the chemiosmotic mechanism.

  • ATP synthase has two actions: a proton channel, and ATP synthesis.
  • Making ATP from ADP + Pi is energetically unfavourable; ATP synthase drives it by coupling it to the H⁺ gradient, changing shape to push ADP and phosphate together.
  • ATP is then exported from the mitochondrion to fuel the cell.

Uncouplers and brown fat

  • If ATP synthesis needs the gradient, then breaking the inner membrane or dissipating the gradient should stop it. Both are true.
  • 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) carries H⁺ across the inner membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. Electron transport continues, but the proton-motive force is lost and no ATP is made: it uncouples the two.
  • Brown fat cells do this naturally: most energy from fat oxidation becomes heat. They act as biological heating pads, reviving hibernating animals and protecting newborn babies (e.g. the back of the neck) from cold.

gct/molecular-biology/lec07-endomembrane:
GCT I · Molecular Biology · Lecture 7

The Endomembrane System and Protein Sorting

The membrane organelles that work as one unit (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, endosomes, vacuoles), the biosynthetic, secretory and endocytic pathways, signal sequences, the jobs of rough and smooth ER, the Golgi, lysosomes and peroxisomes, and the diseases added for the midterm.

Labobo topic: MB Lec 7: Protein Sorting & Endomembrane

In 60 seconds

  • Endomembrane system = ER, Golgi, lysosomes, endosomes, vacuoles; not mitochondria or chloroplasts. Discovered with the electron microscope (1940s).
  • Pathways: biosynthetic/secretory (ER → Golgi → out) and endocytic (surface → endosomes → lysosomes).
  • Secretion: constitutive (continuous) or regulated (stored, released on a signal: hormones, digestive enzymes, neurotransmitters).
  • Signal sequence at the N-terminus (6–15 hydrophobic residues) → SRP → SRP receptor on the ER.
  • ~⅓ of proteins are made on RER (co-translational); free ribosomes make cytosolic, nuclear, mitochondrial and peroxisomal proteins.
  • SER: lipids, steroids, detoxification (cytochrome P-450), Ca²⁺ storage (sarcoplasmic reticulum). Reticulons curve SER tubules.
  • Golgi: cis receives, trans ships; makes lysosomes. Peroxisomes: VLCFA oxidation, plasmalogens, H₂O₂/catalase. Zellweger = empty peroxisome “ghosts”.

  • name the parts of the endomembrane system and its pathways;
  • explain sorting signals and the signal recognition particle;
  • compare rough and smooth ER and their functions;
  • describe the Golgi, lysosomes and peroxisomes;
  • describe Zellweger syndrome, Alzheimer’s tau pathology and diabetes mellitus.

The endomembrane system

  • The cytoplasm’s extensive membrane network was discovered after the electron microscope was developed in the 1940s: membrane-bound channels forming connected canals, and stacks of flattened sacs.
  • The cytoplasm is divided into specialised membrane compartments, recognisable from yeast to plants and animals.
  • ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, endosomes and vacuoles work together as the endomembrane system.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts are not part of it.
  • It is dynamic: materials shuttle between compartments in vesicles. Vesicles bud from a donor membrane, carrying selected membrane proteins and soluble proteins bound to receptors.

Biosynthetic, secretory and endocytic pathways

PathwayRoute
BiosyntheticProteins made in the ER, modified in the Golgi, sent to the plasma membrane, lysosomes or a plant’s vacuole
SecretoryThe same route, for proteins that are discharged (secreted, exocytosed) from the cell
EndocyticOpposite direction: cell surface → endosomes → lysosomes, where material is usually degraded

Two kinds of secretion

ConstitutiveRegulated
ReleaseContinuous, straight after synthesisStored in packages, released only on a stimulus
WhoMost cells; builds the ECM and the plasma membrane itselfEndocrine cells (hormones), pancreatic acinar cells (digestive enzymes), nerve cells (neurotransmitters); often in dense secretory granules

Proteins, lipids and complex polysaccharides all travel along the biosynthetic/secretory pathway.

Sorting signals

  • Cargo (secreted proteins, lysosomal enzymes, membrane proteins) reaches the right place thanks to “addresses” (sorting signals) in the amino acid sequence or in attached oligosaccharides.
  • Most ER-bound proteins have a signal sequence at the N-terminus, including 6–15 hydrophobic residues.
  • The signal recognition particle (SRP) recognises it and binds the SRP receptor on the ER, moving the protein into the RER lumen.
  • Later, sorting signals are read by receptors in budding vesicles, sending each protein to the right compartment.
  • Another example: nuclear localisation signals, recognised by nuclear import receptors.

Rough and smooth ER

The ER is a network of membranes through much of the cytoplasm, probably evolved from infoldings of the plasma membrane.

Rough ER (RER)Smooth ER (SER)
RibosomesBound to its cytosolic surfaceNone
ShapeFlattened sacs (cisternae) joined by helicoidal membranes; continuous with the outer nuclear membraneHighly curved tubules, a network of pipelines; curvature made by reticulons (few in RER)
SharedMany proteins and some activities, such as synthesis of certain membrane lipids
Abundant inProtein-secreting cells: pancreas, salivary glandsSkeletal muscle, kidney tubules, steroid-producing glands

Functions of the SER

  • General: makes membrane lipids (phospholipids, cholesterol).
  • Steroid hormones in the gonads and adrenal cortex.
  • Detoxification in the liver (barbiturates, ethanol) by oxygenases, including the cytochrome P-450 family; chronic use makes liver SER proliferate.
  • Ca²⁺ storage; in muscle it is the sarcoplasmic reticulum, whose regulated Ca²⁺ release triggers contraction.

Bound vs free ribosomes

RER (membrane-bound) ribosomes: ~⅓ of proteins, co-translational translocationFree ribosomes
Secreted proteinsCytosolic proteins (glycolysis enzymes, cytoskeleton)
Integral membrane proteinsPeripheral membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin)
Soluble proteins of the ER, Golgi, lysosomes, endosomes, vesicles, plant vacuolesProteins for the nucleus, peroxisomes, mitochondria, chloroplasts

Golgi apparatus

  • A stack of flattened membrane discs that sorts, modifies, packages and ships ER products, like a post office.
  • In plants it also makes carbohydrates (polysaccharides, glycosaminoglycans).
  • Two faces: cis receives vesicles from the ER; trans releases repackaged products in new vesicles.
  • Products go to other parts of the cell or are exocytosed (the vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane).
  • The Golgi packages hydrolytic enzymes into lysosomes.

Lysosomes

  • Contain hydrolytic enzymes from the Golgi; vesicles form new lysosomes or fuse with existing ones.
  • Digest unneeded parts, such as old or damaged organelles: autophagy (“self-eating”).
  • Digest foreign material: white blood cells phagocytose bacteria and deliver them to lysosomes. Phagocytes have many lysosomes.
  • In damaged cells, lysosomes may burst and release enzymes into the cytoplasm, killing the cell: autolysis.

Peroxisomes

  • Simple membrane vesicles (0.1–1.0 μm), sometimes with a dense crystalline core of oxidative enzymes; more than 50 enzymes.
  • Jobs:
    • oxidise very-long-chain fatty acids (24–26 carbons);
    • make plasmalogens (one fatty acid joined by an ether bond), abundant in myelin; defects cause severe neurological disease;
    • firefly luciferase is a peroxisomal enzyme.
  • Named for hydrogen peroxide: made by urate oxidase, glycolate oxidase and amino acid oxidases (using O₂), and destroyed by abundant catalase.

Diseases for the midterm

Zellweger syndrome
  • Rare inherited disease: neurological, visual and liver problems; death in early infancy.
  • Liver and kidney cells seemed to lack peroxisomes, but actually had empty membrane “ghosts”: enzymes fail to be imported and stay in the cytosol, useless.
  • Caused by mutations in at least 12 genes, all for peroxisomal enzyme import.
Alzheimer’s disease and tau

Defined by extracellular amyloid-β (cut from APP), neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau inside neurons, and neuron loss. Normally tau, a microtubule-associated protein, assembles and stabilises microtubules; in AD and other tauopathies it forms insoluble filaments.

Diabetes mellitus
Type 1Type 2
Share5–10%90–95%
CauseAutoimmune destruction of β cells by self-reactive T cells (perhaps triggered by a virus); can’t make insulinHigh-calorie diet + sedentary life → chronically high insulin → insulin resistance
OnsetUsually childhood; 10–20% of β cells may remain at diagnosisIncreasing worldwide
TreatmentDaily insulin; still risk of kidney, vascular and retinal diseaseLifestyle, drugs

Most complications (cardiovascular disease, blindness, kidney disease, amputations) come from blood-vessel damage.

Watch out

Watch out: peroxisome size

Slide 27 says peroxisomes are “0.1 to 10 μm”. Karp gives 0.1 to 1.0 μm; the “10” is a typo.

Watch out: autolysis and apoptosis

Slide 26 links lysosomal autolysis to apoptosis. Apoptosis is mainly driven by caspases and mitochondria; uncontrolled release of lysosomal enzymes is more typical of cell death by necrosis. Remember the term autolysis = self-digestion by the cell’s own lysosomal enzymes.

Exam traps

Exam trap
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts are not in the endomembrane system.
  • Signal sequences are at the N-terminus and are hydrophobic.
  • Peripheral membrane proteins (spectrin) are made on free ribosomes.
  • Cytochrome P-450 detoxification is in the SER.
  • The cis Golgi faces the ER; trans ships out.
  • Zellweger peroxisomes are present but empty.

Key terms

Endomembrane system
ER, Golgi, lysosomes, endosomes, vacuoles working together.
Biosynthetic pathway
ER → Golgi → destinations.
Endocytic pathway
Surface → endosomes → lysosomes.
Signal sequence
N-terminal hydrophobic address for the ER.
SRP
Signal recognition particle.
Cisternae
Flattened membrane sacs.
Reticulons
Membrane-bending proteins of the SER.
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
Muscle SER storing Ca²⁺.
Co-translational translocation
Moving a protein into the ER while it is being made.
Autophagy
Digestion of the cell’s own parts by lysosomes.
Plasmalogen
Ether phospholipid made in peroxisomes.
